130.chip: Trades off bishop, squanders edge (queen recaptures)
130.label: The player captures with their bishop and is recaptured by the opponent's queen, liquidating a key (usually attacking) bishop and throwing away a winning or better position.

125.label: In a losing/holdable endgame the player gives up their only defensive bishop—usually by exchanging it for a knight or grabbing a pawn and being recaptured—collapsing into a lost pawn or bare-king ending.

132.label: The player captures/exchanges (most often a rook, but also bishop or queen) to simplify, voluntarily entering a lost pawn endgame where the surrendered active piece was the key defensive/winning resource.

131.label: A move that walks away from a defensive duty or into a tactic, losing the player's own material — but the piece lost varies (queen in 4/8, knight in 6/10, pawns in 5) and boards 2/3/7 are purely positional, so it's a fuzzy 'hangs a piece' rather than one specific piece.

126.label: In a winning/better position the player squanders it by mishandling a rook-and-queen tactic on a central file (usually the e-file) — about half the boards MISS the winning rook move (Re6/Rad1/Rfd1/Rde8/Rce8) while the other half are self-inflicted (hanging a rook by abandoning its defender, or walking into a back-rank/king mate), so the direction is genuinely mixed even though a rook on a central file is the recurring element in ~8/10.

97.label: In a clearly winning endgame the player makes a position-wrecking move—sometimes hanging own material to a fork/skewer/recapture, sometimes simply skipping a free capture—converting a win into a draw or loss; the lost piece varies (queen and rook both appear), so no single piece can be named.

137.label: In every position the player played a materially-safe but passive move and missed a winning queen check on h4/h5 (sometimes with a follow-up fork) that exploited the opponent's weakened, f-pawn-less kingside.

136.label: A greedy queen capture-with-check (often a Scholar's-Mate-style Qxf7) onto a defended square that loses the queen for a pawn or minor piece in the opening.

144.label: Plays an unsound Fried-Liver-style knight sacrifice on f7 (or f2) that the opponent simply takes with the king (Kxf7/Kxf2), losing a knight for a pawn in the opening.

141.label: In all 10 positions the player played a quiet/greedy move and overlooked a forcing queen shot — almost always a queen capture with check (Qxa1+/Qxc1+/Qxg8+/Qxe1+) or a queen mate — that won decisive material or forced checkmate; the captured target varies (rook, bishop, knight, or mate), so it's a missed win rather than a hung piece, with the queen consistently the delivering piece.

138.label: A quiet/developing move that ignores a forcing threat against the player's own king (typically Qxh7+, Qxf7+, or Qxh2+/Qxf2+), allowing a sacrifice or capture that exposes the king and wins material or mates.

107.chip: Slow move hangs material (skips rook trade)
107.label: In a middlegame with rook tension on an open file, the player makes a passive/slow move instead of the critical forcing rook exchange (Rxe8+/Rxe1+), allowing the opponent to win the player's own material over the next few moves.

143.label: In the opening the player plays a quiet/natural move (O-O, h3, Bb3, h6) and misses a winning tactical sacrifice—overwhelmingly Bxf7+ exploiting the uncastled king and a loose bishop on g4—squandering a near-winning advantage into equality.

133.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece hanging — to a direct capture or a follow-up fork — losing material for nothing (piece varies: queen, knight, or bishop), with one outlier walking the king into mate.

146.label: In winning/winnable endgames the player reflexively plays a check (rook or queen, 100% of moves) instead of the direct converting move, typically losing tempo or giving the enemy king extra squares — though notably several flagged checks are actually fine (0cp), so severity is inconsistent and the only true 100% invariants are 'endgame' and 'check'.

140.label: Plays a tactically losing move that drops its own piece to a refutation (deflection, unsound sacrifice, or removed/overloaded defender), usually a couple of moves later; the hung piece varies between knight and bishop, so it's 'a piece' rather than a specific one.

142.chip: Missed forcing tactical win (often knight fork)
142.label: In all 10 positions the player makes a quiet developing or retreating move instead of a forcing tactical shot—most often a knight fork or check, sometimes a discovered check or winning trade—that would have won material.

152.label: The player leaves their own queen en prise — almost always to an enemy knight (Nxd8/Nxf6/Nxd1/Nxf7) — by ignoring the direct attack on it while making a developing, capturing, or castling move.

150.label: Plays the queen (or removes its defender) onto a square where it is immediately captured, losing the queen for nothing or for grossly inadequate material.

147.label: In every position the player skipped a forced winning continuation—usually a check, often outright mate—commonly by grabbing material instead of delivering the decisive blow.

139.label: In a winning opening position, the player plays a safe developing/pushing move instead of capturing a hanging enemy piece (usually a knight), throwing away the material advantage.

156.chip: King wastes tempo in pawn race
156.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, moves the king to blockade or centralize instead of advancing its own passed pawn, losing a critical tempo in the promotion race.

149.chip: Hangs own material to tactic (squanders edge)
149.label: From a winning or equal position the player makes a move—usually a greedy capture of a seemingly free piece/pawn, sometimes a king or pawn move—that loses their own material to a tactical refutation (often a discovered attack or recapture-with-check), but the material hung varies (pawn, exchange, rook) so no single piece can be named.

154.label: In a winning/already-decisive position the player passes up a forced checkmate—typically an immediate queen check—by instead playing a quiet retreat or grabbing material, throwing away the mate (2 of 10 instead hang their own piece).

155.chip: Hangs a piece by opening a line
155.label: A capturing/recapturing move opens a file or diagonal that lets the opponent win the player's own piece (rook or queen) — a self-inflicted material loss — though a few of the boards are missed-win omissions instead.

151.label: Instead of the available knight capture/zwischenzug (Nxf3+/Nxf6+, the best move in essentially every board), the player makes another move that leaves their own piece — most often a knight, occasionally a bishop or pawn/advantage — hanging to a simple capture.

160.chip: Hangs corner rook to Qxa1+ check
160.label: The player vacates a defender or diagonal-blocker of their a-file corner rook, allowing the enemy queen to capture it with check (Qxa1+/Qxa8+) and win a full rook.

158.chip: Hangs h-file rook, misses Rxh8+ check
158.label: In every position the player skips the winning rook capture-with-check on the open h-file (Rxh8+/Rxh1+) and instead plays a greedy or passive move, leaving their own h-file rook undefended so the opponent wins the race by capturing with check first.

135.label: The player throws away a winning or clearly better middlegame/endgame by losing or mistrading a minor piece (bishop and knight roughly evenly split), typically leaving it en prise or simplifying into an equal/lost ending.

163.chip: Allows enemy pawn to promote (passed-pawn endgame)
163.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player makes a move (often a greedy capture or stepping off the promotion file) that loses the promotion race and lets the opponent's pawn queen.

148.label: A piece move (often a greedy capture or wrong move-order) that abandons a defender and lets the player's own material fall in a forced rook-exchange / back-rank sequence — the hung piece varies (bishop, knight, rook, even mate), so no single piece is named.

162.label: A middlegame move that hangs the player's own material — the dropped piece varies (rook, queen, knight, bishop) — collapsing a winning/equal position, though the set is impure (one board is actually the best move and a couple are pawn-loss/bad-trade rather than clean hangs).

157.label: In the opening the player plays a natural developing move that ignores an infiltrated enemy queen's threat and hangs their own material — most often the corner rook to Qxh1/Qxh8, but also bishops or a pawn.

164.label: In the opening, plays a move that leaves the player's own piece undefended, allowing a free capture — the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, or queen), and two boards are instead a greedy trade and a missed win.

159.chip: Loses material: greedy grab or missed capture
159.label: A careless material-handling move — frequently a greedy pawn-grab that hangs the player's own piece a move or two later, or an oversight that skips a free winning capture/mate — with the piece and direction (hung vs. missed) varying across the ten positions.

145.label: The player walks into a forced checkmate—usually by greedily grabbing material or pulling a key piece off king defense—rather than addressing the mating threat.

153.chip: Missed winning capture/tactic (often quiet queen move)
153.label: In every position the player passes up a forcing winning move—usually a material-winning capture or mating tactic—in favor of a quieter, non-forcing move (most often a queen move), though in ~4 cases that move also hangs their own material, so the missed-win vs self-inflicted direction is genuinely mixed.

174.label: Across all ten boards the player skips a winning queen capture of an undefended rook on a8/a1 (Qxa8/Qxa1) along an open diagonal, playing a safe developing or recapturing move instead and throwing away a large material-winning advantage.

166.label: The player repeatedly overlooks an undefended enemy queen sitting en prise, declining the free capture and instead playing an unrelated move that allows a forced mate.

167.label: In already-winning endgames (often featuring a passed pawn), the player makes a safe tempo-losing/repositioning move instead of the decisive continuation — a promotion push, winning capture, or pawn break.

161.label: Player throws away a winning position—most often by snatching a central pawn with the bishop (Bxd4) and hanging it to Qxd4 in the opening—but the feature is impure: three boards are missed clean wins/zwischenzugs rather than self-inflicted hangs, and the hung piece is only a bishop in ~6/10.

165.label: In a won endgame, the player advances/promotes a pawn (or makes a slow king/rook move) instead of capturing or neutralizing the opponent's only active piece, squandering the cleanest win and occasionally hanging material a move or two later.

177.label: A pawn move (b6/g6/g3) played to chase away the enemy queen instead fatally weakens the king's own pawn shelter, letting the queen (or a sacrifice) crash through for a decisive attack.

169.label: In the endgame the player overlooks a forced winning resource—most often a back-rank/first-rank mate or check—and instead plays a careless king or pawn move that squanders the win.

176.label: In a won endgame, the player repeatedly declines the decisive simplifying trade/exchange (most often a queen trade into a winning pawn endgame, sometimes a rook exchange/sac), instead playing a passive king move that squanders the win — and in a few cases the chosen move even drops material a move later.

170.label: A self-inflicted middlegame move—usually relocating a piece (most often a bishop) off a key active/defensive square—that ends up hanging the player's own material or fatally weakening the position; the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, rook, pawn) and a couple of boards are pure positional/tempo losses or a missed win, so the specific-piece claim can't be made and a human should confirm.

173.label: The move initiates a capture/exchange that loses the player's own material — most often giving up the exchange (rook for a minor piece, recaptured), though sometimes hanging a knight or queen outright; the hung material varies, so it's 'a piece/material' rather than one specific piece (board 7 is near-noise, otherwise 9/10 fit).

172.label: In a winning endgame the player prematurely advances a passed pawn (or plays a tempo check) instead of the precise winning move—usually capturing hanging material or bringing the king first—squandering the win.

184.label: In the opening, plays a pawn/developing move that allows an enemy knight to leap to c7 (mirror: c2) with a royal fork — or a bishop to infiltrate c7 — losing the exchange or queen.

179.label: The move usually leaves one of the player's own pieces (rook, queen, or bishop) en prise in the middlegame, though about two of the ten are missed wins rather than hangs.

180.label: A materially-safe move (king, rook, knight or bishop — the piece varies) that fails to play the one precise forcing resource, usually a tempo-gaining check, fork, or back-rank defense, that would win or save the position, almost always in endgames.

185.chip: Wrong king move worsens lost endgame
185.label: In an already-losing endgame the player makes the wrong king move—most often losing the tempo in a passed-pawn promotion race (sometimes letting the pawn queen with check)—and occasionally just hangs a piece outright.

168.label: A natural-looking move (develop, centralize, grab, apply pressure) that ignores the opponent's most urgent threat and gets refuted decisively — sometimes hanging own material (bishop/rook/queen/knight vary) and sometimes allowing a mating attack or breakthrough — so the specific thing lost is inconsistent and a human should review.

175.chip: Needless check, missed precise endgame win
175.label: In a winning endgame the player gives an unnecessary or premature check (rook or queen, ~8/10) that loses tempo and the clean conversion instead of the precise quiet/centralizing move, sometimes letting the win slip to a draw; materially safe with no piece hung, so it's an omission rather than a hang, but several boards lose ~0cp so it warrants review.

186.label: A move meant to win or grab material (capture/fork) instead abandons defense and hangs the player's own piece — the hung piece varies (queen, rook, knight, bishop) — almost always in the middlegame.

178.chip: Ignores mating threat, allows mate (king safety)
178.label: In critical or already-losing positions, the player makes a slow pawn or king move instead of the only defensive resource, most often allowing a forced checkmate (king-safety/back-rank collapse), though a few boards instead simply hang a piece — so the hung 'thing' varies and the unifying core is failing to address a decisive threat.

188.label: Player captures a piece (greedily, often the queen or rook) while overlooking an available forced checkmate — usually mate-in-one.

187.label: A knight move—usually a greedy capture of a central d4/e5 pawn—that loses the player's own material (the hung piece varies: knight, bishop, or pawn), though a few boards are instead missed material-winning shots.

182.chip: Premature check fails, often hangs piece
182.label: The player consistently fires a tempting/forcing check (~all 10 boards) instead of the precise winning move; in ~6 it hangs the checking piece (usually a knight) and in the other ~4 it merely throws away a forced win, so the direction is genuinely mixed and needs human review.

195.label: The played move pulls a defender (rook, king, or bishop) off the back rank/key defensive square, allowing the opponent an immediate or forced back-rank checkmate.

193.chip: Trades rook into drawn/lost pawn endgame
193.label: The player captures with the rook (usually with check), trading it for a minor piece and liquidating into a king-and-pawn endgame that squanders a winning rook-vs-minor advantage into a draw or loss.

183.label: In an already-losing position the player makes a self-inflicted move—most often a queen move that abandons a defensive post or walks into a tactic—converting a survivable loss into a forced mate or decisive material loss.

181.label: Player greedily captures with a pawn in the opening—usually fxe5/fxe4 that opens the king's diagonal to a crushing Qh4+/Qh5+ winning material—though two boards are instead missed-win/positional pawn grabs (dxc4), so direction is mixed.

192.label: Mostly self-inflicted king-safety collapses—moving the king (or a king-sheltering pawn) onto a square that allows forced mate or decisive material loss—though the boards vary (mate, trapped queen, hung knight, one missed drawing resource), so the single shared invariant is fuzzy.

200.chip: Premature pawn push/trade in pawn endgame
200.label: In (usually lost) king-and-pawn endgames the feature fires on a pawn advance or exchange that prematurely liquidates a holding/favorable pawn structure — but ~3/10 flagged moves are actually the engine's best move, so the pattern is fuzzy.

189.label: In a winning opening position the player makes a natural developing/structural move (fianchetto, develop, castle) that ignores the board's critical tactic and squanders the advantage — most boards are self-inflicted (the refutation wins the player's own material, mates, or wrecks structure over 2-3 moves), but ~3 are simply missed free pieces (Nxe5), so both the direction and the piece vary and a human should review.

191.label: In rook/piece endgames the player makes a capture or move that loses material to a simple recapture (and in some cases squanders a winning advantage), with the piece lost varying between rook and knight.

190.label: In already-lost or difficult positions the player makes a self-inflicted move that hangs a piece outright (rook, bishop, or knight all appear—no single piece dominates), with a few cases instead abandoning king defense and walking into forced mate.

201.label: In a won position the player passes up a forced winning combination — almost always a decisive rook exchange/simplification on a file — in favor of a slow positional move, throwing away the win rather than hanging material.

199.label: In the opening the player repeatedly fails to capture a free undefended central pawn with the queen (almost always Qxd4), an omission that flips an equal/winning position into a loss.

171.chip: Hangs material via knight move (often Nd2)
171.label: A knight move (frequently Nd2) that abandons a defender and hangs material to a tactic — often a knight fork by the opponent — though a minority of cases are missed wins rather than self-inflicted hangs.

197.label: The player delivers a tempting but purposeless check (instead of the winning quiet move) that lets the opponent's king escape and throws away a winning advantage — a 'patzer sees a check' error across all ten boards, twice even hanging the checking rook outright.

206.label: A quiet, materially-safe move that overlooks a concrete tactical shot (often a capture like Rxc6/Bxb8/Rxf8) winning a piece or the exchange, letting the opponent consolidate.

205.label: Player moves a rook to contest an open file (or the back rank) onto a square where it loses material—either captured outright or via a forced exchange sequence (frequently a back-rank tactic) that drops material.

208.label: Across all top positions the player declines an immediately available capture of the opponent's hanging/undefended piece (queen, rook, or knight, often with check) in a won endgame, squandering or delaying a decisive material win.

198.label: In an endgame, a king or rook move walks into a deflection/skewer check that wins material outright or forces a losing rook trade into a lost pawn endgame — the hung unit varies (mostly rook, once a bishop), so it's 'a piece.'

214.label: A move (usually a pawn capture or queen placement that opens/exposes a file) leaves the player's own queen on the file undefended, letting an enemy rook win it for a rook — 9 of 10 hang the queen, only board 10 hangs a rook instead.

196.label: In endgames the player repeatedly loses a rook — usually hanging it outright to a free capture or knight fork, sometimes dumping it in a disastrous trade into a lost pawn ending.

204.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight tactic)
204.label: In the opening, the played move usually loses the player's own material to a short tactic (a knight is typically the capturing/forking piece), but the hung piece varies and a few boards are tempo losses or a missed win instead, so this is reviewed.

194.label: A king-safety–motivated move (most often moving the king itself) that backfires by either ignoring a winning capture or walking into a tactic, costing material or the game.

203.label: The player's move—frequently a greedy queen capture or a defender abandoning its post—gives up control of a key square and walks into a forced checkmate against its own king (a few boards instead miss a winning mate or hang material).

202.label: In losing middlegame positions the played move allows or accelerates a forced checkmate, typically by vacating a key defensive square or removing a back-rank/king defender (the specific piece varies, so no single piece is named).

209.label: The recurring mistake is most often surrendering the player's own material — hanging or unsoundly sacrificing a piece whose identity varies (rook, bishop, or knight) — but roughly a third of boards are instead suboptimal endgame king moves (tempo loss or a missed win), so both the piece and the mistake type are too fuzzy to commit confidently.

212.label: Trading or capturing with the queen to 'simplify' that actually backfires — usually self-inflicting material loss (a forked exchange, a hung bishop, an exposed king), with the lost piece varying board to board.

213.label: A mostly materially-safe move that abandons the precise winning continuation (often a key file/square or tempo), collapsing a clearly winning position to equality; a few boards instead hang a piece outright, so the direction is mixed and the squandered piece varies.

210.chip: Throws away winning endgame (often hangs piece)
210.label: In a clearly winning endgame (frequently a forced mate), the player chooses a move that squanders the win — most often self-inflicted, hanging a piece that gets captured (queen in 4 boards, rook in 2), but in several cases simply missing a free capture or the mating continuation, so the unifying invariant is 'winning converted to drawn/worse' rather than one specific hung piece.

217.label: The played move loses the player's own material outright—often immediately, sometimes via a 2-3 move refutation—with the hung piece varying (knight most common) and a knight frequently part of the tactic.

211.label: Promotes a pawn to queen immediately instead of first making the necessary preparatory move (a king-safety step or intermediate check), so the rushed promotion gets the king mated or loses the brand-new queen.

222.label: Plays a quiet, retreating, or repositioning move instead of a decisive tactical strike — usually a sacrifice against the opponent's weakened kingside (Bxg6/Bxh3/Rxg6/Rxh3 type blows).

218.label: A king move that exposes the king to a decisive attack (most often a forced mating net, sometimes losing material via tempo-checks), throwing away the game instead of the available defensive queen-trade resource.

226.label: In the opening, the player leaves their own queen en prise (usually to an enemy knight), losing it outright for a minor piece.

207.label: In an already-lost position, declines the forced defensive queen trade/capture and instead plays a king move or queen sortie that either drops the queen or allows a forced mate.

215.label: The player skips a forcing, material-winning move—almost always a capture or deflection delivered with check (often Qxrook+)—and settles for a worse, non-winning continuation.

228.label: Across the boards the player makes a natural-looking capture, check, trade, or retreat and overlooks a crushing tactic — frequently a pin/trap that wins the opponent's queen — throwing away a winning advantage rather than hanging their own material.

219.chip: Loses material or king under attack (checks)
219.label: In a critical/losing middlegame the player plays a passive or greedy move that fails the only defense, letting the opponent win decisive material or mate via forcing checks; the lost material varies (king, rook, queen, pawn), so no single piece can be named.

221.label: The player repeatedly chose a natural, greedy, or routine move and overlooked the one precise winning resource available—frequently a quiet move that traps the opponent's queen—though a few cases also bleed the player's own material.

216.chip: Missed winning tactic in opening (knight capture)
216.label: In the opening the player repeatedly squanders a winning advantage by choosing a passive move (often retreating a bishop to h4/h5) instead of a forcing winning capture such as Nxf3 or Nxf6+.

220.label: A self-inflicted opening blunder that drops the player's own material to a simple recapture — most often a centralized/leaping knight, but sometimes a pawn — so the safe core is 'hangs material in the opening' rather than 'hangs a knight'.

229.label: The player repeatedly squanders a forced mate (or decisive forcing line) by grabbing material with a greedy capture instead of playing the winning continuation.

223.label: Plays a quiet, passive, or greedy move that overlooks the critical forcing continuation—sometimes skipping the player's own winning tactic (fork/free piece), sometimes walking into a decisive refutation or mate against their own king.

234.label: Player passes up a materially-safe but winning bishop capture of an undefended rook, letting the opponent rescue it with tempo.

230.chip: Trades active bishop, queen recaptures center
230.label: Needlessly captures with the bishop on d5/d4 (usually a centralized knight), letting the opponent recapture with the queen and dominate the center — surrendering an active bishop in the opening; in two cases it's outright bishop-for-pawn.

225.label: Squanders a winning/decisive position by playing a tempo-losing move (often a queen check) instead of the decisive forcing line—frequently a rook check on an open file—allowing the opponent's king to escape or castle to safety.

227.label: Across the top positions the player makes a greedy or careless move—often capturing/repositioning in the wrong order instead of first inserting a forcing check or rook exchange—that hangs their own material (a rook here, a queen there, a pawn elsewhere) or even walks into mate, so the hung unit varies and the safe call is 'a piece'.

236.label: In every opening position the player overlooked a pawn capture that would have won a hanging enemy knight for a pawn, instead playing a quiet developing or central move that let the knight escape.

235.label: A bishop or knight move in the opening that loses the player's own material — either hung outright to a one-move capture or trapped/won over a short refutation — though a few boards are pure tempo losses or a missed capture rather than clean hangs, and the hung piece alternates between bishop and knight.

238.label: In a clearly winning position the player throws away the decisive advantage with a non-forcing move — wasting a tempo, grabbing a side pawn, or missing a forced mate/promotion — letting the opponent escape to a draw or worse.

231.label: In difficult/losing endgames the player makes a rook or king move that leaves the king exposed to a punishing check, variously dropping the rook or allowing mate (one board is actually the engine's top move).

237.label: A premature queen sortie to an exposed square (a4/a5/h4/h5) in the opening is punished with tempo, losing material as the queen gets trapped or a now-undefended piece falls.

232.label: Player plays a quiet repositioning/king move that ignores the immediate tactic and hangs their own piece (rook, bishop, or knight — it varies), with a couple of boards instead missing a winning capture.

247.label: In rook/king endgames the move fails to control the promotion square, letting the opponent's passed pawn promote (often to a queen, frequently with check).

245.label: In a winning endgame, the player fails to capture an undefended enemy rook that was free for the taking, instead making a non-capturing king or pawn move (a queen capture in one case).

246.label: Plays a quiet, non-checking queen move when the only good resource was a forcing check — usually a saving perpetual, sometimes a winning/mating or material-gaining check sequence.

239.label: Player makes an inferior capture/trade — usually with a bishop — that squanders a winning position, most often by trading instead of grabbing a stronger or free piece, and occasionally hanging own material via the recapture.

240.label: The player moves a piece (usually the queen) to an active-but-irrelevant square, abandoning a critical defensive/offensive duty and leaving their own material — most often a pawn, but sometimes a bishop or knight — to a simple capture, while also passing up a clearly better capturing move.

244.label: A self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material—the dropped unit varies (knight, bishop, rook/exchange, or pawn) and two boards even walk into mate—with a knight almost always somewhere in the refutation; not a materially-safe missed win.

241.label: Player makes a greedy material grab—usually capturing the opponent's queen or trading queens—but overlooks the recapture/zwischenzug or stronger line, either hanging their own queen/piece (7/10) or squandering a forced win (3/10).

242.label: In mostly losing endgames the player repeatedly fails to capture a hanging enemy piece (rook or knight, often with the king), with a secondary cluster of promotion-into-immediate-capture blunders, so the piece and direction vary enough to need review.

251.label: In all ten opening positions the player leaves a bishop (on g5/h4/g4) undefended—either by parking it there or by ignoring it with a slow move—and the standard ...Bxg5/Bxh4/Bxg4, Nx, Qx sequence wins a full piece, with a knight always serving as the recapturing piece in the tactic.

255.chip: Misses free capture of enemy piece
255.label: In every position the player skips an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy piece (most often the queen, sometimes a rook), throwing away a forced mate or decisive material in favor of a quiet/lesser move.

256.label: Most positions feature a greedy capture or unsound sacrifice that loses the player's own material—usually a bishop left hanging due to a move-order error—though a few boards instead squander a winning advantage or walk into mate, so the invariant is fuzzy.

258.label: In most readable boards the player skips a material-winning capture (twice the specific shot Nxh4 against an exposed h4-knight), but one board is instead a self-inflicted trade into a lost pawn endgame, so the direction (missed-win vs. hung-own) and piece are genuinely mixed and need human review.

254.chip: Wastes tempo instead of decisive capture
254.label: In every position the player plays a tempo-losing move—usually a premature check or a non-urgent pawn advance—instead of the one precise continuation (almost always an immediate capture, e.g. Rxa2, Nxa4, Rxh7+, Nxa6, Bxa2), throwing away a won or held position; material is single-ply safe so it is an omission rather than an outright hang, and the hung/captured piece varies, so no specific piece is named.

252.label: The played move ignores the opponent's decisive threat—typically a hostile queen attack—failing to defend or trade, and so self-inflicts the loss of own material or allows a mating attack; the exact piece varies (bishop/rook/knight) and two boards are pure mate, so no single piece can be named.

257.chip: Hangs own piece on a capture
257.label: The player makes a capture (often greedily grabbing the enemy queen/pawn) that loses their own material to the recapture, but the hung piece varies across boards (queen, rook, bishop, pawn-exchange), so it's just 'a piece' — and 1–2 boards are closer to a missed win/fork, warranting review.

250.chip: Loses material ignoring f5 bishop tension
250.label: Plays an unrelated move while the light-square bishop tension on f5/f4 is unresolved, letting the opponent capture and win material (a pawn, sometimes the whole bishop) in the opening.

262.label: In the opening the player gives away a minor piece for nothing — often a bishop walking into a pawn capture (sometimes via a 'free' check), and in a couple of cases a knight that lands on an undefended square.

248.chip: Squanders winning edge, misses key move (Ba3/castling motif)
248.label: A materially-safe but inferior move that throws away a winning or equal advantage — most often by failing to find the one precise move (frequently Ba3 to keep the enemy king from castling), though a couple of boards instead miss a free piece, so the exact corrective motif varies.

264.label: In a winning (mostly rook) endgame the player makes a materially-safe but inferior move — frequently a pointless tempo-losing check or wrong-piece/wrong-square retreat — that throws away the advantage instead of playing the decisive continuation; no own material is actually hung and the squandered piece varies.

261.chip: Imprecise king move in winning endgame
261.label: In already-winning endgames (often king-and-pawn races), the player makes a technically imprecise move — usually a king maneuver escorting a passed pawn — that gives back a little advantage while staying winning, though a minority of boards instead hang material or miss a free capture.

253.label: In almost every position the player skips an available winning capture of an undefended/attacked knight (most often dxc6) and instead plays a natural developing or repositioning move, throwing away a decisive material advantage.

265.label: Prematurely advances a pawn in a pawn/piece endgame, letting it be captured for free or traded off so its strategic value (passed-pawn/restraint/support) is lost.

267.label: In every one of the 10 opening positions the player leaves a knight en prise to a pawn capture (exf6, dxc3 or exf3), dropping a full minor piece for at most a pawn.

249.label: An opening move (often a greedy queen sortie or pawn overextension) that loses the player's own material to a tactical refutation, with the lost piece varying across boards.

260.label: In every position the player declined a required capture of an undefended/attacking enemy piece (usually a knight on c6 or c3 via bxc6/bxc3), either letting it escape or allowing it to win material in return.

263.label: The player makes a quiet or greedy move while overlooking a forcing check or mate on an exposed king — either failing to deliver a winning mate or failing to play the saving check that prevents getting mated.

224.label: In endgames the player makes a passive king or pawn move that worsens the result—usually walking the king toward the edge/corner and accelerating its own checkmate (occasionally squandering a win or draw), rather than dropping material outright.

266.label: Plays a pointless check—almost always a bishop check (Bc5+/Bb6+/Bh6+)—that the opponent simply sidesteps (Kh1/Kh8), wasting tempo and squandering the position, with the consequence varying between hanging/trading the bishop, dropping material a couple moves later, and missing a stronger winning continuation.

271.label: A materially-safe, often quiet move that overlooks an available winning capture or tactic in the opening—most commonly grabbing free material such as the undefended h8 rook on the long diagonal.

269.label: In every position the player makes a move (queen retreat, king step, or pawn/bishop push) that strips the defender from a centralized knight on d4/d5 (once f3), leaving it to be captured—frequently with check along an exposed diagonal—and dropping a clean piece.

243.chip: Hangs material to a tactic (queen exposed)
243.label: A move — typically a queen sortie or a quiet pawn/piece move that neglects an exposed queen — that loses the player's own material to a tactical refutation (trap or fork) over the next 2–3 moves, most often the queen itself, rather than playing the materially-safe alternative.

275.label: Captures into a queen trade that throws away a winning or advantageous position, eliminating the attacking/dynamic potential that keeping queens on would have preserved.

272.chip: Hangs a piece in unsound attack
272.label: An aggressive attacking move (usually a kingside sacrifice or attacking lunge) that self-inflicts a loss of the player's own material—queen in some boards, rook in others—or in two cases walks into a back-rank mate, so the hung piece varies and the unifying invariant is 'a piece falls' rather than any one piece.

268.label: In endgames the player makes an inferior move—frequently a passive or greedy king move—that throws away the result, sometimes by missing a forced promotion/win and sometimes by hanging material to a tactic, with no single piece consistently lost.

270.chip: Greedy queen check, misses faster win
270.label: In a completely winning endgame, the player plays a greedy queen capture-with-check that wins material but overlooks a faster, cleaner forced win (a checkmate in 2 of 3 boards) — the position stays winning, only slower.

274.label: In the opening, the played move leaves two minor pieces (typically a bishop and a knight) exposed to a single pawn advance that forks them, losing a full piece.

280.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player walks the king the wrong direction, abandoning a pawn that the opposing king then captures for free.

278.label: In a winning endgame the player skips the simple capture of an undefended rook (almost always a king recapture like Kxh2/Kxg7), usually playing an aimless check or tempo move instead and throwing away the win.

279.label: In 6/10 positions the player loses their own queen for free—either by moving it onto an attacked square or by opening the diagonal/file that shielded it—while the other 4 boards are omissions (missed queen-based attacks, a fork, or a perpetual-check draw), so the queen is central throughout but the core mistake type is mixed and needs review.

276.label: In the opening the player leaves a bishop undefended or abandons its defense, dropping a full piece for nothing (knight in one case, a fork-won rook in another).

286.label: In the opening the player hangs a knight to an enemy pawn—either moving the knight onto an attacked square or ignoring the pawn's threat—losing a full piece for at most a pawn.

282.label: In an already-losing position, plays a defensive move (often a king move, piece varies) that exposes its own king and allows a forced mate or decisive attack instead of the one saving resource — though two of the ten are merely passed-pawn endgame inaccuracies, so the invariant is fuzzy.

273.label: Across its top-10 the player repeatedly chooses an inferior move — usually a greedy capture or a piece relocation/push — that loses their own material over the next 1-3 moves while ignoring an available stronger tactic, but the lost piece varies widely (bishop, knight, queen, pawn) and several boards are missed-wins or a back-rank mate rather than clean material drops, so no single piece can be named.

285.label: In a (usually already losing) position, the player makes a self-inflicted king-safety blunder — either walking the king into a net or stripping away its key defender/back-rank guard — that converts a defensible loss into a faster forced checkmate.

288.label: In the opening, the player makes a move (often a greedy pawn-grab) that leaves one of their own pieces en prise, losing material to a one- or two-move refutation; the hung piece is usually the queen (6/10) but also knights and bishops, so it's best described as 'a piece'.

281.chip: Missed forcing win in promotion race
281.label: Plays a slow, quiet move (pawn push, piece retreat, king step) instead of the one forcing line — typically a rook sacrifice or check that forces/clears promotion — squandering a winning passed-pawn position.

284.chip: Missed winning pawn capture (endgame, check instead)
284.label: In endgames the player repeatedly skips a winning capture—almost always of a (passed) pawn—typically playing a pointless tempo-check instead of just taking the material.

291.label: The player repeatedly overlooks a free/hanging enemy queen that the best move wins outright (queen-grab in 9/10; mate-in-3 in the lone outlier), throwing away a winning position.

292.label: A natural developing or pawn move in the opening ignores an enemy knight fork of the king and rook, losing the exchange (a bishop in one case).

295.label: Plays a queen capture-with-check that loses the queen (recaptured or hung), throwing away a winning position into a draw.

297.chip: Walks king into attack (exposes own king)
297.label: Plays a losing king move that walks the king onto an exposed square, inviting a forced attack that ends in checkmate or wins material (often the queen via fork/skewer).

287.label: From a favorable or winning position the player passes up the clearly strongest continuation (a more forcing capture, check, mate, or the correct piece/target), shrinking or throwing away the advantage; the missed/hung material varies board to board, so no single piece applies.

290.label: The player repeatedly fails to harass or capture the opponent's exposed/infiltrating queen with a tempo-gaining move (often Rg1/Rg8), instead playing a passive or self-damaging move.

289.label: The player surrenders their own rook — either hanging it outright for a pawn or trading it off — entering a hopeless, usually endgame, position.

294.label: A 100%-opening feature: a move (almost always tied to the f-pawn) that weakens the king/structure and self-inflicts material loss — either by hanging a piece to ...fxe5 or by exposing the king to Qh5+/Qh4+ on the e8–h5/e1–h4 diagonal; the lost unit varies (knight, bishop, pawn), so no single piece can be named.

296.label: In rook endgames the player reacts to an opponent's passed pawn by passively blockading or chasing it (usually with the rook), losing a tempo or a stronger active continuation rather than hanging material — though several flagged boards are actually 0cp/best, so the pattern is mixed.

303.label: The player keeps choosing a slow, quiet move and overlooks a forcing tactical combination that wins material — most often the ...Bxh6/Bxh6 deflection that drags the queen off c3, though the exact shot varies.

304.label: Voluntarily trades pieces (often a capturing check) to liquidate into a pawn/simplified endgame, throwing away a winning advantage or a saving draw — though the piece traded varies and 2 of 10 boards are actually correct trades.

302.chip: Hangs own material in opening (queen punishes)
302.label: An opening move that loses the player's own material for free — either developing/placing a piece on an unprotected square or grabbing a pawn — most often punished by the enemy queen snatching the loose piece or pawn.

301.chip: Misses winning move in won endgame
301.label: In winning/won endgames the player repeatedly fails to play the one precise converting move—most often a free capture of a hanging enemy piece (knight, bishop, or rook), but also a correct promotion or recapture—letting a clearly won position slip to a draw.

259.chip: Mishandles open center, exposed king (queen check)
259.label: In opening positions with an uncastled king in the open center, the player repeatedly mishandles king safety — failing to deliver or defend the key forcing queen check (Qe2+/Qe7+/Qxe4+) and instead hanging material or missing a winning blow — though the specific error splits between self-inflicted hangs (1,4,7,10) and missed wins/checks (2,3,5,6,9), so the exact direction and piece are not consistent enough to commit.

300.chip: Trades away key piece in endgame
300.label: In an endgame, the player makes an unfavorable capture/exchange that surrenders their own active piece (most often the rook) for inadequate compensation, collapsing into a lost or much worse position.

306.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a king move instead of advancing the passed pawn (or using correct king-escort technique), squandering a forced win—often a mate—rather than hanging any material.

283.label: In winning/equal endgames the player picks a natural-looking move that throws away the advantage—sometimes hanging their own piece (rook/bishop), sometimes missing the decisive capture or tactic—instead of the one precise converting move; piece and mechanism vary too much to name either specifically.

307.label: Played a quiet/passive move and missed a winning Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7/h2 (or the resulting mating attack) that delivers a decisive kingside crush.

308.label: The player makes a move that walks into an enemy knight fork or knight capture-with-check, losing their own material over the next 1-2 moves; the lost unit varies (bishop in ~4, rook in ~2, pawn in ~4), so the invariant is 'loses material' while a knight always delivers the punishment.

277.label: From a winning or mating position the player makes a queen move that throws away the advantage—either hanging the queen outright or missing the forced winning/mating continuation.

298.label: In endgames the player squanders a winning or drawing advantage through imprecise king/rook/bishop moves—losing tempo in pawn races or neglecting a passed pawn—rather than outright hanging material; the hung piece varies and 3 of 10 boards aren't actually blunders, so this needs human review.

309.label: Voluntarily trades off (or gives up) the queen — usually with a check or for a rook — collapsing a winning/holdable position into a lost one.

312.label: In already-winning endgames the player makes a materially-safe but inferior move that squanders or prolongs the fastest win (often a forced mate), rather than hanging its own material — though two of the ten positions are not actually mistakes.

305.label: Predominantly king-safety positions where the played move botches a mating situation — most often allowing the opponent an immediate checkmate (boards 5,6,7,8,9), with two cases throwing away the player's own forced mate by moving the wrong knight (2,3) and outliers hanging a queen (4), an endgame inaccuracy (1), and a passive positional error (10); the lost material/piece varies, so this is a 'mishandles king-safety/mate' feature rather than a single hung piece.

299.chip: Missed winning move in won position
299.label: In a winning position the player plays a materially-safe but inferior move, skipping the decisive winning continuation (a promotion, material-winning capture, or critical pawn-race move) and squandering the advantage.

315.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player chooses a move that neglects the opponent's runner, letting it promote and squandering a winning or drawing position — though two boards are actually engine-best moves and one is a missed pawn-capture, so the core is fuzzy.

320.label: A premature pawn push in the opening (e5/e4/d4) that leaves the advanced pawn undefended and simply gets captured for free — self-inflicted loss of material, almost always the pawn itself.

323.chip: Missed free rook on long diagonal (bishop)
323.label: The player skips a free capture of an undefended enemy rook sitting on the open long diagonal with their fianchetto bishop (Bxh8/Bxa8/Bxh1/Bxa1/Bxb1), instead playing a quiet move that lets the opponent block the diagonal and save the rook.

318.label: Plays a natural/passive/greedy move in the middlegame and misses a forcing tactical resource — frequently an exchange sacrifice or a check — that would have won material or saved the position.

313.chip: Bad bishop trade, enemy knight thrives
313.label: The player makes a losing bishop capture/trade — instead of capturing or eliminating the opponent's strong centralized knight — and is punished when the opponent recaptures even-for-even, leaving their knight dominant or relocating it to a superior square.

319.label: A premature or over-aggressive move (knight sortie, pawn break, or hasty castling) that squanders an existing advantage—often weakening the king or abandoning a central/defensive resource—rather than hanging any one specific piece, since the moved piece and the loss type (material vs. purely positional) vary across the boards.

316.label: In a won or safe position the player skips the decisive tactic (the best move is a rook check / back-rank infiltration in 9/10 boards) and throws the advantage away, though ~3 boards instead actively hang own material (bishop/exchange), so the direction is mixed.

324.label: In endgames (overwhelmingly pawn endgames), the played pawn or king move squanders the win or loses the pawn race, typically letting the opponent's passed pawn promote — though two boards are flagged non-blunders and one is a back-rank mate, so the pattern is fuzzy.

326.label: In every one of these endgame positions the player skips a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (a rook in 8/10, also a queen and a bishop), squandering a completely winning position into a draw or loss.

311.label: A queen move (9/10, often a speculative ...Qh3/Qg3 kingside sortie) that abandons a defensive duty and loses material or squanders a winning advantage, though the boards split between actually hanging own material and merely missing/throwing away a win.

327.label: A passive/developing move in the opening that overlooks a winning knight capture (usually Nxe5, also Nxe4/Nxd4) which exploits an undefended piece, throwing away a winning advantage.

322.label: In a losing middlegame, plays a king-safety-weakening move that abandons a key defensive post (often a rook leaving the back rank or an open file), letting the opponent's pieces converge into a forced mating attack rather than prolonging resistance.

330.label: A materially-safe but slow/passive move that fails to grab a hanging central pawn (d4/e4/d5/e5/c6), squandering a clean material win.

321.label: In every one of these 10 opening positions the player declines to capture or recapture an intruding enemy bishop (typically on c6 or c3), and the refutations show the bishop simply retreating to safety while the player stays down a full piece.

328.label: A middlegame move that abandons defense or walks into a tactic, losing the player's own material — the hung piece varies (bishop most often, but also queen via fork/pin), so it's 'a piece' rather than one specific type.

329.label: The player surrenders a rook for inadequate compensation—typically capturing a lesser piece or pawn with the rook (or leaving it undefended) and being recaptured, losing the exchange in the middlegame.

331.chip: Ignores central tension, allows e5 break
331.label: Plays a slow/developing move instead of resolving the central pawn tension (best move is almost always a center capture like exd4/dxe4), allowing a punishing central pawn break — most often e5, sometimes e4 or d5 — that gains tempo and space and in several lines wins material.

335.label: Captures an enemy rook with its own rook on (or beside) a promotion square, letting the opponent recapture with a pawn that promotes to a queen — often with check or mate — instead of first stepping the king off the back rank.

325.label: Throws away a winning/drawn endgame by promoting to a queen too early, letting the new queen be captured immediately (6/10); the rest are related endgame conversion errors — wrong recapture or a missed queen trade — so the pattern is mixed.

310.chip: Squanders win, often hangs a piece
310.label: An inferior move throws away a winning or favorable position; in the majority of cases it hangs own material (knight, queen, or rook) within a couple of moves, but the piece type and whether it's a material hang vs. a missed win vary enough that a human should review.

338.label: In every opening position the player's move leaves their own knight undefended (frequently the e5-knight, captured by Nxe5), allowing a clean capture that wins a full piece.

332.label: The player makes a capture—most often with a knight (8/10 moves)—that hangs or under-trades their own strong minor piece for too little material, throwing away the advantage; the piece lost varies (mostly knight, twice bishop) and one board is actually a missed win, so it's not a clean single-piece feature.

334.label: In a winning—almost always endgame—position the player skips the simple winning continuation (most often a free capture of an undefended piece, but the piece varies) and throws the advantage away.

340.label: A move that leaves the player's own material undefended and loses a piece to a refutation, though the hung piece varies (knight/bishop/rook) and a couple of boards are actually missed winning captures.

339.label: A middlegame blunder that loses the player's own material—usually walking into a fork or a simple recapture (often the queen, sometimes a knight)—though a couple of the boards are instead missed wins or pure positional collapses, so the core invariant is fuzzy.

337.label: A natural-looking opening/developing move that leaves the player's own material undefended and is refuted by a pawn capture, but the hung material varies (pawn most often, also bishop, knight, or queen) so no single piece can be named.

317.label: A move that throws away the player's advantage, most often by overlooking a free winning capture, though several boards instead hang the player's own queen or lose ground positionally rather than missing a capture.

343.label: The feature captures premature simplification—trading or capturing in a way that converts a clearly winning position into equality (and occasionally hangs material via an overlooked zwischenzug).

336.label: The player gives a check (10/10, almost always with a knight) that trades away or hangs their own best minor piece — usually the checking knight itself — losing material, though in two boards the hung piece is a bishop or the trapped knight costs the queen.

342.chip: Squanders win, skips forcing move (heavy piece)
342.label: In the middlegame the player makes a slow queen or rook move instead of the available forcing continuation (check/capture), throwing away a winning position—and in roughly half the cases even hanging own material or walking into mate.

341.label: The player makes a faulty capture or exchange — usually the wrong move-order, wrong target, or a premature simplification — that throws away the advantage, sometimes hanging their own material a few moves later and sometimes just missing the cleaner win.

347.label: The move loses the player's own material — typically by parking a piece on an undefended square or ignoring an already-hanging one, after which a tactic (fork/discovered attack/intermediate check) wins it; the hung piece varies (rook most often, also queen and bishop), and 2 of 10 are purely positional rather than material.

348.label: In an already-winning position the player chooses a slower, non-forcing move that delays or throws away a forced mate, missing the quickest win — frequently a forcing check or capture-with-check.

349.chip: Missed bishop capture winning a piece
349.label: In the opening the player repeatedly plays a safe developing move and overlooks a winning bishop capture (Bxd6/Bxd3/Bxc5) that bags a full, unrecapturable piece, squandering a winning advantage into equality.

350.label: In an endgame, the player skips an immediate capture of an undefended enemy piece (usually a rook, sometimes a queen) — often playing a check or king move instead — and throws away the win.

345.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight tactic)
345.label: In the opening, the player plays a quiet developing/pawn move instead of capturing a loose enemy knight, and as a result hangs their own material — a bishop, knight, queen, or rook — to an immediate capture or a knight fork; the hung piece varies, with a knight always central to the tactic.

344.label: The player makes a move that drops material—most often the c4 bishop (1,2,3,10) or a knight (4,5)—in the opening/early middlegame, with a knight always central to the tactic; however ~4/10 boards (6,7,8,9) are instead missed Nxe5/Nxe4 captures rather than self-inflicted hangs, so the direction is mixed and the hung piece varies, warranting review.

346.label: Across all 10 boards the player skips a winning capture of an undefended enemy piece (mostly a queen or rook), playing an unrelated king/pawn/piece move instead and throwing away a won position.

356.label: A quiet/tempo move (often a king or rook shuffle) leaves the player's own piece hanging by failing to resolve the immediate tactical tension — the lost piece varies (queen, rook, or bishop), so it's just 'a piece'.

354.label: The player makes a move that ignores or steps into an immediate forced checkmate, leaving its own king trapped in a mating net (the specific blundering piece varies: king, queen, rook, pawn-capture).

359.label: In the opening, White plays a move (Qf3, O-O, or a knight jump) that leaves its own knight undefended—usually on g5—allowing Black to capture it for free.

352.chip: Pushes pawn instead of king (K+P endgame)
352.label: In won king-and-pawn endgames, advances the passed pawn (or steps the king the wrong way) instead of leading with the king first, violating 'king before pawn' and letting the opponent's king blockade into a draw.

353.label: The player repeatedly overlooks a forced mate or crushing queen attack against the enemy king (most often Qxh2#), playing a routine move instead.

360.label: The player chooses a quiet, slow, or greedy pawn-grabbing move and overlooks an available forcing tactic (frequently a check, fork, skewer, or deflection) that would win material or preserve a winning advantage.

351.label: The player repeatedly throws away a winning or clearly better position by choosing a natural developing move or a tempting empty check instead of the unique precise continuation the position demanded — though a couple of boards instead directly hang material (queen/piece), so the direction is not fully clean.

357.label: Plays a greedy or passive move that ignores a mating attack on its own king, allowing a forced checkmate (or king-hunt winning decisive material).

363.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, plays a passive king move (or inferior pawn push) instead of the one decisive pawn break/breakthrough, throwing away the win or the draw.

361.chip: Passive king move loses tempo (pawn endgame)
361.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player repeatedly puts the king on a passive/wrong square, squandering a critical tempo or the opposition and accelerating an already-losing position (no material is hung).

364.label: A self-inflicted middlegame move that flips a holdable/equal position into a lost one — usually by hanging material (rook, bishop, pawn, knight — the piece varies) or by walking the king into a decisive attack/mate, so no single piece can be named.

365.label: In already losing or winning endgames the player makes a position-worsening king move (wrong direction, abandoning a key pawn, or stepping into harassment) or a king-weakening pawn push, which loses material or accelerates the loss — but the specific failure (hung rook/pawn vs. accelerated mate vs. missed win) varies too much to pin down one piece or one direction.

368.label: The player grabs material (usually capturing a bishop) instead of attending to the decisive task, letting an enemy passed pawn promote or missing a mate, turning a win or draw into a loss.

358.label: In a clearly winning (or drawn) position the player throws it away by mishandling material — usually hanging their own piece (rook, knight, or queen vary across boards), though several boards instead miss an available winning capture, flipping the eval from winning to losing.

369.label: In already-winning positions the player grabs material with a queen/rook capture instead of playing the more forcing line (often a check/mate or more precise win), missing the cleaner or faster victory rather than hanging anything.

314.label: Plays a tempo-losing, pointless check that lets the king step to safety and the checking piece land passively, squandering the advantage and skipping a clearly stronger move (the check is usually delivered by a knight).

371.label: In completely winning endgames the feature flags a move (usually a king or pawn move) that fails to convert most efficiently — squandering material synergy, skipping a promotion/capture, or otherwise reducing the advantage — but it's noisy since 3 of the top-10 boards are actually 0cp optimal moves and the 'hung piece 100%' SEE signal is contradicted by the multi-move analyses, so the real invariant is just 'suboptimal endgame conversion' rather than any specific hung piece.

366.label: In the middlegame the player loses their own queen — either moving it to a square where it is captured, capturing into a recapture, or playing another move while the queen sits en prise for little or no compensation.

373.label: In a winning/advantageous position, the player skips the decisive rook move—usually a back-rank or first-rank invasion—choosing a greedy capture or passive piece move that squanders the advantage.

370.chip: Hangs a piece for a pawn (opening sac)
370.label: In the opening, the player sacrifices a minor piece (usually a bishop on f2/f7, sometimes a knight) for a single pawn—often as a tempting check—and simply hangs it to a routine recapture.

355.label: The player throws away a winning or holding position by playing a worthless forcing check (or check-capture) that either hangs a piece outright (rook, bishop) or forces a losing trade/endgame — the hung piece varies, so no single piece can be named, but the harmful check is nearly universal.

374.label: Plays a safe/consolidating or material-grabbing move that misses a decisive winning attack on the enemy king, frequently a rook lift to the third rank (Rf3/Re3/Rd3).

367.chip: Losing king move in endgame (misses only save)
367.label: In endgames the player plays a losing move—usually a quiet king move—that misses the sole holding/saving resource (often the only correct capture), converting a draw or a salvageable position into a clear loss; the punishment varies between a hung piece, an enemy promotion, or mate, so no single piece is named.

379.label: The player repeatedly fails to capture an undefended enemy bishop (usually on g4/g5) that could be won for a full free piece — a missed win, not a self-inflicted hang.

375.label: The recurring error is choosing an inferior rook move (9/10 are rook moves) that throws away a winning or better position — sometimes missing a forced win/mate, sometimes losing tempo or eventually material — rather than one single consistent hung piece, so the boards are too mixed for a confident specific label.

377.chip: Hangs own piece, throwing away win
377.label: In a winning position, the player makes a move (often an in-between attack or move-order error) that abandons defense of their own piece — usually the queen, sometimes a rook — leaving it to be captured and converting a win into a loss.

372.chip: Misplays pawn endgame, misses key capture
372.label: In endgames the move mishandles the pawn tension — almost always skipping the one precise pawn capture (often playing a king move instead) — and loses the pawn race to an opponent's unstoppable passed pawn.

376.chip: Missed simplifying trade into won endgame
376.label: The player keeps pieces on the board instead of making the simplifying rook/queen exchange that liquidates into a winning (or drawing) pawn endgame.

380.label: The recurring blunder is moving the queen to a square where it can be captured—almost always WITH CHECK and usually as a misguided trade offer—hanging the queen and converting a playable position into a loss or forced mate (9/10 are queen moves; one hangs a rook the same way).

388.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player moves the king instead of pushing the passed pawn to the seventh rank, squandering a forced win into a dead draw.

381.label: In every board the player chose a quiet, materially-safe king/rook move and overlooked a forcing winning tactic — almost always a knight check or fork (Nf3+, Nf6+, Nb3+, Nxe3+), with only one board (Bxg7+) using a bishop instead.

384.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player wastes a tempo on a king move or passive pawn push and misses the one critical pawn break/breakthrough (g4, h5, f5, a4, h4...), squandering a winning or holdable position rather than hanging material.

333.label: The played move ignores a decisive threat to the player's own king (often while grabbing material or chasing an enemy piece), allowing a crushing attack or back-rank mate in most positions, though a couple of boards are simply missed material wins.

391.label: In the opening, plays an undefended bishop to a square where it is immediately captured for free, losing a full piece.

382.label: The player repeatedly skips a stronger tactical move that wins material (frequently the opponent's queen) or forces mate, settling instead for a materially-safe but inferior move.

390.chip: Wastes tempo on flank pawn push
390.label: A slow flank/wing pawn advance (usually an a-, b-, or c-pawn, intended as queenside expansion) wastes a critical tempo, letting the opponent refute by winning material or seizing the initiative; the exact punishment varies across boards.

383.label: In already-lost endgames (often passed-pawn/rook situations), the player makes the decisive losing move that converts a difficult-but-fightable position into forced mate or hopelessness — by hanging the rook, trading it for a pawn, missing a saving capture, or neglecting king safety — instead of the one resilient defensive move.

386.label: In a winning position the player repeatedly fails to grab the opponent's undefended hanging rook—playing a king move, a check, or a lesser capture instead—throwing away a decisive material edge (one board the free piece is a queen, not a rook).

389.label: Plays a slow, materially-safe move (often in an endgame) that wastes the tempo needed for a decisive shot — frequently a pawn break like f5/f4/d4 but also key captures — converting a winning position into a draw.

387.label: In an already-winning or mating position the player gives up material — usually by moving the queen onto, or leaving it on, an attacked square — converting a forced mate/win into merely winning; the lost piece is the queen in most boards (1,2,3,4,7,9) but the queen is not unanimous (board 10 hangs a rook) and several flagged boards (5,6,8) are actually trivial non-blunders, hence the review flag.

378.label: In a drawn or winning position the player skips the one saving/winning move and instead pursues their own plan, ignoring the opponent's decisive threat — most often an enemy passed pawn promoting, sometimes a mating attack or a free capture.

393.label: A slow pawn push—almost always one that kicks an enemy bishop to 'win a tempo'—ignores an immediate decisive threat, wasting the critical tempo and letting the opponent crash through with mate or winning material.

553.label: A check (frequently a speculative Bxf7+/Greek-Gift sacrifice) that loses the player's own piece for little or no compensation, where the simple recapture/quiet move was correct.

584.label: In every position the player skips a winning tactic—in 8/10 a knight fork that wins material (exchange/piece)—by choosing a natural-looking trade, capture, or developing move, squandering a winning advantage.

575.label: A move that loses the player's own material — usually a bishop or central pawn left hanging through mishandled opening center tension — though a couple of boards are instead missed winning captures rather than self-inflicted hangs.

588.label: The move leaves the player's own bishop undefended, allowing an enemy knight to capture it for free.

579.label: Pushes a pawn (usually racing a passed pawn or rushing promotion) instead of the correct move, ignoring the opponent's reply and either hanging own material or squandering the winning advantage.

578.label: A move that loses the player's own material — a pawn via a wrong-way king march in pawn endgames or an undefended knight in the opening — though 2-3 of the ten are instead missed material-winning shots rather than hangs.

590.label: In winning or equal positions the player declines an available capture of material—usually by throwing in a pointless tempo check—forfeiting or badly diluting the win.

595.label: In endgames the player makes an inaccurate move (king move, wrong check or wrong promotion) that throws away the optimal result — letting a win slip to a draw/perpetual/fortress or missing a saving stalemate, and occasionally hanging the queen outright.

610.label: Player repeatedly skips a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (bishop/rook/queen/knight all appear), squandering a clearly winning position into a draw or worse.

607.label: In queen endgames the player plays a slower or non-forcing move—usually a check—instead of the decisive continuation, missing a forced mate or material-winning line and letting the enemy king escape.

604.label: A passive move (usually a queen retreat) in the opening that declines an available winning capture of material — varying among rook, bishop, knight-fork, and pawn — with one outlier case actively hanging the queen instead.

596.label: In endgames the player abandons the blockade/stopping of an opponent's passed pawn — usually drifting a bishop to a 'more active' square — allowing that pawn to promote by force.

616.chip: Hangs a piece on greedy capture

662.label: A superficially natural or aggressive move that throws away the player's standing—hanging material in some lines (pawn, bishop, or rook) and merely losing tempo/position in others—with the moved and lost piece varying too much across the ten boards to name any specific piece or single mistake type.

667.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player fails to stop or capture the opponent's passed pawn, allowing it to advance and promote, though two of the ten boards (a missed knight capture and an opening sacrifice) break the pattern.

664.chip: Missed fastest win in passed-pawn endgame
664.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player picks a materially-safe but suboptimal move — a premature/wrong pawn push or a slow king/knight move (and once a skipped free capture) — instead of the decisive move, throwing away a forced win for a slower or merely-better position.

668.label: The player repeatedly chooses a quiet, natural developing/recapturing move and overlooks a winning knight-capture tactic (almost always Nxe4/Nxe5-type) that wins material or saves the position.

665.label: In nearly every position the player had a decisive winning continuation — very often a forced checkmate — but chose an inferior, materially-safe move that threw away the win (one board instead just hangs a knight).

666.label: The player's move walks into or fails to prevent a forced mate against its own king — overwhelmingly an immediate back-rank checkmate (e.g. Rh1#/Rb1#), whether by moving the king to a fatal square, blocking its own escape, or pulling a defender (often a rook) off the back rank, sometimes while greedily grabbing material.

669.label: An over-aggressive opening move—typically a greedy grab (Nxf2, Qxh7) or unsound sacrifice—that loses the player's own material with no compensation; usually a piece (knight, bishop, queen), occasionally a pawn, so the specific unit varies.

671.label: In every position the player passed up an immediate winning bishop capture (most often grabbing an undefended rook for the exchange on the long diagonal) in favor of a quiet move, throwing away free material.

670.chip: Passive endgame move, no king activation
670.label: In endgames the player makes a passive or wrong-direction move (usually failing to centralize/activate the king, sometimes a non-urgent pawn push) that squanders a winning or drawable position rather than pursuing the active king march.

651.label: In the endgame the player makes a losing move — usually pushing a flank pawn or a passive king move — that fails to address the critical passed-pawn/promotion race (or skips the only saving capture), turning a drawn or holdable position into a loss.

657.label: Across the boards the played move vacates the sole defender of a critical square or piece, self-inflicting a decisive blow—most often an immediate checkmate (boards 2,4,7,8,9), sometimes a forced material win (1,3,5,10)—with one outlier being a tempo-wasting check that squanders a win (6).

659.label: Plays a natural capturing or recapturing move (often a pawn-grab) instead of the strongest move, which in some positions hangs its own material (rook/queen/knight) and in others squanders a forced win or tactic — the consequence and piece vary too much to name one.

678.label: The player makes a move that opens or fails to defend a long diagonal, allowing the opponent's bishop to capture an undefended rook and win the exchange.

680.label: While already winning, the player skips a decisive shot — usually a free enemy piece hanging for capture (rook, bishop, pawn) and sometimes a forced mate — settling for a lesser advantage instead of the clear win.

672.label: The player throws away an equal-to-winning position by failing to play the position's thematic central action (d5/e5/f5/Nxe5/d4), instead choosing a passive or wing move — and on ~4 boards this takes the form of an unsound Bxf7+/Bf5 that simply hangs a bishop.

673.label: In nearly all positions the played move self-inflicts material loss, hanging a piece (bishop most often, but also queen/exchange) to a 2-3 move tactical refutation that usually features an enemy knight capturing with check (Nxf3+, Nxd3+, Nxh6, Nxd6+, Nxf6+).

674.label: In endgames (frequently with passed pawns), the player makes a natural-looking move that fails to find the single precise resource — throwing away a win in some cases and a draw in others — rather than hanging material outright.

683.label: Plays a slow, materially-safe move (king/rook shuffle) that throws away a winning position by ignoring the one decisive shot — a pawn or knight fork, a promotion, or a rook invasion — with the winning piece varying across boards.

682.label: In every position the player overlooks a knight-fork check (Nf2+/Ne2+/Nf3+/etc.) that simultaneously attacks the king and wins the queen, instead playing a passive or routine move that throws away the win.

679.label: Player repeatedly fails to grab the opponent's undefended queen, passing up a free winning capture (8/10 are a hanging queen; the other two miss a back-rank mate and a hanging bishop).

675.label: In a winning endgame the player rushes their own passed pawn one square toward promotion instead of the prophylactic blockading/winning move, allowing the opponent to promote with tempo or mate and squandering the win.

681.label: Player moves the queen to a square where the opponent can force an unfavorable queen trade, dissolving the player's attack or advantage.

684.chip: Missed win in queen endgame (passed pawn)
684.label: In queen-and-pawn endgames (almost always a passed-pawn/promotion race), the player chooses a safe but passive queen move and skips the forcing check or capture that wins — costing a faster mate or, in the worst cases, letting a won position slip to a draw — though half the boards are actually 0cp non-blunders, so the 'mistake' is inconsistent.

687.label: In a winning endgame the player skips the immediate, often check-giving pawn promotion (playing a king/pawn/capture move instead) and lets the forced win slip to a draw or worse.

688.chip: Missed capturing hanging enemy piece (often rook)
688.label: The player repeatedly overlooks an elementary free capture of an undefended enemy piece (usually a hanging rook), throwing away a winning position by playing a passive/repositioning move instead.

676.label: Player makes a capture (almost always on b4/b5) that the opponent answers with a recapture or pawn-grab delivering check against the uncastled king on e1/e8, costing material or a winning advantage.

695.label: In every position the player overlooked a simple capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning position by playing an unrelated move instead.

658.label: A move that abandons the defense of, or directly exposes, the player's own piece—self-inflicting decisive material loss, with the queen most frequently the piece hung and a queen involved in nearly every position.

691.label: Across all 10 boards the player makes a materially-safe but soft/preparatory move and overlooks the concrete winning continuation (a capture or forcing tactic) that wins material or preserves a near-winning advantage; the specific winning piece varies (queen, rook, knight, bishop), so this is a piece-agnostic omission rather than a self-inflicted hang.

693.chip: Weakening pawn push hangs material (chasing queen)
693.label: A pawn push—usually intended to chase away the enemy queen—opens a line or strips a defender around the player's own king, and the refutation wins material (or mates) within a couple of moves.

690.label: In every position the player had a decisive winning continuation (often a forced mate) but threw it away with a greedy capture or a slow, non-forcing move.

685.chip: Hangs piece to f7 knight fork (opening)
685.label: In the opening the player ignores a knight fork on f7 (failing to play Kxf7), hanging material — usually the queen to Nxd8, sometimes the d5 knight after retreating the queen.

696.label: The player ignores an immediately capturable undefended enemy rook (taken by the queen, often with check) and instead plays a slow move, squandering a winning advantage.

689.label: Player plays a passive/inferior move that throws away the position by declining an available winning capture or strong move, though in roughly a third of cases the played move instead outright hangs a piece — and the piece involved varies (rook, knight, bishop, queen, pawn), so no specific piece can be named.

677.label: Player moves the queen onto (or leaves it on) a square where it is immediately captured by a rook—often while greedily grabbing a pawn—throwing away a winning queen-vs-rook or mating advantage.

697.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight involved)
697.label: In the opening the player makes a move (often a premature knight sortie like Ng5 instead of Nxe5) that loses their own material; the lost piece varies (knight, bishop, or d4 pawn), so it's 'a piece', with a knight involved in nearly every position.

694.label: Pushing or capturing with the f-pawn in the opening weakens king safety and loses material, typically to a forcing queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) along the freshly-opened diagonal.

700.label: Self-inflicted material loss: the player hangs their own piece — usually by greedily capturing a defended pawn (mostly a bishop, but knight/queen vary, so 'a piece'), occasionally throwing away a forced mate while doing so.

703.label: In a winning position the player skips a free, material-winning capture (most often grabbing an undefended enemy rook) and plays a passive/safe move instead, throwing the win away — though several boards instead show a bad trade, wrong recapture, or greedy grab, so the exact piece and error vary.

701.label: Player needlessly trades queens, simplifying away a winning or favorable position when keeping the queen (often to grab a free piece/pawn or sustain an attack) was far stronger.
