702.label: A self-inflicted move that ignores the opponent's threat and walks into a forced refutation, losing the player's own material or king — but the punished asset varies (knight, bishop, rook, pawn promotion, and several lines end in checkmate), so no single piece can be named.

699.label: An overoptimistic opening capture/sacrifice — most often an unsound Nxf7 fork attempt — that simply hangs the player's own piece, since the opponent quietly recaptures and emerges up material.

705.label: The player makes a self-inflicting move that hangs their own piece — most often the queen left on an aggressive square (h4/h5/e5) where it's captured for free — though two positions instead skip a forced winning tactic, so the core invariant is 'a piece hangs' rather than any single piece.

707.label: In an already-lost position, plays a move that shortens the path to the opponent's forced mate, most often by walking the king into a mating net.

704.chip: Squanders winning position, hangs own material
704.label: From a winning or drawn position the player plays a careless/greedy move (often a capture) that hangs their own material or fatally exposes their king, throwing away the advantage—but the lost piece varies (rook, queen, bishop, even mate-via-king-safety) and a few boards are pure missed forced wins instead, so the feature is genuinely mixed.

710.label: Player loses the exchange by capturing a centralized enemy minor piece with a rook that is simply recaptured by a pawn, dropping rook-for-minor with no compensation.

698.label: In middlegame positions the player repeatedly loses its own material — leaving a piece en prise or trading/sacrificing it for inadequate compensation (most often a bishop, but the hung piece varies).

712.label: The bishop snatches a seemingly free edge pawn (usually Bxa7, also Bxa2/Bxh2) but gets trapped and lost over the next few moves, sacrificing a full piece for a single pawn.

713.label: In every one of the top-10 opening positions the player loses a bishop for free—either by moving it onto an undefended square on a long diagonal (g7/b7/b2/f5/f4) or by failing to defend an already-fianchettoed bishop—so the recurring mistake is hanging a bishop.

706.label: Against White's queen-on-h5 + knight-on-g6 battery, Black fails to play the only defense ...Nf6, instead playing a move (hxg6, Kd7/Kd8, Nxc3, Nc6) that self-inflicts loss — either Qxh8/Nxh8 winning the h8 rook or a Ne5+/Qf7 discovered-check mate.

692.label: A natural-looking positional/developing move that ignores the live tactic, most often hanging the player's own material — but the piece varies (knight, bishop, pawn, or the exchange) and ~3/10 are instead a missed winning capture, so the invariant is only 'ignores material'.

720.label: Plays a tempo/pawn check that lets the enemy king flee to safety, squandering a forced checkmate (8/10) or otherwise decisive win that the player should have delivered instead.

711.label: In a winning middlegame the player plays a slow or inferior move that throws away the decisive advantage—failing to execute the forcing winning continuation (often the fxg6 pawn break or a forced mate), though in ~2 cases the inferior move actually hangs material.

709.chip: Hangs material chasing a piece (pawn lunge)
709.label: A premature flank pawn lunge intended to chase an enemy piece (almost always a knight) backfires, costing the player their own material or fatally exposing their king.

715.label: A king-safety blunder—walking the king into a mating net or removing the back-rank defender—that allows a forced checkmate, almost always delivered by an enemy rook.

686.label: Instead of the available forcing move (usually a rook exchange/capture or a check), the player chooses a slow, non-forcing move that typically hangs their own material — rook, knight, bishop, or queen vary — or occasionally just squanders a forced win.

719.label: In the opening, the player loses material by declining the correct Nxe5 capture/recapture and instead hanging a piece (a bishop on f2 in several, a knight or other piece elsewhere), with a knight on e5 the recurring tactical element rather than the consistently-hung piece.

708.label: In endgames the player makes a tempting capture or check that squanders the correct result — sometimes hanging a piece (queen/bishop/knight, no single piece dominant), more often missing a forced mate, perpetual, or winning plan.

722.label: In an endgame the player makes a slow/passive move—most often a king move—that skips the decisive pawn break or material-winning capture, throwing away the win or worsening a lost position (no own piece hung).

716.label: Across these positions the player self-inflicts a material/positional loss by making a faulty capture or simplifying trade (often missing a stronger zwischenzug, alternative capture, or saving resource), or by leaving an attacked piece hanging — but the piece involved varies (rook, bishop, knight, pawn) and the mechanism alternates between bad trades and outright hangs, so it is 'a piece' rather than any single type.

718.chip: Misses the only good move (king safety)
718.label: In each position the player overlooks the single critical move — usually a forcing queen check, capture, or precise defensive resource — and instead plays a quiet, slow, or greedy alternative that lets the position collapse (most often into a mating attack on their own king, but sometimes losing material or surrendering a saving perpetual).

714.label: Mostly a queen or rook that abandons a defensive duty or captures unsafely, losing the player's own material or allowing back-rank mate, but the hung piece varies (rook/queen/mate) and 2-3 boards are missed wins or near-perfect, so the core invariant is fuzzy.

726.label: In won endgames the move keeps own material safe but throws away the fastest win (often via underpromotion, wrong recapture, or decentralizing) — an omission, not a hang, and 2/10 boards aren't even mistakes.

725.label: Across mostly endgame positions the player picks an inferior move that throws away a winning or equal position — sometimes missing a free capture (Qxb6, Rxa3, Rxd4), sometimes mishandling a passed pawn or promotion (1,2,5,6,10), and twice walking into mate (g3, Re3) — so the only shared invariant is botching the conversion of an endgame edge, with no single hung/missed piece common to ≈8/10 boards.

724.label: Across all 10 boards the player throws away a winning or equalizing position by choosing a natural but inferior move instead of the forcing/winning continuation — about half simply MISS the win (often a tempo-gaining check like Re1+/Bc5+/Bb2+) while the other half SELF-INFLICT material loss (hanging a bishop, queen, or rook, sometimes only after a 2-3 move refutation), so direction is mixed and no single hung piece dominates.

733.label: Plays a passive or routine move, missing a winning bishop sacrifice against the enemy king (consistently Bxf2+/Bxh7+/Bxf7+/Bxh2+).

717.chip: Hangs material via pawn push (tempo grab)
717.label: A pawn move — typically a push to gain tempo on the enemy queen or open lines — hangs the player's own material (usually a pawn, sometimes a piece falling over 2-3 moves), often punished by a capture-with-check against an uncastled king.

732.chip: Hangs a piece with an unsound check
732.label: Plays a forcing check that sacrifices/hangs the player's own material unsoundly (most often a rook, but bishops and queens too), losing material rather than achieving the hoped-for attack.

727.chip: Passive blockade misses active save (passed pawn)
727.label: Repeatedly chooses a passive blockading/quiet move—most often parking the queen on a1/a8 in front of a passed pawn—instead of the active forcing resource (usually a perpetual check or a saving king move), throwing away the draw or win.

723.chip: Hangs a piece in the opening
723.label: In the opening the player makes an unsound move that loses their own material — most often a refuted bishop sacrifice on f7/f2, sometimes a knight grabbed or trapped in the tactic — so the piece type varies (bishop ~6/10, knight ~4/10), making the invariant simply 'hangs a piece'.

728.label: In winning/equal endgames the player makes a passive king or rook move instead of the one precise pawn break (usually d4 or e6), squandering the advantage.

721.chip: Hangs a piece via quiet move (knight tactic)
721.label: Instead of the forcing tactical capture demanded by the position (most often Nxf3+), the player makes a quiet developing/castling move that fails to resolve the tactical tension, hanging a piece within two or three moves (a knight is the pivotal piece in nearly every line).

737.label: In every one of the top-10 positions the player passed up a winning knight fork (Nc2+/Nc7+) that checks the exposed king on e1/e8 and wins the rook (the exchange), instead playing a quiet developing/castling or material-grabbing move that lets the opponent cover the fork square.

731.label: Plays the queen to a vulnerable, often open-file square where it is won — frequently via an intermezzo check or discovered attack that deflects its defender — though in a few boards another piece falls instead.

729.label: A mostly-queen repositioning/retreat that abandons a key square or defensive duty and throws away a winning advantage — usually by missing a forced tactic, though in ~3/10 boards the move directly hangs own material.

735.label: Plays a slow developing/expanding move that ignores an active opponent threat, hanging the player's own material (piece varies — knight, bishop, rook; often king-safety related).

743.label: The player overlooks a forcing queen move — almost always a check, frequently Qxc6+ — that wins material by force, instead playing a quiet, safe, or developing move.

740.label: In an endgame the player makes a faulty pawn advance or premature promotion that throws away a drawn or winning position — sometimes hanging the newly-promoted queen (boards 3,6,10), more often a tempo/structure loss (boards 1,2,4,5,8) or a missed saving resource (7,9).

738.chip: Hangs own material by abandoning defense
738.label: A move that walks a defender off its post (or onto a captured square), leaving the player's own material hanging — but the hung unit varies (queen, rook, bishop, pawns) and several boards instead just miss a faster win, drawing resource, or allow decisive passed pawns, so the feature is mixed.

736.chip: Declines saving queen trade, hangs piece
736.label: In a losing or inferior position the player passes up the forced queen trade that was the only way to limit damage, instead playing another move (usually a king move) that leaves their own piece — most often the queen, but sometimes a rook — hanging.

734.label: Most boards show a move that loses the player's own material (the hung object varies — pawn, knight, queen, bishop), but ~2-3 boards instead miss a forced win/mate, so the core mistake is only loosely shared and needs human review.

741.label: In the opening the player passes up a winning tactic that punishes the opponent's exposed queen on f3/c3 (frequently a knight fork or ...Nd4), playing a quiet developing move instead and squandering a winning advantage into equality.

745.label: The move leaves the player's own piece en prise (usually a bishop or queen, hung directly or via a short 2-3 move tactic), though ~2/10 boards are instead missed wins rather than self-inflicted hangs.

750.chip: Hangs a piece grabbing central pawn
750.label: In the opening, captures a defended central pawn (almost always d4), hanging its own piece — a bishop or knight depending on the position — for just one pawn.

739.chip: Misses critical tempo move in endgame (often a check)
739.label: In a rook endgame, plays a slow move—frequently failing the one saving/winning check—that surrenders critical tempo, letting the opponent's passed pawn promote or a back-rank mate land.

744.label: In winning endgames the player fails to capture the opponent's only remaining active piece (knight or bishop), letting it escape and converting a win or forced mate into mere advantage; one outlier instead hangs its own queen.

742.label: In a winning or clearly advantageous position the player repeatedly throws away the win by choosing a routine/materialistic capture or passive move instead of the precise forcing continuation—mechanism varies (missed tactic, missed mate, bad trade, even a self-inflicted hang), so no single piece or capture is the true invariant beyond 'squandered advantage'.

753.label: In a won position the player passes up a free winning capture (most often the opponent's completely undefended queen) and instead plays a pointless forcing check, throwing away mate or a decisive material edge.

752.label: In nearly every position the player skipped a forced win — frequently a forced checkmate (Ne7#, Rd1#, Qh7#, mate-in-3/6) or a decisive tactic like Ne2+ or Nxf2 — and instead played a materially-safe but inferior capture/positional move, throwing away the advantage.

748.label: Across all 10 boards the played move allows a one-move checkmate (usually Qxg7# or Qxg2#, occasionally Qxh2#/Qxb2#), either by greedily capturing a piece that was the king's last defender or by ignoring an already-present mating threat — a self-inflicted king-safety collapse rather than a missed win.

747.chip: Self-inflicted blunder: hangs material or allows mate
747.label: A move that fails to address a concrete threat — hanging the player's own material (piece varies: rook/queen/pawn) or walking the king into a mating net — though several boards are softer positional/tempo losses, so the specific disaster is not uniform.

751.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight tactic)
751.label: A developing/repositioning move in the opening that self-inflicts material loss—most often refuted by a knight capturing with check (Nxf3+/Nxe2+/Nxe3) after the player skips the safe Nxd4—but the hung piece varies (bishop, knight, pawn, rook) and a couple of boards are missed captures or king-safety lapses rather than clean hangs, so this needs review.

746.label: In a (usually winning) position the player passes up the decisive continuation—frequently a forced mate or a crushing attacking/material-winning shot—in favor of a quieter developing, retreating, or simplifying move, though in a few boards (Nf4, Nf3, Qxb7) the chosen move also outright hangs the player's own piece, so the direction is mixed and the hung piece is not consistent enough to name.

754.label: In each top position the player passes up the single precise best move—frequently a promotion-with-check, but elsewhere a key capture or equalizing resource—playing a passive king/piece move instead; the mistake is an omission of a win/save, not a self-hung piece.

760.chip: Missed winning attack on king (queen check)
760.label: A materially-safe move that skips a forced mate or decisive attack against the exposed enemy king, typically a forcing queen check (Qxg3+/Qxb6+/Qg6+).

749.label: A tempting bishop check (always a bishop, always a check) that backfires—most often the bishop itself gets trapped or captured a move or two later, though in a few boards it's instead a wrong-capture/bad-trade that squanders a bigger win.

758.label: In every position the player chose a quiet developing/retreating move and overlooked a forcing winning shot — often a checkmate, usually delivered by a bishop check (Bb5+/Bh5+/Bxe6#) — squandering a clearly winning tactic.

757.label: In the opening, the player abandons an advanced/infiltrating bishop by playing a routine developing move instead of capturing or trading it, letting the opponent win the piece for free (9/10 bishop, 1/10 knight).

762.label: In all 10 positions the player plays a safe quiet move (developing, castling, or a pawn push) and overlooks a forcing capture-with-check that wins material against the exposed/uncastled enemy king — the check is delivered by the queen in 9/10 (most often Qxc3+), so the win is omitted rather than any own piece hung.

755.label: In the opening the player repeatedly grabs the knight fork Nxf7 instead of the correct Bxf7+, and the refutations show this loses material a couple moves later (knight gets trapped on h8, or a rook/bishop falls, or the king is mated) — the hung piece varies, so the certain core is 'hangs material via Nxf7 over Bxf7+'.

761.label: Player drifts the queen to a passive square, missing a forcing material-winning queen capture of a rook (often an exchange/queen sacrifice such as Qxe1).

764.chip: King to wrong square in endgame
764.label: In an endgame the player walks the king to the wrong square — declining a key capture or losing the opposition/defensive zone — turning a draw or holdable position into a loss.

768.label: Player inserts a flashy 'check first' move (zwischenzug) instead of the clean winning capture, hanging the checking piece — bishop, knight, rook or queen — for far less than it was worth.

759.label: A greedy/loosening capture in the opening that backfires self-inflicted, costing the player's own material or allowing mate; the specific piece lost varies (rook, queen, knight, or a mating attack), so it cannot be pinned to one piece.

765.label: In each middlegame position the player's move neglects the critical defensive duty—removing a defender, blocking the king's escape, or placing a piece passively/in harm's way—letting the opponent crash through with forced mate (boards 1,2,4,7,9) or decisive material loss (boards 3,5,6,8,10), but the piece moved and the thing lost vary too much to name a specific piece or single outcome.

769.label: In every position the player throws away a won game by giving an aimless queen check instead of the decisive queen capture/trade that simplifies into a clearly winning (usually pawn) endgame.

766.label: In a winning position the player makes a tempting capture (often a knight grab) that throws away the advantage instead of finding the one precise winning continuation.

773.chip: Trades rook into lost pawn endgame
773.label: Voluntarily exchanges (or allows the exchange of) the last rook, simplifying a holdable endgame into a lost king-and-pawn ending.

767.label: The player prefers a tempting forcing check over the best move; this usually backfires—hanging its own material or walking into mate—and sometimes just settles for a smaller win, with the only true invariant being that the move is always a check.

756.label: A self-defeating move—usually a pointless check—that hangs the player's own piece (most often a rook) and is captured immediately or within a couple of moves.

763.label: In all ten boards the player held a winning or clearly better position and squandered it with a passive or careless move—often missing a forcing win/mate, sometimes self-inflicting material or king-safety loss—but there is no single consistent hung piece (queen, knight, rook, bishop and pawn moves all appear).

772.label: An endgame blunder—usually a king move—that throws away a won or drawn position (king is misplaced, abandons a pawn, blocks its own pawn, or walks into checks/mate).

776.chip: Hangs material via pawn recapture (opens diagonal)
776.label: A pawn capture in the opening (usually bxc6) opens a diagonal/line that lets the opponent win material with a check or fork — a self-inflicted material loss, most often the exchange to Bxc6+.

781.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe developing/retreating move that misses an available winning tactical strike (often a fork) in the opening, letting the opponent consolidate.

775.label: The played move loses the player's own material — directly hanging a piece (most often a bishop) or dropping it within a 2-3 move tactic — though a couple of boards are closer to tempo/positional losses, so the exact piece varies.

771.label: In a winning middlegame the player throws away the advantage, usually by choosing a quiet or materialistic move instead of the forcing tactical shot (best move is often a bishop capture/sacrifice), though several cases instead outright hang material.

770.label: Plays a tempting, premature CHECK (knight 66% / bishop the rest) instead of the stronger quiet or mating move—the check lets the enemy king escape to safety or releases the attacking pressure, converting a winning/better position into drawn-or-lost, and in several boards (Nd7+, Bxf2+, Nxc7+) the checking piece itself ends up hung or trapped.

780.chip: Hangs a piece capturing pawn (bishop, opening)
780.label: In the opening the player makes a losing capture—most often a bishop grabbing a defended pawn (d7/e7)—that hangs the piece (or surrenders bishop/advantage) for inadequate material.

787.label: The player chose a quiet, non-forcing move and squandered a winning attack, missing a decisive forcing continuation that was almost always a check (often a mating sacrifice).

785.chip: Hangs own piece after capture (queen often)
785.label: A greedy capture in the opening leaves the player's own material hanging to an immediate refutation—usually the queen on the open d-file (Qxd8/Qxd1), though in a few boards it's a rook or bishop lost to a queen check/fork.

774.chip: Bad queen check, not winning Qxd5/Qxf7
774.label: In all 10 positions White plays a tempting queen CHECK instead of the correct simplifying queen capture (Qxd5 / Qxf7+ / Qxf6+); but the consequence is split ~5/5 — in boards 2,6,7,8,9 the checking queen lands on an undefended square and is simply captured (hangs the queen, often into mate), while in boards 1,3,4,5,10 the check is materially safe and merely throws away a won game, so the direction (hung_own vs missed_win) is genuinely mixed and needs human review.

782.label: About half the positions feature a piece move that loses the player's own material to a recapture, fork, or zwischenzug (the hung piece varies — bishop, knight, or queen), while the rest are missed wins (fxe5, c6 break) or advantage-squandering trades/positional errors, so the feature is genuinely mixed and not a clean single-piece hang.

788.label: The played move (often a capture that strips a defender or opens a line) loses the player's own material, with the refutation winning a piece or pawn — the specific unit hung varies, so the invariant is material, not one piece.

791.chip: Hangs own piece with a check
791.label: A check that loses the player's own material (queen or rook, occasionally bishop) — every one of the top moves is a check that hangs the piece or trades it disastrously, throwing away a winning position.

786.label: A move that abandons a key defensive square or compromises king safety — most often a queen or king move — allowing the opponent to deliver checkmate or win material, though several boards (g5, g6, Rf7, Kf1) are really missed wins or positional concessions rather than clean hangs, and the lost piece varies (queen, bishop, king walking into mate), so this is a fuzzy 'self-inflicted loss' feature needing review.

784.chip: Throws away win with a check (piece hangs)
784.label: Plays a tempting forcing check that spoils a winning position — usually the checking piece is simply captured (knight most often, but also rook/bishop), though sometimes the check merely substitutes for a stronger winning capture.

783.label: The played move loses the player's own material—donating a piece or pawn that the opponent captures, often with a tempo-gaining check against an exposed king—rather than choosing a safe alternative; the specific unit hung varies (knight/bishop/pawn), so no single piece is named.

778.label: Greedily captures a pawn with the knight (Ncxb5 / Nxb4) only to be immediately recaptured, hanging the knight for a single pawn in the opening (9/10 are knight grabs; one case hangs a bishop on Bxg4).

793.label: A developing move—most often a bishop (Bb4/Bb5/Bxd5/Bh3)—that leaves the player's own material undefended and losing, though ~3 of 10 are instead omissions that skip a clear win, and the hung piece varies (knight, queen, bishop, pawn/rook), so no single piece can be named.

795.chip: Hangs own piece via capture (often queen)
795.label: In every position the player makes a move—usually a material-grabbing capture—that leaves their own piece undefended and loses it to the refutation, most often the queen but not always.

798.label: In a winning king-and-pawn endgame, plays a premature/wrong-order pawn advance (often dissolving connected passers, allowing a blockade, or under-promoting) that throws away the win rather than hanging material.

794.label: In every position the mistake centers on the queen: the player repeatedly fails to make an available winning/equalizing queen exchange, and in about half the boards literally hangs their own queen — usually by playing a move in the wrong order or ignoring the trade so the queen is captured (Qxa4, Qxf5, Qxh4, Qxe5, Qxb7), while the other half passively keep queens on and squander a win; direction is split between self-inflicted hangs and missed trades, so review is warranted.

779.label: Plays a natural-looking developing move that ignores an opponent's tactical threat in the opening — usually a knight fork on f7/c7 — hanging a piece or the exchange (one board is instead a missed rook capture).

802.label: In all ten positions the player overlooked an available capture of the opponent's queen (usually the only move to avoid mate or save the game) and instead played a losing move.

801.label: In every position the player loses their own rook — usually leaving it en prise for a free capture (Bxh8, Bxe1, Bxa1, Bxe2, Bxf8), and otherwise trading it badly for a bishop — squandering a winning position.

789.label: Advances a knight to a central outpost (often d4) that the opponent simply trades off, collapsing the position — sometimes positionally, sometimes losing material.

796.label: A move (usually the king itself) exposes the king to a decisive attack, either walking into checkmate or getting checked/forked into losing material (often a rook).

777.label: A tactical move that loses the player's own material—the piece varies (knight, bishop, queen, or rook, often via pin or overload)—though about three of the ten positions are missed-win omissions rather than self-inflicted hangs.

800.label: In endgames the player picks a slow, materially-safe continuation while overlooking a faster forcing win (rook check, fork, or pawn break), though several flagged boards are actually 0cp non-blunders.

730.label: A move that overlooks the opponent's tactical refutation and loses the player's own material or winning advantage, with the piece lost varying (bishop, knight, queen, or pawn).

799.label: In a winning middlegame the player skips the single critical winning resource (very often a knight move like Nxd4/Nf5+), letting a won position slip to lost or drawn.

807.chip: Trades rooks into lost pawn endgame
807.label: The feature captures rook trades that liquidate into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame, where eliminating an enemy passed pawn by exchanging rooks removes the defender's only counterplay and lets an outside/connected pawn promote unstoppably.

804.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the king goes the wrong way, wasting a critical tempo and losing the passed-pawn promotion race rather than hanging any material.

813.label: A materially-safe developing or castling move is played in the opening, missing a forcing tactical shot (often a queen check like Qb4+, or a knight/queen fork) that wins material or a decisive advantage.

797.label: In the opening the player plays a slow developing or pawn-grabbing move instead of a forced winning tactical breakthrough — most often the e6 pawn break — letting a winning advantage drain to equality.

792.label: At critical pawn-endgame and promotion moments the player chooses the wrong move—losing a pawn race, hanging a freshly-promoted queen, or skipping the immediate promotion (boards 1-6)—while two boards instead miss the Bxg7 winning-exchange tactic, so the boards do not share one clean specific mistake.

790.label: In a losing rook endgame, plays a move (usually a misplaced rook) that fails to blockade or stop the opponent's passed pawn, allowing it to promote — though a few boards instead allow a mate or hang a rook.

805.label: The move ignores the forcing queen trade or queen capture the position demands, and is punished by hanging the player's own piece, allowing mate, or simply losing material.

806.chip: Missed winning capture in won endgame (often rook)
806.label: In a winning endgame the player advances a pawn or king toward promotion instead of making the simplest winning move (usually a free capture, frequently of a rook), throwing the win away.

809.label: In the d4-vs-e5 opening tension, Black plays an unrelated move instead of the forced ...exd4, allowing White to win the e5 pawn (sometimes escalating to a full piece) by Nxe5/dxe5 or a Bxf7+ shot.

814.label: A middlegame move that loses the player's own material to an immediate or short-term capture (the hung piece varies — queen, rook, or knight — so no single piece dominates), with a couple of boards instead just missing a material-winning capture.

812.chip: Quiet luft pawn move skips tactic
812.label: Plays a slow prophylactic pawn move (h3/g3/h4/g6) instead of the decisive move — usually missing a winning capture or forced mate, but in several boards failing to save its own attacked piece — with the material involved varying (rook/bishop/knight/pawn).

816.label: In the opening, the player captures a pawn with a knight (Nxe5 or Nxe4) that is then simply recaptured, hanging the knight for a pawn.

810.label: A middlegame material error — most often failing to capture a free/forking enemy piece, but sometimes hanging its own piece; the specific piece varies (bishop, knight, pawn) and a knight is usually somewhere in the tactic.

808.label: The player overlooks an undefended enemy bishop that could be captured for free, instead making a quiet move that lets the bishop escape to safety.

803.label: The player throws away a winning or drawing position with a hasty forcing move (often a check, wrong-move-order capture, or greedy grab) that usually hands back own material — most often the queen, but also rooks and passed pawns — though a few cases are pure missed wins.

815.chip: Trades active bishop for passive knight
815.label: Player captures a passive/undeveloped knight with their active bishop, an unfavorable trade that surrenders the superior minor piece (and occasionally drops material in the follow-up).

822.label: From an already-winning position the player makes a materially-safe but suboptimal move that throws away a forced mate or a decisive material gain, converting the win into a merely large advantage.

817.label: The player repeatedly squanders a winning advantage by choosing a slow or passive move instead of the decisive tactic/capture (mostly missed wins, though a couple of boards instead hang the player's own material), with no single piece consistent across positions.

827.label: Advances a (passed) pawn prematurely in an endgame instead of activating the king or choosing a sounder plan, squandering a winning or drawn position; two boards instead just hang a piece.

823.label: A materially-safe move that skips a winning material capture — almost always a queen capture (frequently of an undefended rook on d4) — turning a winning or holdable position into an inferior one.

820.chip: Abandons a defender (king or piece falls)
820.label: The move pulls a piece off its defensive role (or pushes a shielding pawn), after which the thing it was guarding collapses — about half the time a piece (usually a knight) hangs and half the time the king is exposed to a mating attack.

819.label: In endgames (often pawn/passed-pawn races) the player makes a losing move — most commonly marching the king the wrong direction so it can't escort or stop a passer — but the rest are a mixed bag (releasing pawn tension, hanging a knight/bishop, abandoning a hung knight), so there is no single clean piece or unified mechanism.

828.chip: Trades queen via capturing check, missing win
828.label: Player plays a queen capture-with-check that gets recaptured by the king, needlessly trading the queen for inferior material (rook/minor/pawn) and squandering a forced mate or winning attack.

832.label: In pawn/passed-pawn endgames the player makes a tempo or move-order slip in a promotion race (e.g. wrong king move or pawn push) without losing material, though several of the top boards are barely-suboptimal 0-1cp moves rather than real errors.

824.chip: Allows mating attack, neglects king defense (rook)
824.label: In already lost or difficult positions, the player (most often via a rook move) abandons a defensive duty and ignores the opponent's immediate threat, most frequently allowing a forced checkmate, though a few boards instead simply drop material.

821.label: Across all 10 boards the player skipped an available winning capture of an undefended enemy piece (most often a bishop, usually grabbed by the queen), playing a quiet or positional move instead.

826.label: A move that loses material—most boards hang the player's own piece by abandoning its defender or capturing with the wrong piece (bishop/knight/rook all appear), usually punished by the enemy queen, but several boards are instead missed winning captures, so the direction is genuinely mixed.

836.label: Plays a move that hangs the player's own material instead of taking the available simplifying queen trade that would neutralize the threat.

811.label: In the opening with the queen on d5 and Bg4 pinning Nf3, Black repeatedly skips the equalizing/material-winning 7...Bxf3 (or 6...Qxd4 / Qh5) in favor of a passive queen retreat, getting punished by 8.d5 advancing with tempo against the c6-knight (one board instead hangs the g4-bishop to hxg4).

829.chip: Hangs knight on the rim (pawn grab)
829.label: A piece—almost always a knight—wanders to a rim or corner square (often to snatch a pawn) where it gets trapped and lost over the next couple of moves, throwing away the player's advantage.

825.label: The player makes a greedy or loose move — usually a tempting capture or an aggressive knight sortie that pulls a defender away — which neglects their own king safety, allowing forced checkmate in about half the boards and hanging their own material in the rest.

837.chip: Missed winning capture in opening (knight captures)
837.label: In the opening the player repeatedly declines a free, material-winning knight capture (most often Nxe5 against an undefended piece/pawn) in favor of a quiet developing move, throwing away a winning advantage.

838.label: In passed-pawn and king-and-pawn endgames, the player makes an inferior king (occasionally knight) move that loses a tempo in the pawn race—failing to stop or escort the passer—rather than hanging any specific piece.

841.label: In every board a bishop is left on a square controlled by an enemy pawn (usually c5/f4/c4/b4/f5) and is captured for free in the opening — a self-inflicted hung bishop, even on boards 8 and 10 where the played move (O-O, Re8) ignores the already-attacked c5 bishop.

842.label: Moves a knight to an undefended square (g5/g4/h5/h4) in the opening where it is captured for free, almost always by the enemy queen.

839.label: In drawn/defensible endgames the player passively blockades or centralizes instead of playing the only saving active resource—usually a perpetual or defensive check (rook in ~9/10, queen once)—and loses; one board (Kd2) isn't actually a blunder, lowering consistency.

835.chip: Hangs own piece, skips winning capture (often a check)
835.label: In a winning position the player throws the game away by hanging their own piece — frequently with an unnecessary forcing check — instead of making the simple winning capture; the hung piece varies (rook/queen/bishop), so it's 'a piece', not one specific piece.

834.label: Voluntarily trades or gives up the active rook — the piece providing the winning counterplay — converting a winning/better position into a draw or loss (one board hangs the queen instead).

847.label: In nearly every position the player overlooks a free capture of a hanging enemy piece—almost always an undefended rook taken by the king—throwing away a winning material advantage.

846.label: Plays a premature, pointless queen check that—across all ten boards—drives the enemy king to safety while losing tempo, hanging the queen along a rank/diagonal, or skipping a forced win/mate.

845.label: An over-aggressive piece move (usually a rook, sometimes the queen) that chases or attacks an enemy piece while abandoning a critical defensive square or duty — sometimes hanging material over a few moves, sometimes just collapsing the position.

833.label: The feature mostly fires on premature pawn promotions (usually to a queen) that are immediately captured by a rook on the open file, throwing away a winning endgame when an intermediate check (zwischenzug) was needed first — though a few boards instead show a hasty check/capture that trades away a forced mate, and one board isn't a blunder at all.

852.label: The player delivers a check with the queen onto a square defended by an enemy piece (almost always a bishop), and the queen is simply captured next move.

831.label: A move that fatally weakens or exposes the player's own king, allowing the opponent a forcing series of checks (usually forced mate) instead of keeping the king safe or holding the initiative.

850.chip: Hangs a piece or misses win
850.label: Each position is a single blunder that flips the evaluation, but the feature is mixed: roughly half the moves hang the player's own material (most often the queen, though rook/bishop/pawn also occur) and roughly half are omissions that skip a forced win or mate, so neither the direction nor the piece is consistent enough to name precisely.

853.label: A rook move that abandons a defensive duty and lets the player's own material fall (or exposes the king to mate), with the specific hung piece varying across boards (queen, rook, bishop, knight) — plus a few cases that are pure missed tactics.

848.label: The player grabs material with a capture but overlooks the tactical refutation, hanging their own material — often allowing a recapture with check or even mate — and squandering the position.

840.label: A blunder that converts a drawn-or-winning position into a loss — often a careless king move — but the specific error varies across boards (hanging a rook to a fork, hanging a bishop, a greedy pawn-grab losing the exchange, two outright missed wins, and lost endgame/positional technique), so no single piece or single direction (hang vs. miss) can be honestly named.

854.chip: Missed forcing win, grabbed material (exposed king)
854.label: Across all 10 boards the player skips a forcing checkmate or king-hunting attack against an exposed king, instead playing a slower/greedy material grab (frequently snatching a rook in the corner with the queen).

849.chip: Hangs piece via wrong capture order
849.label: The recurring mistake is a move-order error—grabbing a piece (usually with a pawn) before inserting the necessary intermezzo (typically trading bishops first), which leaves the player's own piece hanging; in ~8/10 boards this self-inflicts material loss, with the hung piece most often a bishop but occasionally a knight, while 2 boards are merely missed wins reaching equality.

861.chip: Wrong king move in endgame (loses tempo)
861.label: In king-and-pawn (and a few piece) endgames the player marches the king to the wrong square, conceding a critical tempo or key promotion square — though several flagged moves are actually negligible/optimal and one walks the king into a skewer that drops a bishop.

859.label: The player repeatedly fires off an inferior queen check (always queen, always check) that lets the king escape into safety or perpetual, missing the stronger move — often a forced mate or winning sequence — that the position demanded.

855.label: The queen leaves a critical defensive duty—most often guarding the king, sometimes a hanging piece or key pawn—to chase offense, allowing a decisive attack or material loss.

844.label: In a winning or equal opening, the player passes up a clearly stronger move — most often a winning queen capture or even mate — either purely missing the win (≈6/10) or, in the rest, allowing their own piece (queen or knight) to fall to the refutation; the piece moved and the piece lost both vary, so no specific piece can be named.

856.label: In the opening, plays an unsound sacrifice or 'tempo-loss' move that drops the player's own material — bishop, queen, or pawn varies (often via an early queen sortie or f2/f7 theme) — though two of the ten boards instead miss a winning tactic.

860.label: Played a quiet, non-forcing move and skipped the available decisive forcing continuation — almost always a queen check that delivered mate or won material — squandering a winning position.

843.label: In the opening the player declines to recapture a sacrificed/hanging bishop with the king (almost always Kxf7), letting the opponent retreat the piece and squandering a free win.

830.chip: Hangs a piece (pawn attacks enemy piece)
830.label: A quiet pawn push—usually one attacking an enemy piece—that hangs the player's own material (knight, bishop, rook or pawn varies) or, in a few boards, simply misses a forced winning tactic/mate.

858.label: Plays a slow, purposeless move (king shuffle or quiet pawn move) instead of the time-critical push of a passed pawn, wasting the one tempo needed and letting the pawn be blockaded — turning a winning or drawn position into a lost one.

864.label: A king move to an exposed square (or, in 2/10, a pawn push that strips the king's shield) walks the player's own king into a decisive check sequence — perpetual check that throws away a win, outright mate, or checks that win material.

869.chip: Wrong king square in pawn endgame
869.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player misplaces the king (loses the opposition or fails to occupy the pawn's promotion/blockade square), though roughly half the flagged king moves are actually 0cp non-blunders, so the feature is fuzzy and needs review.

870.chip: Missed capturing free hanging piece (opening pawn-grab)
870.label: In every one of the 10 opening positions the player declined a simple pawn capture of an undefended enemy piece (a knight in 8, a bishop in 2), giving it a tempo to escape and converting a winning material advantage into equality.

862.label: A greedy material capture or careless king move exposes the player's own king and allows a forced mate or decisive king attack (frequently a back-rank or promotion-check mate).

863.label: The player repeatedly chooses a simplifying capture or queen/piece trade and squanders a winning position—about six boards are material-safe moves that miss a stronger winning tactic (missed win), while the other four are self-inflicted captures/moves that hang the player's own material, so the direction is genuinely mixed and the hung/missed piece varies (queen, rook, bishop).

867.chip: Gives up queen unfavorably (sac or trade)
867.label: A queen move that unfavorably surrenders the queen — in 6/10 cases an unsound sacrifice/check that simply hangs it (e.g. Qh7+ Nxh7, Qh2+ Kxh2), and in 4/10 a premature queen trade that throws away a winning advantage; the piece given up is always the queen, but the direction splits between outright hang and bad trade.

873.label: In a won endgame the player throws a tempo-losing, usually pointless check (most often with the queen) that lets the opponent's king escape or counterplay arrive, reducing or squandering a decisive/forced-mate advantage instead of the precise consolidating move.

871.label: Plays a counterproductive check (almost always a rook check) that loses a tempo, lets the opponent's king improve to a safer/more active square, and squanders the player's winning or better position — occasionally hanging the checking piece outright.

865.label: In the opening the player botches a capture decision (knight usually the focal piece): most often it declines a free hanging enemy piece, but in ~4/10 it instead develops into a self-hang — direction is genuinely mixed, so flag for review.

851.label: In a winning or mating endgame the player throws the result away with an inferior king/queen move — often outright hanging the queen, but sometimes only missing the fastest win — with a queen central to every position.

875.label: A move that loses the player's own material—usually by stripping away a key defender or walking into a tactic/king attack—where the hung unit varies across boards (pawn, bishop, knight, rook, even the queen), so no single piece can be honestly named.

868.label: In nearly every position the player loses the queen—in 7/10 boards by leaving it en prise on a square attacked by an enemy rook, knight, or queen (e.g. Qd7→Rxd7, Qd4+→Nxd4, exf5→Rxe7, Qe3→Rxe3+), and in the other 3 by voluntarily trading queens in a way that drops material or throws away a won position—collapsing the evaluation; the queen is the invariant piece, but the hang-vs-bad-trade split warrants review.

866.label: Plays a move that loses material—usually self-inflicted, dropping its own piece within the refutation (knight frequently in the mix), with the specific hung piece varying and a couple of cases being missed winning tactics instead.

884.label: The queen greedily captures a piece that is defended (often capturing a rook), and is immediately recaptured—frequently with check or mate—losing the queen for inadequate material.

877.label: The move directly drops the player's own material — leaving a piece (most often a rook, but also bishop or knight) en prise for a free capture, frequently via a pointless 'spite' check or greedy grab that ignores the hanging unit.

882.label: A tempo move meant to attack/chase the opponent's queen instead leaves the player's own piece (queen, rook, or knight — it varies) hanging and lost by force.

881.label: A move that abandons a defensive duty or steps onto an attacked square, losing the player's own material (the specific piece varies — pawns, rook, bishop, or knight) over the next one-to-three moves.

878.label: In every position the player passed up a clearly winning capture (most often of a bishop) in favor of a quiet, retreating, or wrong-move-order move that squandered the material/advantage.

879.chip: Trades off knight into lost endgame
879.label: Liquidates the knight—the only active/defensive piece, often for just a pawn—turning a drawn or defensible position into a lost pawn or rook endgame.

883.label: A move (frequently a king move) that exposes the player's own king to a decisive attack — checks leading to a skewer, fork, or mating net that wins material or forces mate; the exact piece lost varies (queen in some, mate in others), so the invariant is king exposure rather than one specific hung piece.

876.label: In winning endgames the player fails to convert—either hanging its own queen or missing a forced winning capture/mate—with a queen central to most tactics, though 3 of 10 boards are not even mistakes and the direction is split.

880.label: The player squanders a won position—frequently a forced checkmate—by choosing a slow, natural rook maneuver (doubling rooks on an open file or a rook lift) instead of the decisive forcing move, and in a couple of cases the slow rook move even hangs a piece.

888.label: A self-inflicted check — almost always a knight check (Ng4+/Ng5+/Nxe5+) — that loses the player's own material, since the opponent calmly captures the checking piece (or wins material in the short refutation) rather than fearing the check.

889.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material—most boards hang a piece outright (knight, queen, or bishop) or grab a pawn greedily and drop more, but the hung piece type varies and a few positions are really positional/missed-win errors rather than clean hangs, so it can't be pinned to one piece.

874.label: In all 10 positions the player ignored a hanging or dangerous enemy rook (the clear best move was always to capture it — Rxf2, Qxg7, Nxe7, Qxe2, Qxc3, Nxe6, Nxg2, etc.) and instead made a lesser capture or pawn grab, squandering the win or inviting a losing counterattack.

857.label: A middlegame move that throws away a winning or equal position — about half the boards self-inflict material/king loss (Bh4, g7-bishop, c7/e3 pawns, mate-in-2) while the other half are clean missed wins (the Qxd1+/Nf2+ fork twice, Qh6 mate threat, free Rxd4), with no single consistent direction or piece, so the only reliable core is 'queen/piece moves to a bad square and squanders the edge.'

872.label: In a winning/forcing position the player chooses an inferior move — frequently a premature check or a move-order/tempo error — that hands the opponent a defensive resource, throwing away a much larger win, a forced mate, or letting own material fall (the squandered/hung piece varies: pawn, bishop, rook/exchange), so no single piece can be named and the direction is mixed between missed-win and self-inflicted loss.

886.label: The player squanders a winning or defensible position by playing a quiet, natural-looking move instead of the available forcing move (in ~8/10 boards a check that wins material, forces a won trade, or mates), often then allowing a decisive counterattack against its own king.

887.label: From a winning opening the player skips a decisive tactic—almost always a knight blow like Nxg6 (or Nxb3/Ng3+)—and the advantage collapses, though in several boards the played move actually lets a piece (knight or queen) hang, so the missed-win vs hung-own direction is mixed.

885.label: A move—often a capture, pawn-grab, or king centralization—that overlooks a tactical refutation and usually hangs the player's own material (hung piece varies: knight, queen, or walking into mate), though ~3/10 are instead missed winning captures, so the direction/piece is fuzzy and needs review.

895.label: Across all ten boards the player throws away a winning position by playing a slow/passive move (or a careless trade) instead of the forcing line that removes the blockader and pushes the passed pawn to promotion.

893.label: Throws away a winning or favorable position by choosing an inferior continuation — most often a wrong/needless trade or a missed stronger tactic, occasionally an outright greedy capture that hangs material.

891.label: In most positions the player shuns or fumbles a queen exchange that was the engine's best move, instead playing an active (often queen) move that hangs material or squanders the advantage; the specific material lost varies (pawn, knight, or none), so the true invariant is the missed queen trade rather than any one hung piece.

892.label: Plays a forcing check that captures a rook with the queen, but the queen is immediately recaptured, trading queen for rook and throwing away the game.

894.label: In a winning or transitional position the player plays a move—often a king step-off or a greedy capture—that leaves a piece (usually but not always the queen) undefended or walks into a knight fork and loses it, though a couple of the boards are actually missed wins rather than hangs.

903.label: Recaptures/trades a rook to 'simplify,' removing the last back-rank defender and walking straight into a forced back-rank checkmate (one board instead loses to passed pawns after the same first-rank capture).

899.label: The rook captures a single pawn on a defended square and is immediately recaptured, throwing away the rook (usually a full exchange) for just a pawn.

901.label: In the opening, the player hangs an unprotected piece — most often the queen, but a bishop in several cases — by making a developing/supporting move that ignores an existing attack or steps onto an attacked square.

897.label: In nearly every board the player advances a KNIGHT to attempt a fork/attack, but it abandons a key defensive or blocking role and is refuted — most lines lose the player's own material (bishop or knight) while several instead allow a forced mating attack, so the punished outcome is mixed (hung piece vs. mate) and no single hung piece dominates.

900.chip: Losing king move in passed-pawn endgame
900.label: In endgames dominated by a passed pawn, the player (usually with a king move) mishandles the situation and worsens an already-losing position — variously hanging a rook/knight, letting a pawn promote, or missing the only saving/winning path — so the unifying error is a losing endgame king move rather than one specific hung piece.

905.label: A move that loses the player's own material — most often hanging a piece (knight in 3, bishop in 2, a pawn in 1), but mixed with several tempo-loss/missed-win omissions, and the hung piece varies too much to name one.

906.label: A move that abandons a defensive duty or exposes the king and lets the opponent win the player's own material — but the hung unit varies (rook, knight, or pawn), so no single piece can be named.

902.label: In an endgame the player makes a self-inflicted, losing major-piece move that either hangs the piece outright (≈6/10, rook or queen) or trades into a lost king-and-pawn endgame (≈4/10), turning a drawn/holdable position into a loss.

896.label: An opening move — often a flank pawn poking an enemy bishop while ignoring central tension — that hangs the player's own material via a short tactic (the specific piece lost varies, so it's 'a piece', not one consistent piece).

907.label: From a clearly winning position the player blunders the advantage—usually by missing the single forcing/winning continuation (often a passed-pawn breakthrough in the endgame), sometimes instead by hanging own material—turning a win into a loss.

910.label: A queen check in the endgame that backfires—most often forcing a queen trade into a lost pawn endgame, but in other boards merely wasting tempo to help the enemy king or outright hanging the queen.

904.label: Plays a material-grabbing capture that removes a critical defender (or ignores a stronger in-between threat), collapsing the player's own position within a few moves.

909.label: The player makes a capture (9/10) that removes a key defender or opens a line, exposing own material or the king to a decisive tactic — but several boards are already lost positions where the move is near-best, so the core mistake is not cleanly uniform.

890.label: A faulty forcing move—frequently a tempting check—that throws away a winning position, in roughly half the cases by missing a forced win/mate and in the rest by hanging a piece (queen or rook), so no single piece or pure direction holds.

908.chip: Hangs a piece in winning position
908.label: A move that leaves the player's own piece (rook, bishop, knight or even queen) en prise, throwing away a winning position; the specific piece varies across boards, so no single piece is named.

913.label: A slow, passive, or 'tempo-wasting' move that ignores a live tactical threat and lets the player's own material fall — usually self-inflicted, though the hung unit varies (queen, knight, or pawn) and a couple of boards are instead a missed capture or an allowed mate.

918.label: The player repeatedly skips a forcing tactical win — usually a queen check delivering mate or winning material against an exposed king — in favor of a quieter, non-forcing move.

920.label: In all ten positions the player skipped a free capture of the opponent's hanging queen (most often with Nxd4/Nxd5-type knight grabs), playing a quiet developing move and throwing away a winning advantage.

915.label: Prematurely advances a passed pawn instead of activating the king/pieces first, letting the pawn be blockaded or captured and throwing away a winning or drawing advantage.

924.label: Develops a bishop to g4/g5 in the opening where it is completely undefended and simply captured for free by the opposing queen, losing a full piece.

919.label: In a winning endgame the player repeatedly overlooks the decisive forcing continuation (a forced mate or material-winning tactic) and plays a passive/greedy move that lets the win slip to a draw or even a loss.

914.label: A positionally poor move—usually a passive or misplaced rook—that converts a drawn/holdable (often endgame) position into a loss, in some boards by directly hanging or trading the rook into a lost pawn endgame.

912.label: From a winning/won position the player fails to play the decisive move (frequently a free capture of the enemy queen, or a forced mate), either missing the win outright (boards 1,2,6,7,9) or playing a move that hangs their own piece — usually a rook (boards 3,5,8,10) or queen (board 4) — so the recurring core is 'throws away the win', but the direction (omission vs self-inflicted hang) and the piece involved both vary, hence low confidence.

898.chip: Abandons key pawn, blows won endgame
898.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a king or capture move that abandons a strategically critical pawn or square, squandering a winning (or drawn) position.

916.label: In passed-pawn endgames, plays an imprecise move that loses the promotion race—failing to advance or support its own passer (or to stop/clear the blockader of the opponent's) when one exact move was required.

917.label: A self-inflicted move—often a structure-weakening f-pawn push or an undefended developed piece—that loses the player's own material, but the unit lost (rook, bishop, knight, or pawn) varies too much to name one.

921.label: A materially-safe move that squanders a winning or drawn position by missing the forcing material-winning continuation, almost always in the opening, with the winning target varying (bishop, knight, pawn) and one outlier that actually hangs its own piece.

928.label: A materially-safe but passive move that overlooks an available winning tactical shot (often a knight capture/fork), forfeiting a clear material advantage — an omission, not a hang.

931.label: In endgame pawn races the player mishandles the opponent's passed pawn — walking the king into promotion-with-check, failing to capture/blockade the runner, or trading off the only defender — letting it promote.

925.label: An opening bishop sortie to g4 or g5 that loses material — most often the bishop itself is won after a defender is deflected (Nxf6+) or a pawn (f3/f6) kicks it, though a couple of cases are pure tempo loss or a missed Ng5 win.

932.chip: Missed faster win in endgame (king move)
932.label: In winning endgames the player makes a king (or slow) move that squanders a forced mate or promotion instead of converting cleanly, keeping the position won but throwing away the fastest/forced win.

923.label: From a winning position the player misses a forcing knight capture on the c-file (Nxc6/Nxc3) that wins material, instead playing a slow or wrong-move-order move that squanders the advantage.

929.label: An opening move that loses the player's own material — usually a hung minor piece (knight or bishop) — frequently by ignoring an f3-knight/Bg4 pin tension (Bxf3 was best), though ~4 of the 10 boards instead crack king safety/structure rather than drop material outright, so the piece and even the core direction are not clean.

933.label: A greedy/distracting capture (usually a pawn grab) abandons a defensive duty and lets the player's own piece fall, turning a winning or holdable middlegame into a loss; the hung piece varies (queen, rook, bishop, knight).

922.label: An active-looking move that collapses a good or equal position into a losing one—most often by hanging the player's own material (rook or queen) or walking into a tactic, though several boards are instead positional weakenings or a missed win, so the hung piece is not consistent.

926.chip: Hangs queen, throwing away forced mate
926.label: In every position the player gives up their strongest piece to a simple king recapture (Kx... on all 10 boards)—queen in 8, rook in 2—abandoning an available forced mate/win and converting it into a 'merely winning' position; queen is the typical piece (~80%) so the rook cases warrant a human glance.

934.label: A self-inflicted opening blunder that loses the player's own material to a forcing capture/recapture sequence (the specific piece varies — knight, bishop or queen — with a pinned f3-knight recurring in several lines).

935.label: In a winning opening, the player makes a safe-looking retreat or developing move instead of capturing the undefended enemy knight on h5/h4 with the queen (8/10), squandering a free piece — with two boards instead missing a Bxf7+ tactic.

936.label: Across all ten boards the player passes up the elementary h-pawn capture (almost always hxg4) that wins a hanging enemy bishop on g4, instead playing a quiet developing or pawn move and squandering a winning material advantage.

939.label: The move loses the player's own material by overlooking a tactic (recapture/fork/discovered attack), but the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, queen) and 2-3 boards are instead missed wins or losing trades, so a human should review.

927.label: In the opening, the player ignores an enemy pawn attacking one of their minor pieces and plays another move (often a pawn push), leaving the piece to be captured for free.

911.label: A capture or aggressive move that throws away a winning/near-winning position — most often by leaving the player's own piece hanging (frequently the queen), but in several boards instead by missing a free piece or a forced mate; direction and hung piece both vary, so review is needed.

945.label: In a won position the player passes up an available forced checkmate (usually mate-in-1 or mate-in-2) by making an irrelevant pawn push or prophylactic king move, though two of the ten boards are instead self-inflicted material hangs (e7 dropping the queen, Rc1 allowing Bxb4+).

947.label: In every position the player overlooked a forced checkmate-in-one delivered by a queen capture (most often Qxg2#) and played an irrelevant move instead, throwing away the immediate win.

942.chip: Hangs material on bishop sortie (vs queen)
942.label: A bishop is developed to harass the enemy queen with false tempo in the opening, usually hanging the player's own material (a pawn or the bishop itself via a Nxf6+ deflection), though in a few cases it merely misses a stronger move.

938.chip: Hangs a piece grabbing a pawn
938.label: The played move is a capture—frequently grabbing a passed pawn or trading off a defender—that backfires in the middlegame and self-inflicts loss of material (most often a rook or the exchange via a recapture/opened file, occasionally walking into mate).

937.label: A move that neglects the king's defense — often abandoning a critical square near the king (f7 recurs) — allowing the opponent a decisive attack, frequently forced checkmate.

941.label: Each move directly hangs the player's own material with no compensation (mostly a full piece, occasionally a pawn), but the lost unit varies across boards — knight, bishop, rook, and pawn — so the invariant is self-inflicted material loss rather than any one specific piece.

940.label: In nearly every position the player fails to play the tempo-gaining knight jump to the d5/d4 central outpost (often setting up the Nxc7 fork), instead choosing a passive/wrong move that squanders the advantage or invites the opponent's own Nd5.

943.chip: Squanders advantage with passive move (forcing queen trade skipped)
943.label: The player throws away a winning or equal position by choosing a slow, non-forcing move instead of an available forcing capture/trade (frequently a queen trade), with outcomes split between hanging own material and simply missing a win.

953.label: In a winning position the player skips a forced mate or material-winning tactic, instead playing a slow/tempo move (frequently just chasing the enemy queen).

952.label: The played move self-inflicts material loss by leaving the player's own piece en prise (most often the queen, sometimes a rook traded/given into a lost position) for immediate capture.

948.label: A self-inflicted move that drops the player's own material—most often the queen, but sometimes a rook/exchange—to a tactical refutation that frequently arrives via an intermezzo or discovered check.

944.label: A greedy material grab or careless move that hangs the player's own piece — varying between rook (≈6/10) and queen (≈4/10) — to an immediate recapture or short tactic, turning a worse position into a lost one.

954.label: Captures material (most often snapping off the opponent's queen) instead of playing the available forced checkmate or stronger winning tactic.

950.chip: Misses the winning move (often a fork)
950.label: Repeatedly fails to play the precise winning continuation — frequently a knight/bishop fork — squandering a winning or clearly better position by choosing a passive or greedy alternative instead.

930.label: Player repeatedly declines the engine's Bxb2/Bxb7 capture of the undefended b-pawn on the fianchetto long diagonal, missing a free pawn — though in several boards the chosen move also hangs the player's own material.

949.label: In a winning opening position the player plays a quiet developing or retreating move and overlooks a decisive queen move — almost always a check or capture (Qxe5+, Qh5+, Qxd4+, Qa4+, Qxf7#) — throwing away the win and drifting to equality.

962.label: A queen move that offers or allows a queen exchange, liquidating the player's most powerful attacking asset and converting a winning or holding position into equality or loss.

951.label: Plays a tempo-wasting move—frequently a pointless check—instead of the forcing capture that wins or holds material, throwing away the advantage.

946.label: A knight move—usually retreating or recentralizing the attacked knight instead of the correct central break (often ...d5)—that loses material or throws away the advantage in the opening; the knight is the acting piece but only ~2/10 actually hang it outright.

957.label: Plays a materially-safe move that overlooks a tactic (Rb1/Ra1/Bc3/Rb8/c6-type) which traps or wins the opponent's exposed queen, letting it escape and squandering a winning advantage.

963.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player plays a slow king move instead of the decisive pawn break (often ...f5 or e5), missing the win or the only draw — though several of the boards are actually non-blunders.

965.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly passes up a winning free capture of the opponent's undefended (usually fianchetto-flank) bishop on h6/h3, playing a routine developing/castling move instead of grabbing the hanging piece.

960.label: In a winning passed-pawn endgame, the player advances a pawn (or makes a slow move) instead of capturing the lone enemy piece blockading/stopping promotion, throwing away the win.

961.label: A move that pulls a piece off its critical defensive duty (or the king's safe square), self-inflicting either a lost piece/pawn or a forced mate, usually in an already-losing position.

967.label: The player makes a materially-safe queen move (often a check) that squanders an available forced mate or material win, missing a more forcing line — typically with another piece (rook/bishop/knight) — that was clearly winning.

964.label: A move that walks into the opponent's immediate refutation (usually a queen check, pin, or trap), self-inflicting loss of material or even checkmate; because the hung material ranges from queen to bishop to exchange to outright mate (and one board is a missed win), no single piece can be honestly named.

955.label: The player skips a material-saving exchange — almost always a defensive queen trade (Qxc6/Qxe6/Qxd6/Qxf6/Qxe7/Qxe3, etc., with two rook-trades) — and the move played instead hangs a piece or invites a decisive attack.

959.label: An irrelevant or mis-placed move that leaves the player's own piece hanging in a middlegame tactic — the hung piece is most often a rook but varies (bishop, queen, knight), and the move also frequently skips a winning capture, so the core invariant is self-inflicted material loss rather than any one specific piece.

956.label: A move that collapses a winning/holdable position — in the opening by grabbing a piece (dxe7) but hanging the queen to Bxf2+, and in the endgame by mishandling the king/pawns so the opponent's passed pawn promotes — but the mechanism and piece vary too much to name one specific thing hung.

969.label: In a winning or drawn endgame, plays a careless move (often a reflexive check) that leaves the rook en prise, hanging it and converting the result to a lost king-and-pawn ending.

973.label: The feature fires on rook moves—usually an early 'rook lift' to the 3rd or 6th rank—that leave the rook undefended on an exposed square, where it is simply captured (typically by a bishop) for the loss of the exchange.

978.label: In all ten middlegame positions the player makes a safe but passive move and overlooks a winning knight fork (usually Ne2+/Nd6+/Nb6+) that would win the enemy queen — a clear omission, not a self-hang.

972.label: In nearly every position the player skips a simple, available capture of a hanging enemy piece (or a winning pawn break) that wins material, instead playing a materially-safe but non-winning move.

970.label: Player chooses a slow, greedy, or 'natural' move that overlooks a decisive forcing resource — most often a checkmate in one (5/10) or an allowed/defendable mate (2 more) — while the remaining boards instead miss a winning/drawing resource in passed-pawn endgames.

975.label: A move that fatally compromises the player's own king safety—most often castling directly into a prepared attack, but also pawn pushes/captures that strip the king's shield—exposing the king to a decisive assault or forced mate.

968.chip: Weakening pawn push in lost endgame
968.label: In an already-losing endgame the player makes a pawn advance or capture that either concedes the pawn or wrecks their own structure, hastening the loss rather than holding the line.

974.label: The player makes a capturing exchange (usually a rook, frequently with check) that simplifies the position and throws away a forced mate or winning tactic that a more precise non-trading move would have delivered.

966.label: In a clearly winning or much-better position the player blunders it all away — most often by missing a decisive capture/continuation (boards 1,3,5,6,8,10) or, in a sizeable minority, by an active move that hangs own material into a mating net (boards 2,4,7,9, frequently while greedily grabbing a 'dangerous' pawn) — so the direction is genuinely mixed (missed-win vs self-inflicted hang) and the piece involved varies (rook/bishop/knight/queen), warranting review.

971.label: From a winning or clearly better position—usually an attack on the enemy king—the player picks a slow, greedy, or move-order-flawed move that throws away the win, letting the opponent defend, escape, or counterattack (a couple of cases instead simply hang own material).

979.label: A move that loses the player's own material — most often a piece or pawn the opponent simply captures after an over-eager attacking/developing move — though the hung unit varies (bishop, queen, knight, pawn) and two boards are tempo/missed-tactic rather than clean hangs.

977.chip: Missed winning move in endgame (often promotion)
977.label: In endgames with a clearly decisive resource available—an immediate promotion, a free capture, or a forcing queen trade—the player chooses a materially-safe but passive move and throws away the win.

983.label: Voluntarily exchanges rooks (Rx-) into a lost or drawn endgame—usually a king-and-pawn endgame—surrendering the rook's active counterplay, while a non-trading rook move was best.

985.label: Plays a slow or preparatory move instead of the critical pawn capture that resolves the pawn tension (central, queenside, or kingside), letting the opponent break favorably on their own terms and squandering the advantage.

988.label: A materially-safe slow developing move (often Nbd2) that skips the forcing central pawn break — usually d4 — which would exploit the opponent's uncastled king to win material in the opening.

984.chip: Misjudged trade into lost pawn endgame
984.label: In an endgame, the player captures/trades or pushes a pawn into a simplified king-and-pawn (or knight) endgame that is actually lost or drawn, misjudging the resulting position.

989.label: Instead of a decisive centralizing knight move (often Nd5/Nxb5) that wins material or the initiative, the player chose a slow, passive, or preparatory move and forfeited the win.

976.label: Across its top positions the played move skips an available capture of the opponent's rook—typically winning the exchange (Nxe7/Bxd6/etc.)—leaving the decisive material-winning (or in 7-8, position-saving) capture on the board.

981.label: A move that exposes or stops defending its own material, hanging a piece (most often a bishop) and flipping a playable position to losing — though several boards are instead pure tempo/positional squanders or a missed mate.

986.label: In winning or must-hold endgames (often passed-pawn positions), the player squanders the result by playing an inferior move — frequently a premature check or passive king move — instead of the one precise decisive continuation.

991.label: Plays a developing or repositioning move that fails to resolve the central pawn tension, allowing the opponent's pawn break to win material or seize a decisive positional advantage.

997.label: In the opening the player loses their own bishop, either leaving an attacked bishop en prise (often to b4xc5 / d5xc4 / e5xf4) or sacrificing it unsoundly.

992.label: The player consistently chose a quiet, non-forcing move and missed a forcing tactical check (often the Nd3+ knight fork, sometimes a bishop sacrifice like Bxh2+) that would have won material or saved the position.

994.label: In a winning endgame, the player wrecks the conversion — usually promoting or pushing a pawn prematurely (so the new queen or pawn is captured) or skipping a free capture — turning a win into a draw.

1000.label: The move overlooks a forced checkmate (mate-in-one in 9/10 boards, the lone outlier being a winning-but-imprecise move), with the missed mate delivered by a rook in every mating case.

995.chip: Ignores lethal threat (hangs queen or allows mate)
995.label: The player makes a move that disregards the opponent's immediate decisive threat, either walking into forced checkmate (boards 1,2,4,9) or leaving the queen en prise to be captured (boards 3,5,6,7,10), with one board losing material via an opened diagonal — a self-inflicted catastrophe whose victim varies between mate and the queen, so the specific piece can't be confidently named.

993.label: The move neglects the critical passed pawn — failing to blockade, eliminate, or out-race it (or to create a counter-passer) — letting the opponent's pawn become unstoppable and queen.

1002.label: In every position there was a free, undefended enemy piece (knight, rook, or queen) available to capture, and the player instead played a non-capturing move (often a king step), squandering a winning advantage by overlooking the simple grab.

980.label: Plays a slow, non-forcing move that squanders a winning or better position instead of the stronger/forcing continuation; the piece involved varies and a few cases worsen into allowing a tactic or mate.

996.label: Prematurely captures with a central pawn, releasing the central tension and opening lines/diagonals that the opponent exploits—usually to win the player's own material over the next moves.

982.chip: Gives up a piece, loses advantage
982.label: Across the top-10 the player repeatedly converts a winning or good position into an equal/losing one by surrendering a piece — sometimes hanging it outright (boards 5,6,8,9), sometimes trading off a strong/active piece or grabbing material into a refutation (boards 1,2,3,4,7,10); the mechanism and the piece both vary (a knight is most often the piece, ~6/10, but bishop and rook also appear), so it is honest only to say 'a piece' and the direction is mixed between self-inflicted hangs and missed/blundered exchanges.

999.chip: Bad trade surrenders dominant piece (knight often)
999.label: The move voluntarily trades or captures with a strong, well-placed piece (most often a dominant/blockading knight) into an inferior position—giving up control of passed pawns, an attack, or a winning endgame—rather than truly hanging material outright, though a couple of boards instead hang a piece/pawn directly.

1004.label: The move self-inflicts material loss—most often the queen falls to an unblocked attack on an open diagonal (boards 1,2,3,4,6,9), but the hung piece varies (bishop, knight) and two boards are king-safety collapses, so the specific piece can't be pinned to ~8/10.

998.label: In the opening the player mishandles the central pawn tension — failing to play the freeing/correct break (usually ...d5) and instead retreating, developing passively, or grabbing on the wrong square — letting the opponent resolve the center favorably and, in most cases, win material over 2-3 moves (hung piece varies: pawn, bishop, or knight).

1007.chip: Hangs piece to pawn-fork recapture (knight capture)
1007.label: The player captures a centralized piece with a knight, but the pawn recapture creates a fork that wins back material and nets the loss of one of their own pieces.

990.label: In an endgame the player captures a pawn (often a passed pawn) with a rook or queen, but the recapture wins back the piece and throws away the winning/drawn result.

1009.label: In the opening the player plays a safe/materialistic move (usually a knight) and misses the crushing queen check Qh4+/Qh5+ that exploits the enemy's exposed king, often a forced mate.

1013.label: Captures with the bishop in a premature exchange (almost always BxN on f3/f6) that releases the tension, surrenders the bishop pair/active piece, and activates the opponent's recapturing bishop on the long diagonal, squandering the advantage.

1005.label: Instead of the available queen trade/capture, the player retreats the queen (occasionally a bishop), abandoning a defender and hanging material — usually a pawn, but sometimes a knight or rook.

1011.label: In every position the player overlooks a free capture of the opponent's en-prise piece — a rook in 9 of 10 boards — and instead plays a non-capturing move (most often a king move), letting the material escape.

1006.label: The player makes a move—often a greedy pawn grab or wrong capture—that self-inflicts material loss by hanging one of their own pieces (queen, bishop, or knight varies), mostly in the middlegame, though two cases are instead missed bigger captures.

1010.label: A queen relocation/centralization that loses the player's own material—often the queen gets trapped or won over a couple of moves, sometimes abandoning a defended knight or pawn (hung piece varies, so not a specific piece).

1015.label: Reflexively plays a purposeless pawn check that loses tempo and worsens the position — improving the enemy king, fixing/weakening the pawn structure, or even giving away material — instead of the quiet best move.

1008.label: In every position the player chose a quiet/passive move (often a king step) instead of an available forcing best move — a capture, check, or promotion — that would have won or saved the game, making this a pure omission rather than a self-inflicted hang (material safe 100%, own piece hung 0%).

1003.chip: Allows forced mate on own king
