1003.label: A king-safety blunder—either walking the king into the open or pulling a defender away from the king zone—that abandons the only saving resource and allows a forced checkmate.

1001.label: Captures a (usually poisoned) piece next to its own king — most often gxh6 — ripping open the king's pawn shield and allowing a decisive queen attack (frequently Qxh6) or mate.

1014.label: In losing endgames, the player skips an available capture—usually a king recapture of a hanging rook or a dangerous passed pawn—and plays an idle king move or pawn push instead.

1016.label: Plays a quiet/developing move instead of a forcing check that wins material or mates by exploiting the opponent's exposed or uncastled king (two boards instead self-hang material).

1022.label: A materially-safe but passive move (bishop retreat, rook shuffle, or rim knight) that skips a winning central knight capture (Nxd4/Nxd5/Nxe5/Nxe4) — an omission, not a hang.

1020.chip: Hangs piece via wrong capture order
1020.label: The player grabs a capture (often a flashy check or fork) in the wrong move-order, ignoring a more urgent threat and hanging their own material — usually the queen or the exchange via the opponent's counter-capture.

1018.label: The player makes a self-inflicting move — either retreating a knight that was shielding the e-file or stepping the king onto an open line — that allows a devastating discovered check and hangs material (most often the queen).

1021.chip: Misses the only good move, squanders edge
1021.label: The player throws away a winning or equal position by choosing a plausible but inaccurate move instead of the single precise good move available; the pieces involved vary (rook, knight, queen, bishop, pawn) and a few cases (Nxh5+ twice, Rb5) actually hang material rather than merely omitting a win, so the feature is mixed and worth review.

987.chip: Ignores threat, allowing mate or material loss
987.label: The player makes a non-defensive move (most often a passive king walk, but also a queen redeploy/capture or pawn push) that fails to address the opponent's decisive threat, resulting in either immediate checkmate (~5/10) or the loss of a piece/material (~5/10) — the hung piece and the disaster type both vary, so no single piece can be named.

1019.label: The player throws away a winning advantage by making a premature, unfavorable trade — usually capturing with/exchanging off a strong active bishop for a passive enemy piece (releasing tension or opening lines) instead of a stronger advancing/developing move.

1012.label: The player moves the king (9/10) to a natural-looking but fatal square that walks into a decisive attack — usually a mating sequence, occasionally blocking an escape/retreat square so a piece is lost — a self-inflicted king-safety blunder from a winning position.

1024.label: Plays a greedy capture or pawn push that ignores the opponent's decisive threat, typically leaving its own queen en prise (8/10 hang the queen; the other 2 instead walk into a kingside mating attack).

1029.chip: Exposes king by walking into center
1029.label: The player voluntarily marches the king to an exposed central/open square (Kd2/Kd7/Ke7/Ke2/Kd1, or the related g6xh5 capture opening the king), walking into a decisive series of checks and a mating net or material loss, typically instead of the only defensive resource g6/g3.

1026.label: Player makes a materially-safe move—usually greedily grabbing material—while overlooking a stronger forced win (frequently a forced checkmate).

1031.label: Captures/trades a rook immediately instead of first inserting the intermediate move (zwischenzug — a check or pin) that would win extra material or force mate.

1025.label: A thematic but premature knight move in the opening (often to the rim, e.g. Nh5/Nh4/Na5) that leaves the knight undefended or abandons a defender, losing a piece — usually the knight itself.

1017.label: Plays a greedy capture or loose king/piece move that leaves its own material—usually a rook—hanging on an open file or rank, converting a winning position into a loss.

1036.label: Plays a slow, safe, or tempo-losing move that squanders a forced mate or winning king-side attack — usually missing a forcing sacrifice (Qxh7+, Rxg7+, Rxh2+) that delivered checkmate.

1033.label: In every position the player had a strong capture available—almost always a queen capture (Qxd4, Qxf3, Qxg5+, Qxg4, Qxe4, Qxf4, Qxf5+, Qxd2) that won material or staved off mate—but played a quieter/different move and missed the win.

1039.label: In every position the player overlooks a one-move capture of the opponent's undefended/hanging queen, squandering a winning position.

1023.label: In the endgame the player makes a move that loses material or the game outright—most often hanging a piece (frequently a rook) by capturing/relocating greedily, and in several cases abandoning the defender of a promotion square so the opponent queens.

1030.label: The move abandons a critical defensive duty — a defended piece/pawn, an open file, or a key square — letting the opponent break through to win material (a pawn, the exchange, or even the queen) or land a decisive attack; the lost material varies (pawn/bishop/rook/queen) and several boards are purely positional or king-safety, so no single piece can be named.

1038.label: Plays an unsound bishop sacrifice on the king's wing (Bxf7+/Bxh7+/Bxh2+/Bxf2+, or fails to rescue the f2-bishop) that the opponent simply accepts, leaving the bishop hung for at most a pawn.

1042.label: Plays a forcing check with the queen (or a queen-promotion) that hangs the queen to an immediate capture, throwing away a forced mate or won position.

1032.chip: Inferior king move in lost endgame
1032.label: In already-lost endgames (mostly rook endings) the player makes a king move that fails to maximize defensive resistance — sometimes allowing a faster forced mate, but in half the cases the move is only marginal or not actually a mistake, so the recurring element is the lost-endgame king move rather than any single hung or missed piece.

1034.label: The player overlooks a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen (or grabs a lesser piece), throwing away a decisive, often forced-mating, material win.

1044.chip: Missed pawn win in opening (central tension)
1044.label: In the opening, plays a slow developing or prophylactic move that ignores central pawn tension, missing an immediate capture that wins a clean pawn.

1043.label: This feature fires on premature queen exchanges (usually a capture-with-check) that liquidate into a lost king-and-pawn endgame, surrendering the queen's last checking/counterplay resources—though a few boards are actually fine trades and one (board 10) instead hangs a passed pawn via a rook move, so it warrants review.

1040.label: In every position the player overlooked an immediate capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning material grab (often a forced mate).

1041.label: In the opening, the player moves a bishop to an undefended square (often a greedy pawn-grab on c7/a6/b7/h6) where it is immediately captured for free, losing a full piece for nothing or for a single pawn — 9 of 10 are bishop hangs (one is a knight).

1045.label: Captures/trades off the last defensive piece (queen or rook) into a king-and-pawn endgame that is lost because the opponent's passed pawn promotes.

1027.label: The player repeatedly fails to neutralize the opponent's dominant knight, in most boards hanging material over 2-3 moves (most often the rook to an Ne3+ fork, occasionally a pawn), though a few boards instead just concede a dominating knight without immediate material loss — so the hung piece varies and direction is mixed, warranting review.

1050.label: A knight is moved to an undefended square in the opening and is immediately captured for nothing (almost always by an enemy bishop), losing a full piece.

1028.label: Plays a move that abandons a key defender of a piece, pawn, or king square, hanging own material (or the king) to a tempo-gaining capture—often with check; the specific piece lost varies (knight, bishop, queen, pawns).

1037.label: Across nearly all boards a passed pawn is one step from queening, and the player makes a losing move around it—wrong move order, wrong capture, or vacating a key square—but the actual error type is mixed (hanging own material in 3/8/10, missing a winning shot in 5/9, simply allowing promotion in 1/2), so the only certain invariant is the passer-near-promotion setting rather than a single uniform mistake.

1047.label: A move that neglects king safety and walks into a forced checkmate—most often a back-rank mate (7/10), sometimes a king-hunt mate (5,10)—throwing away an equal or winning position; only board 3 differs (a trapped rook rather than mate).

1055.chip: Wastes tempo in won pawn endgame
1055.label: In a completely winning endgame, plays a slightly inefficient king or pawn-push move (delaying promotion or suboptimal centralization) that loses only a tiny amount of tempo/centipawns rather than hanging any material.

1181.label: In most positions the player plays a passive move and overlooks a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen, while a couple instead hang their own rook.

1183.label: In a drawn or holdable endgame the player makes a move — often overlooking the single saving resource (a capture, trade, or king centralization) — that converts the position into a loss or forced mate.

1180.label: Across the boards the recurring fault is a self-inflicted losing move — dropping the player's own material (knight, pawn, queen, rook, or the exchange) or fatally exposing the king to mate — but the specific piece hung varies too much to name one, and a couple of boards are actually a missed win or a non-blunder, so it needs review.

1186.label: In the opening the player loses their own material self-inflicted—either leaving a piece en prise or removing its defender (most often a knight, sometimes a bishop or pawn)—turning an equal position into a losing one.

1179.chip: Hangs a piece or allows mate
1179.label: A losing blunder that ignores the critical threat — most often leaving a piece (frequently a rook) hanging, and in several cases walking the king into a forced (often back-rank) mate.

1185.label: Squanders a winning advantage by playing a quiet, materially-safe move instead of a forcing knight tactic (Nxf7/Nxf2/Nxc3/Nxe4/Nxd2 sac or capture) that exploits the opponent's exposed/uncastled king.

1168.chip: Hangs a piece opening king attack
1168.label: An unsound capture/sacrifice intended to open lines against the enemy king (often on g6, usually a bishop move) that instead loses the player's own material; the hung piece varies (mostly bishop, but also rook and queen), and a few boards are really missed wins.

1192.label: The player voluntarily captures into a queen trade that liquidates their winning advantage—usually killing an attack on the enemy king or, in one case, declining a mate/free piece—turning a winning position into equality or worse.

1182.label: A move that throws away a clear (often winning) advantage in a position where a knight is the central piece — about half the boards hang the player's own knight while the other half fail to capture/trade/reposition a key knight, so the precise error (hang vs. omission) varies and only the knight involvement is constant.

1188.label: In winning endgames the player repeatedly plays a materially-safe but inferior move and misses the precise winning continuation (often a forcing check such as d3+), though a couple of boards instead hang material over 2-3 moves.

1200.label: In rook-and-pawn endgames, plays a passive or poorly-placed rook (occasionally king/pawn) move that surrenders a tempo and lets the opponent's passed pawn run to promotion, rather than the active rook placement that would stop it.

1187.label: The player makes a move that abandons defense of their own king (removing a key defender or skipping the only prophylactic move), allowing a decisive attack that is usually forced mate, though two boards instead simply squander a winning advantage.

1191.chip: Ignores threat, allowing mate or material loss
1191.label: The move neglects the opponent's one forcing threat, walking into either a forced checkmate (king exposed) or decisive material loss, with no single piece or attack type dominating across the boards.

1193.label: In the opening the player makes a move (usually a greedy capture) that hangs one of their own pieces for at most a pawn—the piece varies (knight ~7/10, bishop ~3/10), so it's 'a piece'—losing material to a simple recapture.

1198.label: In a winning endgame the player ignores the unique saving/winning resource (usually a knight or bishop maneuver/sacrifice) and instead plays a natural-looking move — advancing the king, promoting into a capture, or giving a useless check — squandering the win.

1204.label: A king move that exposes the king and walks it into a forced checkmate (or, in a couple of cases, decisive material loss via an unstoppable check).

1199.chip: Missed capturing a hanging piece (usually rook)
1199.label: In nearly every position the player overlooks a simple one-move capture of an undefended enemy piece (most often a rook) and plays an unrelated pawn or king move instead, throwing away a winning material advantage.

1206.label: In pawn/passed-pawn endgames the player chooses the losing side of a pawn race — sending the king the wrong way (or pushing a pawn) instead of using it to stop/escort the decisive passer — converting wins or holds into losses, with no material actually hung.

1190.label: In a worse middlegame the player makes a non-forcing move (usually a rook) that abandons a critical rank or file instead of trading off the dangerous rook, allowing the opponent to crash through with a decisive tactic — back-rank mate, a fork, or a forced win of material.

1201.chip: Misses free capture of hanging piece
1201.label: Repeatedly ignores an elementary capture of an undefended/hanging enemy piece (most often a rook, sometimes a bishop/knight/pawn, frequently a pawn-take in the endgame), throwing away free material or a forced win.

1196.label: In the opening, plays a natural quiet developing or repositioning move that ignores the position's urgent demand (an unresolved threat, a pin, central tension, or a winning tactic), squandering the advantage — but the piece moved and whether material is hung vs. a win is missed vary across boards, so no single piece or direction can be honestly named.

1203.label: Plays a quiet opening developing move and overlooks a forced material win — almost always a bishop grabbing an undefended pawn on the long diagonal (Bxg7/Bxg2) to win the exchange.

1194.label: The player repeatedly makes a losing queen move — either hanging the queen (often to a knight fork) or making/offering a disadvantageous queen exchange (e.g. queen-for-rook) — that squanders material or a winning position.

1210.label: In every position the player skips a simple capture of an undefended enemy knight (f4/e4/d5/d4/e5), passing up a free piece — a clear missed-win omission, not a hang of their own material.

1197.label: Player repeatedly prioritizes a material capture (or own plan) over the strongest continuation, most often a forced mate or decisive attack, squandering a won position; in a few cases the greedy move itself hangs material.

1195.label: A critical-position move that throws away a winning or drawn game, most often by hanging the player's own material (variously a bishop, queen, or pawns), though a few boards instead miss a forced win rather than losing material outright.

1208.label: A move that loses the player's own material to a refutation within 1–3 moves, but the hung unit varies widely (knight, rook, bishop, queen) and two boards are more positional (king-weakening/tempo loss), so the safe label is 'hangs a piece/material' rather than any specific piece.

1213.label: In opening (often King's-Gambit) positions with central pawn tension, the player makes a quiet developing/preparatory move instead of the winning capture fxe5/dxe5(/fxe4), squandering the advantage — frequently letting the unresolved tension drop a pawn a move or two later.

1217.label: Plays a bishop to an attacking/pinning square (Bg5 or Bg4) attempting to pin a knight, but the pin is illusory and a knight-based tactic wins the bishop within a few moves.

1205.chip: Losing endgame move (hangs piece or pawn race)
1205.label: In the endgame the player makes a position-losing move—most often hanging a piece (rook, bishop, or knight) but sometimes squandering a tempo in a pawn race or removing a key defender—converting a drawn or merely difficult position into a clear loss.

1216.label: On every board the player declines the engine's best move—a piece exchange (a rook trade in eight positions, a queen trade in two)—throwing away a winning or equal position by avoiding the simplifying capture.

1211.label: A slow, passive, or greedy move that throws away a winning/advantageous position instead of the precise forcing continuation; the piece moved and exact mechanism vary, so no single hung piece can be named.

1220.label: In a winning endgame the player plays a materially-safe king move that squanders the win (often a forced mate or pawn promotion) instead of the one precise winning continuation.

1202.label: Player plays a slow/passive move instead of an available forcing tactic — almost always a check (Qh5+, Qh4+, Bb5+, Qc6+, etc.) — that wins material or mates; in about half the boards the passive move also lets their own piece fall a move or two later, but the invariant across all 10 is the squandered forcing win.

1218.label: In a losing endgame, plays an irrelevant pawn push, king walk, or passive piece move instead of the only defense (capture, blockade, or tempo-check) that stops the opponent's passed pawn(s) from promoting.

1212.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material — hanging a piece (rook, bishop, knight, or queen) to an immediate recapture, discovered attack, or losing trade, mostly in the middlegame; the specific piece varies so it's 'a piece', not one named piece.

1225.label: The player ignores a direct attack on their own queen and plays an unrelated move (development, pawn push, or a queen move into capture), allowing the queen to be taken for nothing or a minor piece in the opening.

1209.label: The player makes a slow/passive move (usually a queen retreat or shuffle) that fails to find the demanded active continuation — surrendering the initiative and either missing a winning/saving shot or letting the opponent's attack crash through.

1214.chip: Avoids forcing queen trade, hangs material
1214.label: On all 10 boards the best move was a forcing queen trade (Qxe2+/Qxd2+/Qxe7+/Qxa5); the player instead developed or attacked, and the refutation wins material (often the queen, sometimes a knight or pawn a move or two later).

1222.chip: Hangs piece on center capture (pawn-recapture fork)
1222.label: In the opening the player captures a centrally-posted piece (usually a knight, on e4/d5/e5/d4), but the opponent's pawn recapture forks/double-attacks two pieces and wins material back with interest — a self-inflicted hang where the specific hung piece varies (bishop, knight, or pawn).

1215.label: The player repeatedly blunders in positions revolving around a queen that is en prise—usually either leaving its own queen/material hanging by removing a defender (boards 1,2,3,4,5,8) or failing to grab the opponent's free queen (boards 6,9), with two king-safety/queen-trade variants (7,10)—but the direction (self-hang vs. missed capture) and the hung piece (queen, rook, or bishop) vary too much to commit to a single specific label.

1207.label: From a winning position the player throws away the advantage, and the boards split almost exactly in half: ~5 SELF-INFLICTED hangs (Qe6+, Qxe2, Rf4, Bb4, g3 dropping queen/rook/bishop) and ~5 OMISSIONS missing a decisive capture (Qxd8+, Bxf8, Rxa3+, dxe5) — the mechanism and the piece both vary, so this is a mixed 'blunders the win' feature, not a clean hang or a clean missed-win, and needs human review.

1229.label: Across all ten endgame positions the player skipped a winning knight-check tactic (fork/discovered attack/clearance, usually winning a rook) and instead played a passive or pawn-grabbing move that let the advantage slip to a draw or near-equality.

1219.chip: Missed bishop capture of hung rook
1219.label: Repeatedly missed a bishop capture of an undefended enemy rook (winning the exchange or a full rook), instead playing a slow developing or structural move.

1234.label: Plays a passive or wrongly-directed king move in a king-and-pawn endgame, losing the king-activity/march race rather than hanging material (several boards are near-zero-loss, so the pattern is fuzzy).

1227.label: The player squanders a winning or drawn position by playing a natural capture/developing move instead of a forcing intermediate check that wins material or mates (a minority of boards instead self-inflict a hang).

1226.label: An opening move that fatally exposes the player's king—most often allowing a devastating Qh5+/Qh4# on the opened light-square diagonal (7/10 boards), while three other boards instead lose the queen to a ...Bb4 pin against the king on e1, so the exact mechanism is mixed.

1221.chip: Hangs a piece or blunders advantage
1221.label: A mixed 'blunder' feature: about half the moves directly lose the player's own material (bishop ×3, queen ×2) to a tactic 1-3 moves later, while the rest are positional/king-safety errors that throw away a winning or equal position — no single hung piece dominates, so it must stay generic.

1230.chip: Squanders win with quiet move (kingside attack)
1230.label: In nearly every position the player held a large or winning advantage and threw it away by playing a slow, natural move (passive rook/queen developing move) instead of the strong continuation — most often a crushing kingside attack (Qh5 / b1-h7 battery) — making this an omission/missed-win feature rather than a material-hanging one (hung-own only ~33%).

1223.label: An early queen sortie (Qb3/Qb6/Qf3) in the opening that gets punished tactically — most often by a knight fork (Nd4/Nd5/Ne5) or a Bxf7+ break that wins the player's material, though a few boards instead skip a winning tactic (Bxf7+/Nxe5), so the direction is mixed and the lost piece varies (rook/bishop/queen-pressure).

1228.label: At a critical tactical moment the player skips the decisive forcing move (usually a winning check, capture, or sacrifice) and plays a slow or materially losing alternative, squandering a winning advantage or the game.

1239.label: A materially-safe move that ignores an immediate capture of the opponent's undefended queen, squandering a winning advantage (9/10 boards miss a direct queen grab).

1224.label: Moving a piece (usually the knight off e4) clears the e-file, allowing a discovered check from the e2-queen to the e8-king that wins the player's own queen in the opening.

1238.label: A self-inflicted endgame blunder—usually a capture that grabs material or removes a key defender—which loses the player's own piece (varied: rook most often, but also bishop/knight) to a tactical refutation, frequently a check or back-rank threat.

1241.label: The player moves a piece to a square where it loses material—either captured outright or refuted by a follow-up tactic—and although the moved piece is most often a knight (~7/10), it is sometimes the queen or bishop, so the invariant is self-inflicted material loss rather than any single piece.

1231.label: In the opening Black greedily grabs a central pawn with a knight, a self-inflicted material loss that is punished by a tactic (usually Qa4+ or a recapture) winning back the knight or the exchange.

1232.label: A self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material — but the hung piece varies (exchange/rook, knight, queen) and 2-3 boards instead allow a mating attack or miss a win, so it's only loosely 'hangs a piece' rather than any specific one.

1233.label: An active-looking move (check, capture, trade, or pawn push) that throws away a winning or equal position—in most boards self-inflicting material loss (a piece hung immediately or within a couple of moves), though several instead just miss a stronger winning tactic; the piece involved varies (knight/bishop/rook/queen), so no single piece can be named.

1237.label: A premature knight sortie to the rim (almost always ...Na5 hitting the c4 bishop) that neglects king safety and loses material, typically refuted by the Bxf7+ sacrifice exploiting the now-undefended f7.

1243.chip: Hangs rook chasing queen with g-pawn
1243.label: A g-pawn push (g6/g3) to chase the enemy queen off h5/h4 opens the e-file and long diagonal, letting the queen check (Qxe5+/Qxe4+) and capture the now-exposed corner rook.

1235.label: Every position ignores a one-move queen checkmate against the castled king (Qh7# or Qh2#/Qg2# along an open diagonal), playing an unrelated/greedy move instead of the forced defensive block and getting mated next move.

1240.label: Plays a premature forcing check (or wrong move-order) that throws away tempo or hangs the player's own piece — frequently a bishop — instead of first making the necessary capture/trade; but several of the boards are not actually blunders, so the pattern is fuzzy.

1242.chip: Overlooks decisive move, throws away advantage
1242.label: In a critical position the player overlooks the one decisive move (a free capture like Qxg5/Nxh4, the saving castle, or a forcing check/combination) and instead plays a passive or wrong move that squanders the win or walks into mate — but the direction is genuinely mixed (≈4 boards are self-inflicted hangs/back-rank mates rather than pure omissions), so it needs review.

1247.label: A middlegame move—often a greedy capture or careless reposition—that loses the player's own material, with the hung piece varying widely (rook, knight, bishop, or queen) rather than one specific piece.

1250.label: A move leaves an own pawn or piece undefended, allowing the opponent's knight to win the material—frequently via a fork or capture-with-tempo.

1245.label: A move that throws away a clearly winning or large advantage — about half the time by skipping the only strong continuation (positional/tempo omission), the other half by hanging material outright, with no consistent piece.

1249.label: Across the boards the player makes a passive or tempo-losing move (retreat, flank pawn push, or grabbing a side pawn) that abandons a key defensive or attacking role and skips a forcing winning continuation, surrendering the advantage — sometimes letting their own material (a piece, varying between knight/rook/pawn) or king fall a few moves later.

1236.chip: Hangs material via weakening opening move
1236.label: A premature/weakening move in the opening—most often a pawn push (h6, h5, e6)—that throws away equality by letting the opponent win material or shatter the player's structure (commonly a capture/sacrifice on g6 against the kingside bishop), but the specific piece lost varies (g6 bishop, d3 bishop, rook, knight, pawn) and two boards aren't pawn moves, so the only firm invariant is 'self-inflicted material/positional collapse in the opening.'

1248.label: The player plays a quiet, non-forcing move and overlooks an available forcing check (usually a queen or bishop check) that wins material or saves the position.

1253.label: The player plays a natural-looking developing, trading, or 'tempo' move that throws away an immediately available forced mate or winning combination — a materially-safe omission rather than a self-inflicted hang.

1244.label: In a winning/advantageous middlegame the player skips a concrete forcing tactic (often a check or capture) and plays a slow or weaker move, throwing away the win — the missed material varies, so no single piece is named.

1259.label: Pushes a bishop into a square where it is captured for free (or sacrificed on f7 for a single pawn) in the opening, losing a full minor piece across all ten positions.

1258.label: In the opening, the played move hangs an undefended piece (most often a bishop, sometimes a knight or queen) to a simple pawn capture.

1255.label: In every position the player squandered a winning advantage by playing a passive or aimless move instead of an available material-winning capture, which in 9/10 cases was a bishop capture (often netting a full piece).

1260.label: A materially-safe, non-forcing opening move (castling, retreat, or quiet pawn move) that squanders a concrete winning knight tactic — most often Nxf7, sometimes Nxc3/Nxf2 — turning a near-winning position into equality.

1246.label: The played move is a self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material — a piece falls (queen, rook, knight or bishop, varying board to board) either immediately to a free capture or within 2–3 moves of the refutation, so no single piece can honestly be named.

1256.chip: Pawn capture opens lines toward own king
1256.label: Resolving pawn tension with a pawn recapture/capture that rips open a file (usually toward the player's own king), handing the opponent a decisive attack rather than losing material outright.

1252.label: A move that fatally exposes or neglects the player's own king, inviting a decisive attack that ends in checkmate or heavy material loss.

1265.label: A safe move that overlooks an immediate capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning position.

1251.label: In a clearly winning position (usually an endgame) the player makes a tempting forcing move—often an impulsive check or a material grab—that throws away the cleanest win (a forced mate, a free piece, or a superior endgame) yet stays winning, so the recurring error is a missed/squandered win rather than a single consistently-hung piece.

1254.label: From a winning position—almost always an endgame involving a passed pawn or promotion race—the player throws away the advantage (a pointless tempo-losing check, allowing the enemy pawn to queen, or skipping the only winning move), flipping winning into losing/drawn; the moving piece and exact mechanism vary, so no single piece is hung.

1261.label: The recurring mistake is a move that leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended and lost — but the hung piece varies (knight on d5/a5 in some, the g4/g6 bishop in others) and a few boards are instead a missed-win capture (3), a tempo slip (8), or a bad positional trade (9), so it's best named generically as 'hangs a piece'.

1270.label: Player leaves a rook undefended on an open line where the enemy queen captures it for free, hanging a full rook (or the exchange) in nearly every case.

1268.label: Captures a dangerous passed pawn with the rook, allowing an immediate recapture that loses the rook for a single pawn in a losing endgame.

1266.label: Plays a greedy or passive move—usually grabbing a pawn instead of a forcing rook check—throwing away a forced mate or winning attack.

1257.label: Plays a slow, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo — instead of the precise forcing shot — and is then punished either by missing a win or by allowing the opponent a decisive tactic or king attack.

1263.label: A move that throws away a winning (or drawing) advantage — in most boards the played move self-inflicts material loss within a few moves (the hung piece varies: knight, queen, etc.), while in a few it merely misses the decisive/saving continuation.

1267.label: A move that ignores an enemy knight (often skipping ...Bxe5) and lets a knight fork/infiltrate, costing the player material — bishop, knight, pawn, or exchange — within a couple of moves; a knight is the operative piece on every board, but the hung piece itself varies.

1272.label: In a winning or clearly better position, the player plays an inferior/slow move that throws away the advantage instead of the available decisive continuation (frequently a forcing capture or check), rather than hanging a specific piece.

1274.chip: Missed winning capture in endgame (often a hanging rook)
1274.label: In a winning endgame the player chose a materially-safe but passive move, skipping a clear winning capture (most often grabbing a free rook, sometimes a knight fork) and throwing away the won position.

1271.label: Throws away a won position by prematurely exchanging or playing a slow move instead of establishing/exploiting the pin (usually on the f3- or f6-knight).

1276.label: In endgames the player mishandles a passed pawn—skipping the key capture of its supporter, the needed blockade, or the correct king route in the race—allowing the pawn to promote and turning a defensible loss into a decisive one.

1273.label: In every position the player makes a materially-safe but imprecise endgame move (a slow king move or wrong capture) instead of the one precise winning continuation—most often a timely pawn break like b4—squandering a winning or equal position without hanging any material.

1281.label: The recurring mistake is advancing a pawn that weakens the player's own pawn structure or king safety (or liquidates a winning pawn majority), squandering a draw or win — a purely positional error, with no piece actually hung.

1275.label: From a winning (mostly endgame) position the player fails to find the decisive winning continuation—typically a pawn promotion or a simplifying rook trade/sac (Re1+, e1=Q+/R+, Rxf2+)—letting the opponent escape with perpetual check, while a minority of boards (8,9,10) instead hang material outright, so the core invariant is 'won position thrown away' rather than a single hung piece.

1269.label: In the opening, the player makes a move—usually a knight move—that leaves one of their own pieces (most often a knight) hanging to a simple pawn capture or short tactic, losing material for little or nothing.

1280.label: In winning passed-pawn and pawn endgames, the player resolves the pawn tension by capturing (or delays the decisive break with a slow move) instead of advancing/locking the pawn, throwing away a forced mate or winning advantage — though several flagged boards were actually 0 cp non-blunders.

1282.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material—either marching a piece into capture or abandoning a defender so a piece falls over the next move or two—most often a knight but sometimes a bishop or the exchange, so the safe specificity is 'a piece'.

1277.chip: Releases pawn tension, ruins structure (enemy passer)
1277.label: Captures with a pawn that releases the tension or blockade and wrecks the player's own pawn structure—typically handing the opponent dangerous (often passed) pawns—rather than a true hung-piece tactic, since every board resolves as a structurally losing trade/recapture.

1286.label: In Italian-style openings the player makes a developing or tension-ignoring move (d4, castling, Qf3, Re8, Ng4) that leaves their c4/c5 bishop undefended, losing it to a simple capture.

1279.label: Plays a counterproductive check — almost always letting the enemy king capture the checking unit (pawn 73%, bishop 27%) — that hands over material or releases the king, squandering the advantage.

1264.label: The player moves a piece (usually a knight, ~7/10) off a critical defensive/guarding square — often to grab a pawn or piece — abandoning its duty, and the refutation shows the player's own king getting mated or their own material falling over the next moves.

1262.label: The player makes a self-inflicted move that loses their own material—hanging a piece (queen, knight, or rook) by ignoring a threat or moving it to a captured square; the exact piece varies, so it's 'a piece' not one specific type.

1283.label: A suboptimal move that throws away a winning or clearly favorable position, most often by missing a stronger material-winning or tactical continuation, though several boards instead hang a piece or trade off a key restraining bishop into an enemy passed pawn.

1284.label: Advances a pawn prematurely—usually with a check—letting the enemy king blockade it (or hide behind it as a shield), squandering a winning position.

1278.label: A passive, non-forcing repositioning move (often the queen, sometimes the king) that ignores a critical resource—a saving queen trade, a free capture, or a hanging piece—and is punished by losing material or squandering the win; both the lost piece (pawn/knight/queen) and the Hangs-vs-Missed direction vary across boards, so this needs human review.

1292.label: The player delivers a queen check that loses the queen for inadequate compensation — either captured outright for a pawn/nothing or traded into a hopeless deficit — with the move always being a check in all 10 boards.

1287.label: Plays a non-forcing or materialistic move that overlooks a winning checking move — frequently a forced checkmate — squandering a decisive advantage.

1291.label: In rook endgames the player mishandles material—sometimes hanging their own piece (rook on b5c5, bishop on f2e3), sometimes failing to win/save material (missed exd5, missed forced Rxe7+ exchange)—but the direction (self-inflicted hang vs. missed win) and the piece both vary, so only the broad 'endgame material error with a rook on the board' is reliable.

1294.label: A materially-safe but passive move that overlooks a winning tactical shot—almost always a bishop move (Bb5/Bb4/Be6/Bg4) that pins or deflects to win the enemy queen—in the opening.

1295.label: The played move leaves the player's own queen en prise, where it is captured by an enemy knight for inadequate compensation.

1285.label: In every position the player makes a premature simplifying capture (usually a queen trade with check) that cleanly converts a winning position into a smaller edge, passing up a more decisive tactic — frequently a knight fork.

1293.label: The played move self-inflicts material loss by leaving a piece capturable—either placed directly en prise or by abandoning its defense—though the specific piece varies (rook, bishop, knight, queen) and two boards deviate (one is a wrong-capture trade into a lost endgame, one squanders a forced mate).

1302.label: In most of the top positions the player overlooked a decisive winning move — either a forced checkmate (boards 1,5,6,7) or a capture/fork winning the opponent's queen (boards 2,3,4,8) — choosing a lesser materially-safe move instead, though two boards (9,10) instead self-inflicted a hang of the player's own material, so the core 'Missed win' invariant covers only ~8/10.

1299.label: An inaccurate move — most often a kingside pawn push in an endgame — that loses tempo or wrecks the player's own pawn structure and squanders a winning or equal position, rather than cleanly hanging a specific piece.

1289.label: A defensive/trade-offer move (usually the queen) backfires, exposing the king to a forcing check that wins the player's own material — they should have stepped the king to safety instead.

1288.label: In a drawn or winning position the player throws away the result by playing an inferior move—frequently failing to grab a hanging enemy queen or piece—instead of the available winning move, though several boards are positional collapses rather than missed captures.

1304.label: In materially-safe, already-winning positions the player repeatedly skipped a forcing rook check (skewer or back-rank, ~9/10) that won material — but the prize varies (rook, queen, bishop), so no single captured piece is named; it's a missed win, not a hang.

1300.label: A pawn advance (8/10) that wrecks the player's own position in an endgame — sometimes squandering a winning advantage, sometimes hanging material a few moves later — but the damage varies (positional weakening vs. material loss) and two moves aren't even pawn pushes, so the exact mistake isn't a single clean type.

1303.label: In the opening the player leaves the central e5 pawn hanging — developing or pushing elsewhere instead of advancing ...e4 — and it falls (boards 8 and 10 are instead early-Bd3 tempo losses, and board 9 hangs a piece, so the e5-pawn invariant is only ~7/10).

1301.label: Plays a quiet, safe repositioning move (retreat/develop/castle) instead of an available winning tactical strike, most often a bishop capture such as Bxd4+ or Bxe6.

1309.label: Promotes a pawn to a queen on a square where it is immediately captured (or, in one case, ignores a mating threat), hanging the freshly-promoted queen and squandering a winning position instead of playing the prep/intermezzo first.

1290.label: An unsound speculative capture/sacrifice in the opening — overwhelmingly a knight (Nxf7/Nxf2/Nxe4/Nxe5), once a bishop (Bxf7+) — that hangs the player's own piece for at most a pawn, cleanly refuted by a simple recapture with no attacking follow-up.

1296.label: The player voluntarily trades/captures with the queen to simplify when a stronger continuation (keeping queens on, a winning capture, a fork, or mate) was available, throwing away a winning position into roughly equal/drawn material.

1298.label: An exposed, tempo-losing move (often a piece to a rim or awkward square) that in most positions lets the player's own material fall within a few moves, but the hung item varies (knight, bishop, pawn) and a few cases are purely positional, so the core is fuzzy.

1314.label: In every position the player chose a slow/passive move and overlooked a forcing pawn advance — almost always a check, frequently the f5+ king-and-rook fork — that wins material outright.

1310.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe move that squanders a winning advantage by overlooking an available material-winning tactic (capture, fork, or double attack).

1317.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly fails to grab a free, undefended enemy bishop (typically on b5/g4/b4/g5), playing a safe but passive move instead and throwing away a winning material advantage.

1319.label: Plays a move that ignores an existing/created attack and leaves one of its own pieces (varying — bishop, queen, knight, or rook) hanging for a free capture.

1342.label: The played move usually loses the player's own material—commonly a bishop but also an exchange or pawn, often by abandoning an active piece or exposing it to capture—though several boards instead simply miss a winning tactic, making the feature mixed.

1347.label: The player makes a capture or unsound sacrifice that loses their own material—a piece (knight or bishop, sometimes the exchange)—usually in the opening, refuted by a recapture or zwischenzug.

1324.label: Plays a careless active/material-grabbing move that ignores an immediate mating threat against its own king, allowing forced checkmate (or in 2 cases throwing away a won position via the same overlooked forcing line).

1343.chip: Hangs material in losing endgame (king move)

1349.label: A materially-safe move that skips an available winning capture; the material won varies (queen, rook, pawn, exchange), so no single piece is named.

1339.label: In a winning opening, the player loses their own knight — usually a greedy pawn-grab (Nxe5/Nxf4/Nxd5) that gets recaptured, or a knight left undefended; 2 of 10 are instead pure tempo/king-safety squanders rather than hung pieces.

1356.chip: Queen abandons defense, king exposed (often pointless check)

1350.label: Plays a slow, passive, non-forcing move that ignores the position's concrete demand (a threat, central tension, or a defender's duty), ceding the initiative and frequently allowing the opponent to win material — but the piece lost varies, so no single piece can be named.

1357.label: A move that loses the player's own material to a tactic (fork/deflection/overload), but the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, queen) and a few boards are instead missed winning captures rather than hangs.

1359.label: In a winning middlegame, the player throws away the advantage by choosing a tempting forcing move — almost always a check, often a discovered check — instead of the simple, decisive winning continuation.

1352.label: A non-critical/slow pawn move (very often a flank push to harass an enemy knight) that ignores the position's real demand — grabbing a hanging piece, defending, or counterattacking — and throws away the advantage; a knight is involved in every position, but the resulting loss is sometimes a missed winning capture, sometimes a hung own pawn, sometimes just a positional/king-safety collapse, so the direction is mixed.

1355.label: From a winning (mostly endgame) position the player throws away the advantage with an inferior move — about half the boards hang the player's own material (rook, knight, queen, pawn — it varies) and about half simply decline a clean winning capture/tactic, so neither the direction nor the piece is consistent enough to name.

1364.label: A move that neglects king safety—pulling a key defender away (or grabbing material while the king is exposed)—and is punished by a decisive kingside attack, frequently a forced mate.

1365.label: In the opening, plays an aggressive or greedy move (often abandoning a guarded bishop) that leaves an own piece — most often a bishop, sometimes the queen or a knight — undefended and lost to a simple or short-tactical capture.

1361.label: A slow, tempo-wasting move (usually a pawn push) ignores the urgent need to contest open files or trade rooks, most often letting the opponent double rooks on the 7th/2nd rank and seize a decisive initiative.

1351.label: A move that throws away a winning or clearly better position by playing an inferior continuation instead of the available strong line — usually missing a material-winning move, occasionally hanging own material or blocking/misplacing a piece; mechanism and piece vary across boards.

1368.label: The player snatches a pawn with a knight that is immediately recaptured (sometimes after a 1-2 move intermezzo), losing a full knight for a pawn.

1371.label: The player repeatedly passes up a clearly winning move—usually a free capture of queen, rook, or pawn—in favor of a tempting but pointless check that lets the opponent's king escape and squanders the advantage (the 'patzer sees a check' reflex).

1376.label: On every board the player makes a routine/reflexive recapture instead of a stronger forcing move — a zwischenzug, tactic, or outright mate (most often a check) — squandering a winning advantage.

1366.label: A natural-looking move that squanders a winning or better position — roughly half the boards hang the player's own material (pawn/exchange/bishop, no consistent piece) and half miss a winning capture or necessary defense, so neither a specific piece nor a single hang/miss mechanism dominates.

1378.label: Plays a tempting/forcing check (100% of boards) instead of the stronger quiet capture or winning move, throwing away the advantage — but the consequence varies (sometimes hangs own knight/rook/bishop, sometimes just misses a clean win), so no single piece can be named.

1381.label: In an endgame the player exchanges off the rook (usually by capturing a pawn/piece), eliminating the sole defensive or blockading resource and converting a holdable position into a lost one — though a few boards are non-trade endgame slips (a tempo-wasting check, a pawn move, an allowed queen trade).

1380.label: In endgames the player makes a passive or misplaced king move (or wastes a tempo on a pawn push) instead of the correct king activation/retreat, deteriorating an already difficult position rather than hanging material.

1370.label: A move—frequently a pointless check—that wastes the critical tempo and squanders a winning (occasionally drawn) position, the suboptimal play usually letting the player's own material (pawn, rook, or queen, no single piece dominating) fall over the next few moves.

1383.label: In king-and-pawn / promotion endgames the player chooses an imprecise (usually king) move that throws away the only drawing or winning line, though several of the top-10 boards are actually 0cp non-blunders, so the pattern is fuzzy.

1379.label: In endgames the player makes a decisive king move that either misses a winning/drawing resource or hangs material — the error type and piece vary (roughly half missed-win, half self-inflicted), so this is a general endgame-blunder feature rather than one specific mistake.

1382.label: The player loses a bishop — almost always the dark-squared bishop on g5/h4 — by failing to resolve its exposure (typically with Bxe7), letting it be trapped by ...g5 or captured outright.

1297.chip: Neglects own king while attacking (often a check)

1393.label: In king-and-pawn endgames, plays a tempo-wasting king move or wrong pawn-capture/push order that loses the critical passed-pawn promotion race, converting a win or draw into a loss or draw.

1391.label: The player delivers a forcing check that places the queen (8/10) on a square defended by an enemy piece — usually an f6/e5/e7 knight — hanging it for free; every board is a check, and the rare exceptions hang another piece (knight) or lose material over a couple moves.

1389.label: Plays a slow, quiet, or developing move instead of the position's urgent concrete action (a pawn break, defense, or active continuation), letting the opponent seize the initiative or win material.

1386.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a king move (occasionally a pawn move) that misplaces the king or loses a tempo, letting the opponent's passed pawn(s) decide — but it's fuzzy because several top boards are already lost with ~0cp loss (not real blunders) and two are pawn pushes rather than king moves, and no specific piece is ever 'hung'.

1392.label: Plays an unsound pseudo-sacrifice grabbing a pawn (typically Nxf7 or Nxf2) that simply hangs the knight to recapture, losing a full piece for a pawn in the opening.

1387.label: The player makes an irrelevant move — frequently a tempting check or material grab — instead of capturing or blockading the opponent's passed pawn, allowing it to queen with a decisive (and the recurring) mistake.

1398.label: A quiet, passive or retreating move that overlooks an available winning tactical shot, squandering a decisive advantage.

1388.label: In every position a clearly winning move (often a forced checkmate) was available, but the player squandered it by grabbing material or playing a 'safe'/inferior move instead.

1396.label: Advances a pawn prematurely in the endgame instead of the needed king/knight move, throwing away a forced win or drawing resource.

1384.label: The player's move leaves a rook en prise to an enemy knight or bishop, losing the exchange.

1394.label: Plays a quiet, natural-looking move (often a developing queen move) and overlooks an available material-winning tactical shot — almost always a knight capture like Nxe5 — squandering the advantage.
