1819.label: A self-inflicted blunder that loses the player's own material — frequently by removing a defender or opening a line that exposes the king — but the hung piece varies (queen, bishop, or outright mate), so no single piece can be named with confidence.

1832.label: A king/pawn move that throws away a king-and-pawn (or minor-piece) endgame — releasing central tension/blockade or misplacing the king — typically letting the enemy king infiltrate, rather than hanging any material.

1838.label: Player hangs a knight with an unsound pseudo-sacrifice (almost always ...Nxf2, once Nxf7), giving up a full piece for one pawn in the opening on an illusory fork/king-attack that the simple Kxf2 refutes.

1827.chip: Hangs own piece, missing winning capture (queen)
1827.label: With a winning capture available (frequently a free enemy queen), the player instead makes a move that hangs their own material — most often the queen, but sometimes a pawn or rook — squandering a winning position.

1833.chip: King to edge in lost endgame (passed pawn)
1833.label: In already-lost pawn/passed-pawn endgames the king is shuffled to a passive edge square instead of centralizing, capturing the key supporting piece, or inserting the saving check — accelerating promotion or mate.

1837.label: The player gives a queen check that simply hangs the queen, as a rook captures or interposes-and-captures the checking queen for nothing (or for far less).

1830.chip: Hastens own mate in lost position (king exposed)
1830.label: In an already-losing position, the player makes a self-inflicted blunder—usually a king move that walks into a mating net, but sometimes hanging a piece or abandoning a blockade—that converts a fighting loss into a forced mate or decisive material collapse, with the exposed king as the recurring element.

1828.chip: Hangs a piece botching winning tactic
1828.label: In a winning tactical position the player botches the combination—usually capturing in the wrong order or moving the wrong piece—and ends up letting one of their own pieces fall (knight, bishop or queen vary), though in ~3 of the 10 the move is materially safe and merely misses the winning capture (frequently of the enemy queen), so the feature is mixed between self-inflicted hangs and missed wins.

1844.label: The player grabs material with a capture while their own king is under attack, ignoring a decisive king-safety refutation (most often an immediate checkmate).

1839.label: A materially-safe developing or castling move in the opening that skips a winning tactic — most often the Bxf7+ sacrifice or another blow against the f7 square.

1840.label: A materially-safe but passive king/pawn move that overlooks an available winning capture or tactic — most often failing to take the opponent's hanging queen with a pawn, though the won piece varies (queen, rook, pawn, fork).

1841.label: In every position the player ignored a free, undefended enemy piece that the engine wins outright — most often the opponent's hanging queen (8/10), a bishop in the rest — playing an unrelated move and usually walking into a forced mate.

1842.chip: Blunders into mate or hangs material
1842.label: A self-inflicted losing move that either walks the king into a forced mate (boards 1,2,3,7) or hangs the player's own material such as queen/pawn (boards 4,6,8), with the rest being positional/tempo slips or a missed win — so the exact victim and even the mistake category vary across positions.

1845.label: In clearly winning middlegames the player repeatedly overlooks a forcing queen move—often a check delivering forced mate or winning material—and instead plays a slow pawn push or materialistic grab.

1846.label: In the opening, the player's capture or developing move loses their own material — often by stripping the king's pawn cover so a queen check (Qh5+/Qh4+) wins a rook, or by leaving a developed/captured piece undefended — with the lost piece varying (rook, bishop, knight), and one board being a missed win rather than a hang.

1835.label: In the opening the player declines the natural central pawn capture/tension and self-inflicts material loss — most often hanging a knight to an advanced enemy pawn, sometimes just dropping a pawn — though two cases are merely positional.

1847.label: A tempting forcing check that sacrifices the player's own material (or wrecks their position) for insufficient compensation — the checking piece is most often a knight but varies (bishop, queen), so name it only as 'a piece'.

1853.label: A grabbing or developing move that, through a move-order or missed-intermezzo error, hangs the player's own material — the hung piece varies (rook, bishop, knight, or pawn), and a few boards instead show a king-safety lapse or a missed win.

1854.label: A materialistic capture (queen-grab, recapture, or removing own defender) that snatches a pawn/piece but throws away a winning or favorable position—often hanging the player's own material or wrecking king safety—instead of the stronger best move.

1852.label: In passed-pawn endgames the king goes to a wrong square—often the back rank—that fails to catch or blockade the passer, frequently letting it advance/promote with a tempo-gaining check.

1856.label: In the opening the player hangs their own queen—either by leaving it en prise or moving it to a forkable square—and it is typically won by a knight fork or knight capture (e.g. Qe3 allowing Nxc2+).

1858.label: In pure pawn/king endgames the player makes an inferior king or pawn move — often skipping the decisive pawn break (e5/f5/h5) or taking the wrong king route — that turns a draw or win into a loss, with no material hung.

1848.label: The player gives a check (usually with the queen) that the enemy king simply captures for free, hanging the piece outright — 8/10 hang the queen, the other two hang a rook, and in every single board the refutation is the king capturing the dropped piece.

1836.label: The bishop greedily captures a rook to win the exchange, but the grab surrenders a key defensive bishop (usually the long-diagonal guardian) or ignores a tactic, so the recapture/removal exposes the king or loses more material than the exchange was worth.

1849.label: The player moves a piece off a defensive duty, leaving their own material (knight, pawn, rook, or bishop) hanging — though several boards are instead tempo/positional losses or a missed win, so the piece and even the mistake type are not uniform.

1843.chip: Squanders won opening, declines free capture
1843.label: In a winning opening (phase 100% opening), the player throws away the advantage by not grabbing the available free piece (best move is usually Nxe5/Nxe4) — but the direction is genuinely mixed: about half are self-inflicted hangs (notably the recurring Bxf2+ bishop sac, and one Qd8 hanging a knight) while the rest are pure omissions/allowed tactics (a6, a3, Bd3, Bd6→Nxf7, Nxc3→Bxf7+), so neither a single hung piece nor a clean 'hangs vs missed' label is honestly supportable.

1857.label: In most top positions the player skipped a clearly winning move — frequently a free material/queen capture (Rxc6, gxh4, Rxe8) or the only winning king/rook move — an omission rather than a self-inflicted hang, though a couple of boards (Nc5 leaving the rook, Re1 walking into Nf3+) instead hang the player's own piece, and one isn't actually a blunder, so the core is fuzzy and warrants review.

1855.label: A misguided move—usually a king move—that worsens an already difficult/losing position, either walking into mate, self-inflicting material loss, or wasting a critical tempo instead of addressing the decisive threat.

1825.label: A self-inflicted move that neglects or weakens the player's own king safety, allowing a decisive attack or sacrifice — though several boards instead simply hang material outright, so the invariant is fuzzy.

1850.label: An active, self-inflicted move—usually a rook trade or sacrifice (often dissolving a dominant doubled-rook/two-rook configuration)—that gives up the player's own material and throws away a winning position; the surrendered piece is a rook in ~8/10 boards but occasionally the queen, so the exact piece is too fuzzy to name with full confidence.

1864.label: In pawn/rook endgames the player makes a tempo-losing king or pawn move that fails to convert a win or hold a draw (no material is hung), though several flagged boards are near-best non-blunders.

1866.label: In nearly every position the player passes up a crushing queen infiltration to the kingside (usually Qh6/Qxh6, sometimes Qh3/Qf6) and lets a winning attack fade to equality.

1860.label: A self-inflicted move — usually a greedy pawn grab in the opening — that leaves the player's own knight en prise to be won for little or nothing, with two boards instead being a positional/king-safety collapse.

1862.chip: Hangs material on premature kingside attack (bishop to h3)
1862.label: The player launches a speculative kingside attack (often a bishop to h3/h6), abandoning a defensive duty and hanging their own material to the refutation.

1863.chip: Trades rook for knight in won endgame
1863.label: Captures a knight—usually trading a dominating rook for it—and converts a winning rook endgame into a drawn or lost pawn endgame (knight is always the captured piece).

1867.label: Plays a safe but pointless move while the opponent's queen sits hanging (usually capturable in one move), squandering a winning position by failing to take it.

1859.label: A quiet or king move that overlooks the critical tactic and lets the player's own material fall (a piece — knight/bishop/rook all appear — often to a capture-with-check or fork) within a few moves; ~2/10 are instead king-safety blunders that miss a win or allow mate, so this is flagged for review.

1871.label: Squanders a winning position by playing a slow king/rook/pawn move instead of immediately advancing (or clearing the way for) the decisive passed pawn to promote.

1851.label: In the opening the player makes a passive piece retreat or quiet developing move instead of the stronger forcing continuation (a capture resolving tension or a Qh4+/Bb5+ tactic), sliding from equal to losing; in two cases the same passive move also outright hangs material.

1876.label: Plays a quiet/non-forcing move and misses a decisive winning (often mating) queen check such as Qxg7+ or Qh7+.

1861.label: A quiet or misplaced move pulls a piece off its critical defensive/positional duty (or skips the only resolving move), turning a winning/better position into equality or worse; the relocated piece varies (knight, bishop, queen, pawn), so no single piece can be named.

1874.label: In a winning position the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (rook shuffle, knight retreat, king move) and overlooks an immediately decisive tactic—almost always a forcing check, frequently a queen strike to e6/d5—that would win material or deliver mate.

1873.label: The player typically moves or leaves a piece on an undefended square and loses it for nothing, most often a knight (7/10 hung knights), though a bishop, a bad trade, and one missed-win case break the pattern.

1865.label: A flashy capture or check that loses the player's own material—bishop, queen, or knight (varies)—throwing away a winning or equal position, though a few boards are instead missed simple wins.

1879.chip: King fails to stop passed pawn
1879.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player moves the king the wrong way (chasing a pawn, passive blockade, or to the edge) and fails to stop the opponent's passed pawn from promoting, often allowing a forced mate.

1872.chip: Slow king move squanders endgame (forcing move missed)
1872.label: In endgames the player avoids the decisive forcing move (promotion-with-check, forcing check, or winning queen trade) and instead plays a slow king move or wrong trade, losing tempo and squandering the win/draw — sometimes hanging material a few moves later, though what's lost (mate, bishop, pawn ending, or just tempo) varies too much to name one piece.

1878.label: A self-inflicted move that loses the player's own material, where the hung piece varies (queen, rook, bishop) and several cases are king moves that undefend or expose material; two boards are closer to missed-win omissions.

1870.label: The player greedily captures a defended piece (often the queen grabbing a minor) and is punished by an immediate simple recapture, losing material or a winning advantage.

1869.chip: Wrong capture squanders winning position (queen involved)
1869.label: From a winning position the player grabs the obvious capture (usually an invading rook, often with the queen) instead of the decisive move, thereby missing a bigger capture/mate or hanging own material through a move-order error.

1877.chip: Declines saving queen trade, allows mate
1877.label: A king-safety blunder in a losing-but-playable position where the player declines the only saving queen trade/capture and instead plays a move (usually a king step) that walks straight into a forced checkmate.

1875.label: Plays a tempo-wasting move—usually a queen check—that hands the opponent's king a path to safety, squandering a forced mate or clean win instead of the fastest continuation.

1881.label: In a winning position the player overlooks a move that captures hanging material — often an undefended rook or queen, or that wins the exchange — squandering the win, though a couple of boards instead hang the player's own material.

1884.label: Captures/trades the last rook into a misjudged, hopelessly lost pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawn(s) queen faster.

1880.chip: Self-inflicted move exposes own king (allows mate)
1880.label: A self-inflicted blunder that fatally compromises the player's own king (or hangs material), usually permitting a decisive check or forced checkmate — though the specific piece/outcome varies across boards.

1885.label: In the opening, the played move loses material—most often a developing move (Be2/Bf4/Bc4/Nc3/Ne2) that leaves a piece hanging, usually to a pawn capture, with the hung piece alternating between knight and bishop—though three of the ten cases are purely positional pawn pushes that concede space rather than material.

1889.label: In every position the player made a safe but passive move and overlooked a forcing tactic — almost always a deflection/clearance sacrifice delivered with check — that wins the opponent's queen.

1891.label: Player plays a queen move that gives check (usually capturing a pawn) but the queen is immediately recaptured—often by a bishop sweeping a long diagonal—losing the queen for nearly nothing.

1887.label: A capturing move — either a greedy material grab or an unsound sacrifice — that loses the player's own material, with the hung piece varying (knight, bishop, or rook) across positions.

1886.label: A middlegame move loses the player's own material (bishop or rook) to a short forcing tactic, either by abandoning a defender or stepping a piece into capture; two boards are instead positional/missed-win, and the hung piece varies, so it stays 'a piece' and needs review.

1883.label: A move — usually a capture or trade — that self-inflicts a decisive loss by going from winning to losing, almost always punished by a knight landing with a fork, check, or mate (8/10), though boards 7 (bishop x-ray) and 8 (queen) differ and the actual material lost varies (knight/bishop/rook/exchange or outright mate), so neither the hung piece nor a single tactic can be pinned down precisely.

1892.label: A materially-safe king/knight move that skips an available free capture, turning a drawn endgame into a lost one (the captured piece varies — queen or pawn — so it's 'a piece', not a specific one).

1890.chip: Hangs own piece in opening (knight involved)
1890.label: A move (almost always in the opening) that ignores a threat and loses the player's own material — a self-inflicted hang where a knight is involved in nearly every refutation, but since the hung piece isn't consistently a knight (≈7/10) it's just 'a piece'.

1888.label: In every one of the 10 opening positions the player skips a free capture of the opponent's undefended/hanging queen (Bxd8, Bxd1, Nxd8, or Nxd1), playing a quiet move instead and throwing away a winning position.

1899.label: A winning continuation (most often a forced checkmate) is overlooked in favor of a purposeless or greedy move, letting the opponent escape into a perpetual-check draw or equality.

1897.label: In the opening the player passes up a decisive winning continuation—forced mate (3,7), winning the queen (4,6), or winning a piece/initiative (1,9,10)—and instead plays a materially-safe but second-best developing or pawn move, letting a won position slip toward equality.

1894.chip: Hangs a piece via greedy rook move (often Rxh7)
1894.label: A rook move — frequently a greedy ...xh7 pawn-grab — that loses the player's own material, as the rook or its recapturing piece gets trapped or undermined a move or two later.

1893.label: A passive queen move that fails to resolve the standing queen tension—usually the correct Qxd5/Qxf5-type capture or trade—either squandering a win or hanging the player's own material.

1900.label: In completely winning king-and-pawn endgames, the player repeatedly skips the decisive rook-takes-knight sacrifice (Rxf6+/Rxf5+/Rxc6+) that eliminates Black's only piece, instead playing a materially-safe king or pawn move that keeps the win but spurns the cleanest simplification.

1901.label: In passed-pawn/promotion endgames the player chooses a slower or passive material-safe move that misses the fastest forced win (a mate, fork, or capture), though several flagged boards were actually optimal.

1898.label: In every position the player grabs material (or plays a quiet move) and overlooks an available forced win — a checkmate in ~8/10 boards, a decisive queen/material gain in the rest — typically letting the opponent recapture or even mate in return.

1904.chip: Bad queen trade into worse endgame
1904.label: The player captures to trade queens at the wrong moment, simplifying into an inferior (often lost) endgame and throwing away their winning or drawing chances by surrendering the queen's activity.

1882.label: In a won endgame the player repeatedly walks past an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy piece (a rook in 8/10, a queen in the other 2), playing a king move or pawn push instead and throwing the win away.

1902.label: Captures/exchanges a major piece (usually a rook) to simplify into a misjudged, worse-or-losing pawn endgame — though a couple of boards instead just hang a piece outright and one or two are barely-suboptimal, so the pattern is mixed.

1895.label: A passive, retreating, or trading move that throws away the player's winning or drawing result—surrendering rook/queen activity, liquidating into a drawn/lost ending, or letting an enemy passed pawn through—across mostly endgame positions; pieces and exact failure mode vary, so no single piece or mistake type can be named.

1911.label: Tucks the king passively into a corner/edge/back-rank square instead of centralizing or activating it, throwing away endgame draws or wins to checks, pawn promotion, and mating nets.

1903.label: In the opening, while winning, the player grabs material with a tempting capture (bishop, knight or queen) instead of the one accurate move, squandering the advantage—frequently refuted by a zwischenzug or by their own piece falling—so the captured-piece/punishment varies and only the 'greedy capture in a won opening' core is reliable.

1907.label: An ill-timed opening pawn advance (c5/e5/f5/b5/c4) that ignores the central tension—usually leaving a central pawn (e5/e4) hanging in boards 1–5/8, but only conceding space/structure in the b5 and c4 boards (7,9,10)—so the invariant is 'neglects the center' rather than one consistently hung piece.

1909.label: An unsound speculative bishop sacrifice that captures a pawn on h3 or h6 to open a file against the king, but simply hangs the bishop to the recapturing g-pawn with no compensation.

1913.label: An opening move that loses the player's own material to an immediate capture or short tactic, with the hung unit varying (knight, bishop, or pawn) so no single piece can be named.

1910.chip: Hangs own material to ignored threat
1910.label: A natural-looking developing or pawn move that ignores an opponent's tactic/threat and lets them win the player's own material (or deliver mate); the specific hung piece varies across boards (knight most often, but also rook, bishop/exchange, or the king).

1912.label: In an endgame, the player makes a passive or retreating king move that skips capturing free enemy material (the hung piece varies — rook, knight, queen, pawn), or otherwise fails to play the optimal king move.

1918.label: An opening move that leaves the player's own queen en prise, allowing it to be captured for free (often by a knight, e.g. Qh5/Qh4/Qd5 hangs).

1908.label: In a winning position the player fails to play the decisive move—usually an available winning capture—throwing away the advantage, with consequences ranging from back-rank mate to dropping a hung piece or missed fork.

1905.label: The player repeatedly parts with the queen too early — trading or sacrificing it via a check/capture — dissolving a winning attack or mate that a queen-keeping move would have converted; direction is split between outright hangs and safe-but-wasteful trades, so it's flagged for review.

1919.chip: Trades winning piece for a pawn
1919.label: In every endgame the player captures a pawn (usually with check) and is immediately recaptured, trading away the winning piece — rook, queen, or bishop — and converting a won position into a draw or a far smaller edge.

1920.chip: Hastens loss in pawn endgame (passed pawn)
1920.label: In already-losing king-and-pawn (and a couple rook) endgames, plays a king or pawn move that accelerates the defeat—typically by allowing the opponent's passed pawn to advance unchecked or misplacing the king—rather than hanging material or missing a win.

1916.label: From a winning/clearly-better position the player skips a forcing tactic—frequently a checkmate or winning check (Qh7+, Qxh7#, Ne2+, Rg7+)—and plays a passive or greedy move that throws the whole advantage away.

1917.chip: Missed forcing tactic, played quiet move (knight fork)
1917.label: Plays a slow, natural developing move instead of an available forcing tactical shot — most often a knight jump to b5/d5 setting up a Nc7+ fork of king and rook — squandering a winning advantage rather than losing its own material.

1906.chip: Hangs a piece, squandering the win
1906.label: A move (frequently a bishop) that throws away a winning or mating position — most often by leaving the player's own material to fall in the refutation, though a few boards instead simply miss a forced mate or just lose the thread positionally, so the exact mistake is not uniform.

1914.label: A natural opening move that fails to first capture the enemy knight (Bxc3/Bxc6), allowing a knight fork on d4/d5 that wins the player's bishop in roughly 8 of 10 boards.

1921.label: Jumps a knight to an aggressive central/forward square (d4, e5, d5, e4, b4, b5) where a pawn kick traps or wins the overextended knight, costing material or decisive tempo.

1926.label: A natural opening move leaves a piece exposed to an enemy pawn break (most often e5/e4/d4/c5/b4) that forks and wins material; the hung piece varies between bishop and knight, so it's just 'a piece'.

1924.label: Plays an unnecessary, often premature check—almost always a rook check—that the opposing king calmly sidesteps, wasting a tempo and squandering the position instead of the stronger quiet or capturing move.

1927.label: The player repeatedly skips a winning central pawn thrust (d4/e5/e4/d5) that simultaneously attacks the opponent's bishop and knight, playing a safe but passive developing/castling move instead.

1915.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight usually)
1915.label: An opening move that leaves the player's own material en prise—most often a knight captured by a pawn, though the hung piece varies (pawn, bishop, rook by skewer).

1928.label: In the opening, a natural developing or space-gaining move loses the player's own material to a tactic — usually a knight left hanging or a knight fork — though a couple of boards are instead missed wins or purely positional, so the exact hung piece varies.

1922.label: A one-move material blunder—most often hanging the player's own piece (varying among queen, rook, bishop, knight, pawn), but in ~3/10 cases instead failing to grab a free enemy piece; direction and piece are too mixed to commit to a specific 'Hangs X'.

1923.label: Advances a passed pawn one square prematurely instead of first improving piece activity, letting the opponent set up a clean blockade and neutralize the winning advantage.

1932.label: The move compromises the player's own king safety—walking the king into the open or stripping away its defenders/castling—allowing a decisive (often forced-mate) attack.

1929.label: Across the top-10 the player makes an ill-judged capture or exchange that backfires — sometimes hanging material outright (Nxd4, Qxf5, Qxg5, Bb4+) and sometimes trading into a lost pawn endgame or worse position (Nxf4, Rxf4, Rxd5, Bxg5, Nxd5) — and since the piece involved varies widely (knight, queen, rook, bishop) no single piece can be named.

1930.label: While winning, the player throws away the advantage by abandoning or hanging a strongly-placed/infiltrated piece (a knight in most boards, but also queen and bishop) instead of consolidating or making the winning capture.

1933.chip: Hangs own piece (varied; some missed wins)
1933.label: A move that throws away a winning or equal position—most often by hanging the player's own piece (rook, knight, or bishop, no single piece dominant) after moving its sole defender or overextending it, though about a third of the boards instead miss a winning tactic, so the feature is genuinely mixed.

1931.chip: Misses free capture, often hangs piece
1931.label: In nearly every top position the player overlooks a free, winning capture of an en-prise enemy piece (the queen in ~6/10, a rook in the rest) and instead plays an unrelated move that itself frequently hangs its own piece (rook/bishop/knight vary), converting a won or holdable position into a loss; because the mistake splits between pure omission (~half) and self-inflicted hang (~half) and the pieces are not a single clear majority, this needs review.

1938.label: Plays a routine developing move or recapture instead of advancing/promoting an advanced passed pawn (usually cxb7), letting the opponent simply capture the pawn and squander a winning advantage.

1939.chip: Trades rook into lost pawn endgame
1939.label: The feature captures a rook voluntarily exchanging itself (Rxsomething met by Kx) to simplify into a king-and-pawn/minor-piece endgame that is strategically lost, sacrificing the rook's defensive counterplay rather than hanging material outright.

1934.chip: Throws away forced mate (often hangs queen)
1934.label: In a winning endgame the player squanders a forced mate—most often by hanging their own queen instead of playing the decisive capture—turning a forced win into a far worse (sometimes losing) position.

1936.chip: Hangs piece via pointless check (rook checks)
1936.label: Plays a tempting but losing check—almost always a rook check—that either hangs the piece outright or loses material/tempo over a few moves, converting a defensible losing position into a clearly lost one.

1941.label: Player fails to play a winning knight fork (Nd7+/Ne6+/Nf5+ etc. that forks king and rook), instead choosing a passive, greedy, or piece-hanging move and squandering a winning position.

1945.label: Gives a purposeless rook check in a rook endgame that wastes a tempo and invites the opponent's king to advance/centralize, instead of using the move for active king or rook play.

1940.label: The player's queen move loses material (or invites a mating attack) — usually by abandoning a defensive duty or making a losing capture/trade that gets punished with a recapture-and-check on an opened file; the hung material varies (rook, knight, pawns, or king safety), so it's 'a piece' rather than a specific one.

1942.label: A move played to grab material, trade, or gain tempo/double-attack backfires—hanging the player's own piece (rook, knight, queen, or bishop—it varies) or fatally exposing the king—on roughly 7 of 10 boards, while two are outright missed wins and one isn't a blunder, so the exact piece and even the direction aren't consistent enough to commit.

1944.label: A careless capture or move-order error that self-inflicts material loss — the hung unit varies (knight, queen, or pawn), so no single piece can be named — turning a playable or drawn position into a losing one.

1951.label: In every opening position the player skips the crushing Qh4+/Qh5+ check that exploits the diagonal opened by the missing f-pawn, winning material, instead playing a routine developing or recapturing move.

1947.label: In most positions the player makes a materialistic or natural-looking move (frequently a greedy capture, or a piece dropped onto an attacked square) that loses their own material—immediately or within the refutation—but several boards are instead pure missed-wins/defensive omissions and the hung piece varies (knight, bishop, pawn), so the feature is mixed and should be reviewed.

1946.label: Sorties the bishop to h6 (or mirror h3) to trade off the opponent's fianchettoed bishop, a premature/unsound exchange that abandons a key defensive duty and either hangs material or loses critical tempo.

1953.label: The player snatches a 'free' pawn (b2 or b7) with the queen, which then gets chased and trapped over the next moves, losing the queen (typically for a rook).

1950.chip: Weakening flank pawn push (chases enemy piece)
1950.label: A tempo-wasting wing pawn push (h6/h3/g4/g5/a3) that 'puts the question' to an enemy piece but squanders the advantage by loosening the king's pawn shelter (or missing a sharper resource).

1956.label: In every one of the 10 opening positions the player skips an available free capture of an undefended enemy piece (a bishop in ~half, a queen in the other half) and instead plays a routine developing move, throwing away winning material — an omission, not a self-inflicted hang.

1896.chip: Throws away won endgame into draw
1896.label: An endgame move that collapses a winning or forced-mate position into a dead-drawn 0.00 ending — sometimes by hanging a piece (rook or queen) to immediate capture, sometimes by a losing trade, and sometimes by missing the only winning/drawing move.

1925.label: In a winning endgame, the player makes a self-inflicting move (often moving a piece onto a capturable square or playing a pointless check) that hands the opponent their own material for free, usually while a clean free capture was available instead — the lost piece is most often a knight but sometimes a rook, so it's 'a piece'.

1948.label: In a rook endgame, the played king or rook move creates a vulnerable alignment/square that lets the opponent's forcing rook check (skewer, back-rank, deflection, or forced trade) win the rook—or in a few cases deliver mate/stalemate—converting a holdable, drawn, or winning position into a loss.

1957.label: A natural-looking but passive move that ignores the position's critical tactical demand, usually allowing the opponent to win material (frequently via a fork), though several boards instead just squander a winning advantage positionally.

1949.label: In a winning endgame the player makes a non-optimal (often king) move that converts a win into a loss—usually by skipping a free winning capture, though several boards instead hang the player's own piece or are already lost, so the direction and piece are genuinely mixed.

1955.label: Across its top positions, the player squanders a winning (or at least equal) position by grabbing a tempting forcing move — frequently a queen check or trade — instead of the precise winning continuation, sometimes even hanging its own material in the process.

1959.label: A self-inflicting middlegame move that leaves the player's own piece (queen or bishop most often) en prise, losing material to an immediate or short-tactic capture.

1964.label: A greedy/careless move leaves the player's own queen undefended, and it is won by a bishop-sacrifice check (Bxh7+, Bxh2+, Bb5+, etc.) that deflects the defender or clears the line before capturing the queen.

1952.label: In all ten positions the player grabs material with a capture (usually a bishop) intending to win a piece, but the greedy grab overlooks a decisive refutation — hanging their own piece, allowing back-rank/king-hunt mate, permitting a pawn to promote, or dropping into a lost endgame.

1962.label: From a winning/advantageous position the player plays a materially-safe but passive or inaccurate move, missing the decisive tactic or forced win (the winning move varies by board, no single piece).

1960.label: A slow/passive move (usually a pawn move) ignores a forcing tactical threat, allowing the opponent to win material—rook, exchange, knight, or a promoting passed pawn—via a multi-move combination, so the lost piece varies and can't be pinned to one type.

1968.label: A king move in a king-and-pawn (occasionally king-and-bishop) endgame that surrenders the opposition/correct king positioning, throwing away a draw or win rather than hanging material.

1935.label: In a drawn endgame the player makes one decisive losing move — about half the time hanging a piece (bishop or knight) and the rest failing to find the only move that holds, typically letting an enemy pawn promote or material fall.

1965.label: Moves a piece to a square where it gets trapped, forked, or left undefended, losing the player's own material — most often exploited by a pawn break.

1969.label: In nearly every position the player overlooks a free capture of the opponent's hanging (undefended) queen and instead plays a non-capturing move, throwing away a winning position by squandering the material — often also hanging their own queen or walking into mate.

1963.label: A self-inflicted move—often a greedy capture or pointless check—that hangs the player's own material (rook, queen, bishop, or knight, varying by board) or otherwise collapses a defensible/drawn position into a lost one; a minority are pure tempo/endgame slips with no material hung, so the piece can't be pinned down and a human should review.

1973.label: The player repeatedly skips a forced checkmate—most often the Qh6/Qf6 maneuver threatening Qg7#—choosing a materially-safe or tempo-wasting move instead, so the recurring error is an omission (missed mate), not a self-inflicted material loss.

1967.chip: Missed forced win in endgame (often promotion)
1967.label: In winning endgames the player squanders a forced win or mate by grabbing material or promoting a pawn immediately instead of playing the precise winning continuation.

1958.chip: Gives up defensive bishop in endgame
1958.label: The player repeatedly surrenders their only defensive minor piece—usually the bishop—either by hanging it with a king move (boards 1,5,8,10) or trading it for a single pawn (boards 3,6,7,9; knight on board 2), converting a holdable endgame into a lost one.

1972.label: A pawn move played to chase an enemy knight in the opening ignores a tactic and hangs the player's own material (usually the exchange to a knight fork).

1976.label: A materially-safe developing move that omits the crushing queen check (Qh5+ for White, Qh4+ for Black) which exploits the opponent's missing f-pawn and weakened king to win the rook by force.

1974.label: From a winning position the player plays a natural capture or check that abandons a stronger forcing continuation — frequently a forced mate — throwing away the win.

1966.label: A move — most often a king or pawn advance in an endgame — that converts a holdable or drawn position into a clearly lost one, but the exact failure varies (hanging a rook/bishop, allowing a passed pawn, or walking into mate), so no single piece or mechanism is the invariant.

1980.label: In the opening the player loses their dark-squared bishop—either by retreating it to a5 where b4 traps it, or by leaving the b4-pinner undefended to a Qa4+ fork—instead of playing the resolving ...Bxc3+.

1979.label: Plays a quiet, materially-safe move (often a pawn push) and overlooks an available decisive capture or tactic—the won piece/pawn varies (bishop on d6, queen, the d3 pawn, etc.)—throwing away a winning advantage.

1981.label: The played move steps directly into a forced checkmate—almost always a king move walking into mate-in-one—rather than playing the sole desperate defensive resource.

1977.label: A tempting forcing move (a check in 9/10) — most often a premature promotion that walks into a capture or a rook-for-pawn trade — throws away the player's own material or winning advantage and collapses the position.

1982.label: Castling (O-O or O-O-O) that hangs the player's own material — losing it immediately or over 2-3 moves — with the specific piece (knight/queen/bishop) varying across positions.

1971.label: The player throws away a winning or better position by grabbing material or initiating a premature capture/trade instead of the stronger continuation — about half the boards hang the player's own material (queen, bishop, exchange) over the next moves, the other half merely simplify the advantage into equality, and the captured/squandered piece varies (bishop, knight, rook, queen), so neither a single piece nor a single direction is clean.

1983.label: A passive/slow move that squanders a won position by missing a forcing queen tactic or capture (often Qxa7/Qxa2/Qxh7).

1978.label: In a lost-but-survivable position the player ignores the forced-mate threat — almost always failing to capture one of the opponent's two queens (the only defensive resource) — and instead plays a passive/greedy move that converts the game into a forced checkmate.

1943.label: A decisive blunder centered on the queen in nearly every position — the player either hangs their own queen or fails to win/capture the enemy queen — but the direction (self-inflicted hang vs. missed win) is genuinely mixed, so flag for review.

1988.label: A materially-safe quiet/developing move that skips the winning Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2 for Black), allowing the opponent to play ...h6/...Nf5 and permanently close the attack.

1991.label: In endgames (mostly king-and-pawn), a king or passive piece move surrenders a key central square — typically by chasing a flank pawn — letting the enemy king infiltrate and turning a draw/win into a loss; material itself never hangs.

1989.label: The played move ignores an existing checkmate threat — most often a queen-bishop battery on the long diagonal crashing through with Qxg2# (and similar Qxg7#/Qxc7#) — walking the king into immediate mate; a minority of boards instead hang a piece or lose material/tempo, so the single invariant is fuzzy.

1987.chip: Allows opponent's passed pawn to promote
1987.label: The played move fails to blockade or capture the opponent's passed pawn (abandoning the blockade square or ignoring the runner), allowing it to promote and decide the game — typically a rook/king endgame defensive failure.

1992.label: In a won opening the player repeatedly skips the knight strike (usually Nxd5) that wins a free central pawn by hitting the queen on b6, instead playing a safe trade/developing move that throws away the advantage.

1993.label: The model ignores an immediate tactical threat (often a queen capture, sometimes with check) and plays a move that loses its own material—a rook, knight, or pawn depending on the board—though a couple of positions are instead missed-win queen trades, so the hung piece is not a single consistent type.

1984.label: Plays a material-grabbing capture (usually winning a bishop) that ignores a stronger threat, either walking into mate or losing more material than it gains.

1970.label: A self-inflicted middlegame move that abandons a defensive post or duty, losing the player's own material (the specific piece varies — rook, queen, bishop, or knight).

1937.label: In all ten positions the player gives an unnecessary or premature knight check ('sees a check, plays a check') instead of the strong move—squandering a forced mate or winning combination in most boards, but in others (e.g. Nxa7+, Nc7+) actually trapping/hanging the knight, so the direction is mixed.

1994.label: Plays a slow or routine move that squanders a winning advantage instead of the decisive tactic, most frequently the knight capture on e6, though several boards instead self-inflict material loss.

1995.label: The played move ignores the opponent's immediate tactical reply (often a fork or in-between capture), self-inflictingly dropping material — a piece or the exchange — in the middlegame, with the specific piece lost varying board to board.

1985.label: In most boards the player squanders a won position by declining a simplifying trade or sacrifice (usually a queen or rook capture that liquidates into a winning pawn/king endgame) and instead plays a check or passive move that keeps pieces on; a notable minority (~3/10) instead outright hang their own queen, so the feature is mixed.

2001.label: Plays a tempo-wasting queen check that lets the opponent's king escape to safety, forfeiting a stronger winning continuation (mate, material, or decisive advantage).

1986.label: Plays a premature, easily-blocked check (usually a queen on a5/a4 or a bishop on b5) that the opponent simply interposes against with tempo, squandering the advantage — sometimes hanging own material, sometimes missing a stronger winning move.

1996.label: The played move leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended and it is captured for free, most often by an enemy rook, across middlegame and endgame positions.

1961.label: A move (usually with the queen) that abandons a defensive duty and hangs the player's own material or allows mate, where the saving move was typically a queen trade.

1999.chip: King loses tempo supporting pawn promotion (Q endgame)
1999.label: In queen-versus-king-and-pawn endgames the king is moved to a passive square (typically right next to its own passed pawn to shepherd it) that loses a tempo or lets the enemy queen check with gain of time, instead of the optimal king placement.

1998.label: In every position the player plays a materially-safe but passive move, overlooking a forcing tactical shot — almost always a deflecting/zwischenzug check (Bxg7+, Bxf2+, Bxg2+, Bh2+, Qxf1+, Ne7+) — that wins the exchange or a rook.

2002.chip: Trades active bishop prematurely, releasing pressure
2002.label: Makes a premature simplifying capture (almost always with the bishop) that trades off its powerful active piece and releases the tension, allowing a favorable queen trade/simplification that squanders a winning or better position rather than keeping the pressure on.

1990.chip: Hangs piece or misses central break (opening)
1990.label: An opening/early-middlegame central-pawn decision (typically around the d4/e5/e4 break) that goes wrong, but the direction is NOT consistent: ~4 boards hang the player's own piece (bishop in 4 & 7, knight in 8, pawn in 9), ~4 boards are materially-safe moves that miss a winning central break or free capture (d4 forking c3-knight/e3-bishop in 1 & 5, e5 forking f6/d6 in 10, free Bxd6 in 3), and ~2 are positional collapses after a premature e5; the hung piece also varies, so neither a single piece nor a single mistake-type can be honestly committed.

2003.label: A self-inflicted move (often a greedy capture that opens a file) drops the player's own material — queen, bishop, pawn or knight varies — frequently to a rook recapture with check against an exposed king.

2000.label: A self-inflicted move—usually a faulty capture, move-order slip, or removal of a key defender—that loses the player's own material (queen, knight, exchange, or pawn) or fatally exposes the king, with the specific hung piece varying across the boards.

2009.label: A move that leaves the player's own undefended piece — most often the queen — hanging, usually by removing its defender/recapture or ignoring a direct capture threat (with two outliers being king-safety/mate blunders).

2011.chip: Hangs a piece chasing enemy queen
2011.label: Plays a tempo move to attack the enemy queen but leaves an undefended piece (knight, bishop, or rook varies) that the queen simply captures instead of retreating.

2008.chip: Hangs own material via bad capture
2008.label: A self-inflicted material loss—typically an aggressive capture, trade, or check that backfires and drops a piece or the exchange (8/10 are captures); the lost piece varies (knight, bishop, rook/exchange, queen) so no single piece can be named, and a couple of boards are purely positional or lead to mate rather than clean material loss.

2012.label: A bishop move that drops the bishop for nothing—usually to an undefended/attacked square (frequently g4)—where it is immediately captured or lost in a short forcing sequence.

2013.label: A material-grabbing capture pulls the back-rank defender away from the first rank, allowing an immediate (or forced) back-rank checkmate.

2007.chip: Abandons key defense, allows decisive attack
2007.label: The player vacates a critical defensive square with a move that looks active or space-gaining, but it abandons the king/material and lets the opponent infiltrate for a forced mate (most boards) or a winning material grab (the rest).

2014.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a suboptimal king move or premature pawn push (material always safe, nothing hung) that squanders the precise winning/holding line, most often throwing a win away to a draw.

2006.label: The player repeatedly skips a forcing winning move—most often a capture or trade that wins the opponent's queen—settling for an inferior continuation that throws away a decisive advantage.

2015.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player marches the king (or pushes a pawn) in the wrong direction or loses a tempo in the pawn race, squandering a win or draw rather than hanging any material — though several of the top boards are actually 0cp non-blunders, so the shared invariant is the pawn-endgame/king-tempo setting more than a single clear error.

2017.label: In endgames, an imprecise pawn/king/rook move throws away a winning or drawn position — usually by wasting a critical tempo, occasionally by hanging material — though a couple of the boards aren't true blunders at all.

2004.label: In these opening positions the player repeatedly fails to capture or recapture an intruding enemy bishop, leaving themselves a full minor piece behind.

2019.label: The move allows the opponent to win the player's own material, almost always via a knight fork, though the specific material lost (rook, exchange, pawns) varies.

2022.label: Player puts the queen on a square that lets the opponent trade queens or capture and simplify, dissolving a winning advantage and skipping a stronger tactic (frequently a knight fork that should have been played instead).

2005.label: In opening positions the player makes a move that surrenders material or advantage—most often a light-squared bishop on g4 hangs or related f3/en-passant tactics misfire—but the specific mistake varies (direct hangs, a fork, a pin, a missed en passant, and pure positional drops), so the core invariant is only loosely 'a losing opening move centered on the g4-bishop/exf3 structure.'

2024.label: In a clearly winning position, plays a materially-safe but inaccurate move (often a pointless check or a routine capture) that squanders the win instead of finding the decisive promotion/mate/capture.

2023.label: In a passed-pawn endgame the player gives a purposeless tempo-wasting check (or push) instead of the only move that blockades, attacks, or captures the opponent's promoting pawn, throwing away the result.

2016.label: In every board the player squanders a winning or comfortable opening by skipping the critical move, but the mechanism is mixed — ~4 boards hang a piece (knight/bishop, varying), others are passive/greedy moves that miss a forcing continuation — so the only firm invariant is 'wastes the opening advantage,' too heterogeneous to name a piece or a single mistake type with confidence.

2020.label: Plays a premature queen check to h4 or h5 that is refuted by a simple pawn block (g3/g6) gaining tempo, wasting time and—in most boards—hanging material (sometimes the queen itself to Nxh5/Nxh4, sometimes a knight or pawn left undefended), so the hung piece varies and the constant is the unsound queen sortie.

2025.label: The player repeatedly fails to grab an available free or tactically-winning enemy piece (most often a hanging knight), instead playing a non-capturing move that lets the piece escape and throws away a winning position.

2027.chip: Hangs a piece in opening (knight involved)
2027.label: A knight-led opening move that loses the player's own material — usually recapturing/centralizing with the knight so a pawn forks or wins a piece a move or two later — though the specific piece lost varies (bishop+knight, queen, bishop, pawn) and one board is a pure missed win.

2010.label: In a winning position the player throws away the advantage by playing a greedy capture or passive move instead of the forcing continuation—about six times this hangs the player's own material (a varying piece: queen, rook, knight or bishop) over the next 1-3 moves, while the rest are simply missed forcing wins.

2026.label: The player makes a self-inflicting move that loses material or allows mate—most often by exposing its king to a check or discovered attack—but the exact piece lost varies and a couple of boards are simply missed mates, so the feature is mixed.

2034.label: Reflexively trades queens (Qxd8+/Qxd1+) to simplify, surrendering a winning attack or tactic that the queen should have delivered instead.

2035.label: In every position the player skipped a winning deflection tactic—a pawn advance with check (e3+, f3+, d5+, b6+, d7+, etc.) that lures the enemy king off a defender or blockade to win material or promote.

2031.label: A move that fails to control the promotion square, letting the opponent's passed pawn queen (often with check) in an endgame.

2036.label: In the opening, the player repeatedly skips a winning long-diagonal bishop capture (Bxg7/Bxg2/Bxb7) that nets the exchange, instead making a quiet developing move.

2030.label: In every position the opponent's queen was hanging and capturable for a winning material edge, but the player made a king move or wrong capture and missed the free queen—frequently then hanging their own queen or walking into mate.

2018.label: A tempting capture or simplifying trade that gives up the player's own key/active piece and worsens an already difficult-or-lost position, rather than keeping the correct defensive resource.

2037.chip: Hangs a piece on a check
2037.label: The player gives a forcing check that immediately loses their own material — the checking piece (most often a rook, but sometimes a knight or bishop) is simply captured or sacrificed into a lost endgame/mate.

2029.chip: Trades/hangs dominant knight via faulty check
2029.label: Plays a knight check or capture (Nx+) that the opponent's queen simply recaptures, surrendering a dominant or winning knight for insufficient value.

2038.label: The played move ignores an existing forced checkmate threat against its own king—usually while attacking the enemy queen for a tempo—and gets mated in one (the enemy queen delivers the mate in every case).

2032.label: In an effort to eliminate a dangerous advanced/passed pawn, the player captures it and thereby hangs their own material (queen, bishop, exchange or pawn) — or in a couple of cases simply grabs the pawn while missing a stronger winning capture.

2040.label: The player simplifies with a capture/check—most often a queen trade—into a lost or clearly worse endgame, throwing away an available perpetual-check draw or winning chances, though a few boards instead hang the queen, lose the exchange, or just drop a tempo.

2043.label: Across all ten endgames the player advances a passed pawn one square (or auto-queens it) when king activation or defense was better — the pawn is often simply captured or the push wastes a tempo, though it ranges from negligible inaccuracy to outright loss.

2044.label: Plays a slow or irrelevant move (pawn push / king walk / piece centralization) that ignores an opponent's imminent passed-pawn promotion, allowing the pawn to queen and win decisive material.

2021.label: A self-inflicted king-safety blunder where the player's move (often a king move) exposes their own king to a decisive check—frequently a forced mate—or loses material to the resulting attack, though one board is a missed win and two are really piece-hangs.

2039.label: A greedy capture—typically one that opens the d-file or a diagonal—that hangs the player's own queen, though two cases instead walk into mate and one merely misses a bigger win, so the unifying piece isn't cleanly the queen.

2041.label: A self-inflicted king-safety blunder—frequently a king move—that walks into or permits a forced mating attack, though a couple of boards instead drop material to a passed pawn or a back-rank/exchange tactic rather than mate.

2042.label: The player ignores an enemy passed pawn's promotion threat and plays an irrelevant move that abandons or hangs the rook guarding/blockading the promotion square, losing material.

2047.label: In nearly every position the player ignores a forcing tactical resource — typically a queen capture delivering check that wins material, equalizes, or saves the game — and instead plays a passive or natural-looking move.

2028.label: In these opening positions the player repeatedly declines the critical central knight capture (usually ...Nxd4 / Nxe4), choosing a natural developing or slow move that either forfeits a win or invites a punishing tactic.

2045.label: In a winning endgame, plays a quiet or safe move instead of the clearly available winning capture/move (the missed piece varies — rook, knight, bishop, or promotion), squandering a decisive advantage.

2046.label: In sharp positions with one correct move, the player repeatedly throws away a winning or won game—most often missing a forced mate or winning tactic, occasionally by hanging a piece.

1997.chip: Missed win in endgame (slow king move)
1997.label: In winning endgames the player chooses a materially-safe but slow move (usually a king move) that throws away or delays the decisive continuation—missing the forcing pawn push, promotion, or mate—rather than hanging any material.

2033.label: In the opening the player repeatedly fails to capture a free central e-pawn (the winning Nxe4/Nxe5 by knight), playing a slow developing move instead — though ~4/10 boards are outright self-inflicted piece hangs, so both the direction and the hung piece are mixed.
